**Steve Howell** · 2016-09-14 03:32 UTC

Here is a slightly more detailed theory:
* The original test always worked standalone, because the search engine always thought there were few enough "Japan" rows to start going after "Japanese" rows as well.
* The original test was flaky if you ran it after a bunch of other tests, because the search engine was less predictable about its decision that "Japan" was too narrow a search.
* My new test is deterministic failing standalone, because I end up (eventually) feeding enough "Japan" rows to the search engine that it decides not to go after "Japanese".

For the flaky scenario, I have two theories:
* When Django rolls back data after a test completes, the search engine doesn't hear about it, so its statistics get out of date with the actual DB's data.

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-09-18 17:53 UTC

We don't have a strong requirement to stay with `unittest`, but it does have its conveniences since it's integrated with Django; we'd want to use something like https://pypi.python.org/pypi/pytest-django if we were to replace it

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-09-18 17:54 UTC

https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/1.10/topics/testing/advanced/#using-the-django-test-runner-to-test-reusable-applications is probably good reading to understand how `test_runner.py` integrates with the rest of the system

**Steve Howell** · 2016-09-18 19:13 UTC

`unittest` is a real pain to extend, so it might be nice to move away from it, but it's a pretty ambitious project to switch over to a new testing framework with all the Django integration.

For the specific task of making it easy to re-run tests and to specify them more easily, I think there's a way to do it without getting too involved with extending unittest.  I think we can mostly handle it in our wrapper script, `test-backend`.  Converting slashes to dots can definitely be done there.  Also, we could have test failures write out some of hidden file with the name of the test that failed, and then add a `--rerun-failed-test` option to re-run it.  Finally, you could implement a `--broaden` option to `test-backend` that runs the suite instead of the test, or the module instead of the suite, or the directory instead of the module, if you have a hidden file that stores the args, and, again, you wouldn't need to muck with unittest's opaque discovery mechanism.

**Steve Howell** · 2016-09-18 19:21 UTC

If we want to do a smaller experiment with `nose` or similar, it would be worth looking at `tools/test-tools` and the tests it runs.  There we don't have to worry about Django integration, and the suite there has grown enough that the current `unittest` way of running tests has already become cumbersome.

As a sidenote, as part of debugging the casper issues with the administration pages, I learned that like 1/4 of our Casper wait statements were e.g. casper.waitForSelector, which doesn't do what most folks expect (the thing could be invisible and not in view, as long as it's in the DOM)

**Steve Howell** · 2017-03-06 00:16 UTC

@Tim Abbott As we move to using ids instead of names in the main JS code I see three options for maintaining the Casper tests, two of which you mentioned in comments on my recent PR:
* just leave the name attributes to make it convenient for Casper to find stuff
* have some kind of mapping system of ids to names
* change the Casper tests to look for display data instead of internal ids

I think the last option is the most robust testing strategy, but it's probably a bit of work to implement.  I think you can create custom functions that Casper waits on, but I think there are some limitations.  I don't really know off the top of my head.  But I'd be inclined to say with the status quo for now, and if we want to do work on the tests, we should probably skip past the middle option, which seems to be both inconvenient and not entirely in the spirit of testing the actual user experience.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-03-06 00:20 UTC

yeah, that's reasonable.  I guess we can easily see which ones are used by the tests and we can't remove because the tests will fail, but we can purge all references from `static/js` :)

from __future__ import print_function

if False:

def run(check_func):
    # type: (Callable) -> None
    '''
    This decorator simply runs functions.  It makes it more
    convenient to add new checks without a big main() function.
    '''
    rc = check_func()
    if not rc:
        sys.exit(1)

def run_command(args):
    # type: (List[str]) -> None
    print(' '.join(args))

@run

    return True

@run

**Steve Howell** · 2016-09-28 23:30 UTC

I have been spending a little bit of time thinking about where we go next with our backend tests.  Once we have tests that are easy to run, quick to run, and fairly thorough in terms of line coverage, we achieve two very important goals:
* it gets less likely for us to introduce bugs/regressions into the backend
* we can refactor with more confidence

But I think we can then think about leveraging the test suite in some other ways.  With a little bit of instrumentation, tests could generate really cool documentation.

I am wondering if other folks have had brainstorms in this regard.  I don't have any fully-baked ideas on where we take this, but my thought experiment is what do we do with tests in 2021.

When this test runs, https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/master/zerver/tests/test_narrow.py#L1831, what determines the state of the database at that point?

I picked that test because I was debugging that, but it could be any test in general I guess.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-05-17 01:30 UTC

@Sampriti Panda the database comes from `populate_db`, run with the `--test-suite` option.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-05-17 01:31 UTC

The logic for generating the test database all comes from the `tools/do-destroy-rebuild-test-database` entrypoint

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-05-17 01:31 UTC

(follow it a few scripts down and you'll see how it calls `populate_db`)

**Sampriti Panda** · 2018-05-17 01:31 UTC

I see, and the previous tests shouldn't affect that right?

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-05-17 01:31 UTC

Basically, we end up making a template snapshot, and each `test-backend` run does a snapshot restore

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-05-17 01:31 UTC

Additionally, Django is designed to run each test inside a transaction and rollback the transaction after each test

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-05-17 01:32 UTC

So it is possible to leak state from test to test, but mostly through the filesystem (we also change the KEY_PREFIX for memcached with each test)

~~~
#!/bin/bash

# update a bunch of Zulip git repositories

checkout_repo(){
    git checkout master
    git pull upstream master
    git push origin master
    git checkout -
}
for repo in zulip zulip-android zulip-electron zulip.github.io
do
    pushd ${repo}
    checkout_repo
    popd
done
~~~

**Steve Howell** · 2016-10-16 16:28 UTC

So, this is a bit messy, but it turns out that when you call `custom_check_file` on a file, even if the `rules` parameter is an empty list, it still does a check for trailing newlines.  So the current code's behavior is correct, although there might be a way to refactor the code to improve clarity.   Checking for whitespace issues is decidedly **non-custom**, so the name of the function is misleading to the extent that it does non-custom checks.

**Steve Howell** · 2016-10-16 16:30 UTC

It's a little bit of a performance hack that we try to sweep a file all in one pass, both for custom regex things and generic things.  If we separated out those concerns, which would be cleaner for somebody reading the code, then we'd introduce a small performance penalty in that we'd have to open every file twice.

**Steve Howell** · 2016-10-16 16:36 UTC

We could go down a huge rabbit hole trying to clean this up, but I think for now the simple fix is to clarify the comment.  Something like:

```
# It is okay that json_rules is empty, because we will
# still check JSON files for whitespace
```

The current comment is `# just fix newlines at ends of files`, which sort of implies that, but I think we can be more explicit.

## make_stream

*2016-10-20 to 2016-10-21 · 14 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/43-automated-testing/topic/make_stream/with/43209)*

**Steve Howell** · 2016-10-20 05:00 UTC

@Tim Abbott We have this kind-of-hard-to-type-and-remember idiom in 21 places in our test code:

```
stream, _ = create_stream_if_needed(realm, 'new_stream')
```

I'm inclined to change this to be:

```
stream = self.make_stream(realm, 'new_stream')
```

Even if the stream already exists, for most tests, you're only interested in making the setup stuff simple and easy to understand.  Thoughts?

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-10-20 17:37 UTC

I might do `self.ensure_stream`?

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-10-20 17:37 UTC

as the name?

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-10-20 17:38 UTC

I kinda want it to be clear when you're doing something that should fail if the thing doesn't exist

**Steve Howell** · 2016-10-20 17:58 UTC

I could live with `ensure_stream`.  It's harder to guess, but maybe there are other places where we could use `ensure_foo` so that it's a common idiom in our code.  Ok, I may try to knock this out today.  I'm making decent progress on the stream counts, so I don't feel as far behind as yesterday.

**Steve Howell** · 2016-10-21 15:37 UTC

So now I'm thinking we should actually have a `make_stream`, and in my sweep of the 20 places, I can solve three problems at once:
*  I can remove the verbose `create_stream_if_needed` calls
* I can make new streams that don't have any existing attributes that might be brittle.
* I can start to introduce some i18n stuff

I'm thinking of `stream_name = "日本の to English"`, which mixes languages and has whitespace.

I would make `make_stream` throw an error if it already exists.  Thoughts?

**Steve Howell** · 2016-10-21 15:42 UTC

Also, I'm thinking of doing this:

```
def make_stream(self, stream_name, realm_name = None):
    if realm_name = None:
        realm_name = 'zulip.com'
   # ...
```

This will make the calls nice and simple: `stream = self.make_stream(stream_name)`.

When we cut over to `example.com`, this can save effort in some way, but it's also a little bit of a trap, since it's not explicit.  I think the latter concern will be a one-time gotcha, so I'm not too worried about it.

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-10-21 15:42 UTC

What I'd do is replace that `zulip.com` with e.g. self.DEFAULT_REALM_DOMAIN, so it's changeable in a test.

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-10-21 15:43 UTC

I think in general we want to be moving in in the direction of having constants like "zulip.com" moved into variables so we can do an s/zulip.com/example.com/ at some point

**Steve Howell** · 2016-10-21 15:44 UTC

Yeah, that's reasonable.  Also, in individual tests, you still have the option to specify realm_name, of course.

**Steve Howell** · 2016-10-21 15:45 UTC

Not a huge issue, but another thing is whether the optional parameter is realm_name or realm.

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-10-21 15:50 UTC

I'd probably do realm.  One thing worth mentioning in this space is that we're working on eliminating `realm.domain` as a field in the database; instead we'll just have a set of RealmAlias values and the primary string key for a realm will be `realm.shortname` (currently called `realm.subdomain`).

**Steve Howell** · 2016-10-21 15:52 UTC

Ok, sounds good.  I think having an optional parameter with a default will make all this kind of stuff easier to cut over.  The individual tests just want to create a stream, and they don't need to understand realm details for the most part.  But, if they need to fetch a realm anyway (for other reasons), we give them the option to pass it.

**Steve Howell** · 2016-10-21 21:26 UTC

#2099

```
 Webhooks for external integrations.                                                                       
from __future__ import absolute_import
from django.http import HttpRequest, HttpResponse
from zerver.models import get_client, UserProfile
from zerver.lib.actions import check_send_message
from zerver.lib.response import json_success
from zerver.decorator import REQ, has_request_variables, authenticated_rest_api_view

from six import text_type

# Desk.com's integrations all make the user supply a template, where it fills                               
# in stuff like {{customer.name}} and posts the result as a "data" parameter.                               
# There's no raw JSON for us to work from. Thus, it makes sense to just write                               
# a template Zulip message within Desk.com and have the webhook extract that                                
# from the "data" param and post it, which this does.                                                       
@authenticated_rest_api_view(is_webhook=True)
@has_request_variables
def api_deskdotcom_webhook(request, user_profile, data=REQ(),
                           topic=REQ(default="Desk.com notification"),
                           stream=REQ(default="desk.com")):
    # type: (HttpRequest, UserProfile, text_type, text_type, text_type) -> HttpResponse                     
    check_send_message(user_profile, get_client("ZulipDeskWebhook"), "stream",
                       [stream], topic, data)
    return json_success()


```

## new users

*2016-11-18 to 2016-11-18 · 1 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/43-automated-testing/topic/new.20users/with/56772)*

**Steve Howell** · 2016-11-18 23:57 UTC

If you've worked with our tests, you know about Cordelia, Hamlet, and friends.  I just added the users Aaron and Zoe.  (It hasn't hit master yet, but it will soon.)  They are at the front and back of the English alphabet, and they have uppercase characters in their emails, and Zoe has a smaller user id than Aaron.  If you are writing tests, please consider using them as part of your tests, as they can help drive out strange bugs due to case insensitivity and user id ordering assumptions.

If you want to add more users to our test database, we could use some non-English names, particularly names with non-ASCII characters.  Look for "AARON" in the code.  A couple tests will break when you add users, and I leave it as an exercise to the reader to figure out how to fix those.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-11-29 19:43 UTC

`mypy` does a decent amount of inference, so if you use a variable name with one type in one place, and then another later in the file, it'll notice that and complain.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-11-29 19:44 UTC

(I can't remember, but we might only run `mypy` on one of the test suites)

**Max Vovshin** · 2018-11-29 19:45 UTC

So as a general rule, if I use mypy, I cannot assign an already existing variable a new type?

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-11-29 19:58 UTC

Without a `cast()`, yeah.  But it's generally bad style to do that anyway, so I don't find the restriction to be limiting :)

**Max Vovshin** · 2018-11-29 20:23 UTC

@Tim Abbott Cool thanks a lot for the info!

**Neil Pilgrim (neiljp)** · 2018-11-29 20:43 UTC

*2017-01-04 to 2017-01-04 · 72 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/43-automated-testing/topic/linting/with/115530)*

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-04 19:41 UTC

I'm gonna do a little brain dump of our lint-based tools here, in hopes that it leads to some questions that I can help answer.   For starters we have these docs:  https://zulip.readthedocs.io/en/latest/linters.html

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-04 19:43 UTC

For things like Python/JS, we basically use popular open-source linters, and then we also have some customized lint rules.  For our templates and CSS stuff, we use home-grown tools.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-04 19:44 UTC

The main way we check templates is to make sure that they're indented properly.   The tools here is `./tools/check-templates`, which uses `lib/template_parser` to parse out template tags.  (Our template parser can handle Django/Handlebars tags on top of normal HTML tags.)

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-04 19:45 UTC

There's a method called `validate()` in `lib/template_parser.py` that does the indentation checking.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-04 19:47 UTC

For CSS we have a similar library called `tools/lib/css_parser.py`, and we front that with `tools/check-css`, which basically just checks that our CSS is well-formed.

**Tommy Ip** · 2017-01-04 19:48 UTC

Do we have linter for plain `.html` files?

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-04 19:49 UTC

Both of the tools I mentioned earlier are in `./tools/lint-all` and therefore also in `./tools/test-all`.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-04 19:49 UTC

Our linters should work for plain HTML files.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-04 19:50 UTC

We also have some tools that are **not** yet part of our test suite.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-04 19:52 UTC

For example, we have a tool called `./tools/html-grep` that will look for HTML classes among our templates.  This can be useful if you're trying to figure out, for example, how a CSS class actually gets used in our code.  (ping @Alicja Raszkowska )  But we don't actually do any automated testing with it yet.  But potentially some day we could have HTML grepper cross-reference our CSS code automatically somehow.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-06 15:40 UTC

Yeah, that's our linter.  We started off with the XHTML convention, so I think we want to continue to support it for consistency.  For void elements like img, HTML5 doesn't really care if you put the trailing slash there.

**Tommy Ip** · 2017-01-06 15:41 UTC

Yeah i did that, HTML is very loose anyway.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-06 15:45 UTC

We could make the linter simultaneously more relaxed and more strict:
* more relaxed: don't require trailing slash for img, br, etc.
* more strict: complain about trailing slash for div, span, etc.

I don't think we've been inconvenienced/burned by the two above scenarios very often, so it's low priority to fix the linter, but it would probably be fairly straightforward.

Right now the linter doesn't really know the semantics of any particular HTML tags, but I could see us someday doing more semantic things, like prohibiting certain tags that don't fit the Zulip HTML coding guidelines, or something like that.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-06 15:46 UTC

The only tags we treat kind of specially are link and meta.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-31 17:41 UTC

I guess part of the problem here is that tons of tests have somebody log in, correct?  Whereas only one or two tests actually need to verify your feature?

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-31 17:44 UTC

For this particular tests, you could probably do this:

~~~ py
login(...)
self.assertEqual(len(mail.outbox, 1)
# do a bunch of other stuff
self.assertEqual(len(mail.outbox, 1)
~~~

But it sounds like you are looking for a more general purpose solution, which is reasonable.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-31 17:44 UTC

Out of curiosity, are we  going to have a feature flag or realm setting here?

**Akyya Mayberry** · 2017-01-31 17:47 UTC

Exactly. Because my code searches for particular META data in a HTTPRequest which doesn't exist for most of the tests, so I adjusted my code a bit to test for the this data. But, for the test like the one above, I am not sure if I should tweak my code some more or make some adjustments or if the adjustments should be made on the tests. I will like a more general purpose solution, so I don't have to make so many changes. I am not sure about feature flag or realm setting.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-31 17:47 UTC

The reason I ask is that if we put this feature behind a setting, like `SEND_LOGIN_EMAILS`, then we can set that to False in `test_settings.py` and then for the two or three tests where we care, we could do something like...

~~~ py
with self.settings(SEND_LOGIN_EMAILS=True):
    # ....

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-31 17:49 UTC

Then in your function that handles the signal, you could just add this to top:

~~~ py
if not settings.SEND_LOGIN_EMAILS:
    return

**Akyya Mayberry** · 2017-01-31 17:49 UTC

Is this what context managers or or the test_helpers.py is about? Someone mentioned is as a solution.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-31 17:49 UTC

Yeah, `with` statements in Python are context managers.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-31 17:50 UTC

They generally are used for temporary things like opening/closing a file, or temporarily tweaking a settings variable, and they sort of magically "wrap" the block with the open/close stuff happening under the hood.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-31 17:51 UTC

(or in your case, set/unset SEND_LOGIN_EMAILS)

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-31 17:52 UTC

@Tim Abbott should probably weigh in here on how we want to handle this.  It's possible that we really want to handle this at the "signal" layer of Django, and there may be standard Django testing mechanisms for that.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-31 17:54 UTC

I think it's fairly likely that this is going to be an optional feature, where it's either set in settings.py (site-wide), or on the Realm model (organization-wide), or maybe even per-user.  If that's the case, I don't think it's too hacky to take advantage of that in our tests to make it so that tests **ignore** the new feature by default.

**Akyya Mayberry** · 2017-01-31 17:59 UTC

I see. I haven't been able to find much on Django site specifically, but other sites suggest something similar to what Steve has suggested. I will keep looking.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-31 18:07 UTC

Here is a little article on context managers, if you're curious:

http://preshing.com/20110920/the-python-with-statement-by-example/

There are lots of technical details under the hood with context managers, and creating them requires a somewhat advanced understanding of Python, but as far as using them, they are somewhat intuitive.

An example would be

~~~ py

print('this shows blue')
with color_set_to_red():
   print('this shows red'))
print('this shows blue again')
~~~

Whatever deep magic happens in `color_set_to_red()` shouldn't concern you too much, as long as the `color_set_to_red()` context manager is implemented correctly.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-01-31 18:11 UTC

Yeah I think a reasonable approach for this is to create a `SEND_LOGIN_EMAILS` setting defaulting to `True` in `DEFAULT_SETTINGS` in `zproject/settings.py`, set it to false in `zproject/test_settings.py`, and then only for the couple tests where we're testing this feature set it to true with `with self.settings(SEND_LOGIN_EMAILS=True)`

**Akyya Mayberry** · 2017-01-31 18:13 UTC

Thanks. I will surf through Django docs some more and take some time to look over context managers in the shared link.

Going back to the `apply_event` function, that is one of the more subtle pieces of code in the backend.  If events happen **between** fetching initial data and sending the original payload to clients, we actually have to manually munge the event data onto the state data in `apply_event`.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-02-28 19:57 UTC

And then we have tests enforce that.

**Yashashvi Dave** · 2018-02-28 20:10 UTC

Hmm, I get how `apply_events` works, if I am getting it correctly, it updates the data according to received event before sending to client. But I don't understand, how or in which cases an event is generated **between** fetching initial data and sending the origin payload to clients. :thinking_face:

**Steve Howell** · 2018-02-28 20:10 UTC

It's just a race condition, basically.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-02-28 20:10 UTC

After you fetch all the data, events could race in before you send the initial payload to the client.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-02-28 20:12 UTC

In theory we could have architected this differently, and just had the events go the client, but that solution has some pitfalls that I probably couldn't do a great job of describing.  So we just do some patching of the data on the backend instead.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-02-28 20:12 UTC

And then the `do_test` helper is kind of magical in simulating that scenario.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-02-28 20:13 UTC

So if you can get `do_test` to pass, you are 99% confident of having written the correct code for this race condition.

The last 50 commits fits this config:
```
# .gitlint
[general]
ignore=title-trailing-punctuation, body-min-length, body-is-missing

[title-match-regex]
regex=^.+\.$

[title-max-length]
line-length=79

[body-max-line-length]
line-length=79
```
```bash
# lint-commits
echo "Linting commit messages from upstream/master to HEAD."

commit_list=$(git rev-list upstream/master...HEAD)

for commit in $(git rev-list clean | head -n 50); do  # head -h 50 for testing
    commit_msg=$(git log -1 --pretty=%B $commit)

    echo "Linting $commit"
    echo "$commit_msg" | gitlint
done
```

#!/bin/sh
#
# An example hook script to check the commit log message.
# Called by "git commit" with one argument, the name of the file
# that has the commit message.  The hook should exit with non-zero
# status after issuing an appropriate message if it wants to stop the
# commit.  The hook is allowed to edit the commit message file.
#
# To enable this hook, rename this file to "commit-msg".

# Uncomment the below to add a Signed-off-by line to the message.
# Doing this in a hook is a bad idea in general, but the prepare-commit-msg
# hook is more suited to it.

SOB=$(git var GIT_AUTHOR_IDENT | sed -n 's/^\(.*>\).*$/Signed-off-by: \1/p')
grep -qs "^$SOB" "$1" || echo "$SOB" >> "$1"

	 sort | uniq -c | sed -e '/^[ 	]*1[ 	]/d')" || {

}

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-04-23 04:12 UTC

Ahh, OK, I can totally see that.  I bet what's happening is that there's a race: we push to master, Travis CI doesn't run for 10-15 minutes, and we push to master again during the 10-15 minute wait before the build starts.  So Travis gets the new `master` commit ID, but hasn't fetched that into the local repository (since it only fetched what it needed to do the build).

One of the desired outcomes of naming dependencies is to make folks think about the dependencies, but that requires a bit of expertise that is often beyond the scope of fairly simple changes.  In this particular case, for example, we are actually introducing a circular dependency between narrow.js and stream_data.js.  The narrow.js module depended on stream_data.js before, and that's reasonable, but having stream_data.js depend on narrow.js is perhaps something we should avoid somehow, although I don't think there's a particularly clean way to do that now. **Andy Perez** · 2017-12-09 09:22 UTC

I know this issue isn't the most important, but in the odd case anyone is curious as to what's going on here (maybe @Tim Abbott or @Yago González ), I've actually figured this one out, although I'm not sure if we want to act on it.

The output from marked.js does indeed contain `&#39;` as expected.  So does the HTML produced by the handlebars templates.  So... where does it end up going in the end?  As it turns out, later in the code an actual DOM element is produced using jquery, and this is where it vanishes.  When you try `$('<p>&#39;</p>')[0].innerHTML`, you notice that `&#39;` has been unescaped to `'`.  The creation of the DOM element parses the HTML output from handlebars templates, turning `&#39` into its unescaped variant.  In fact, most get unescaped except for a few choice character references, such as `&lt;`, `&gt;`, and `&nbsp`.

As for the original reason for why this was even considered, it seems that "fixing" (there's currently nothing wrong with the output, it's produces identical actual HTML) the marked code or the python markdown code so that they agree could be a good idea.  It would help make the marked output match the bugdown output more often, although there are lots of really annoying cases where something as trivial as attributes being in a different order on some tag somewhere throws it all off.

An idea that came into my mind while typing this is that we could possibly use something like `jsdom`, which lets us create DOM elements as part of our node test.  This means we could take the marked and bugdown outputs, create DOM elements, then test for equality using marked_element.isEqualNode(bugdown_element), and this would circumvent both issues with escaping (like with `&#39` vs `'`) and with differing attribute orders.  It might be something too heavy / cumbersome to employ just for testing markdown/bugdown, though, or a bad idea for reasons I haven't thought of yet.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-12-09 12:15 UTC

@Andy Perez I would be interested in seeing a prototype of using `jsdom` in the node tests for `marked.js`.  I like the idea of asserting for semantically equivalent HTML vs. the naive strings-must-match-exactly approach we have for now.

**Andy Perez** · 2017-12-10 09:07 UTC

@Steve Howell Sure!  I've got https://github.com/PentaHiggs/zulip/tree/issue-4367 which shows it in action.  Right off the bat, there are six `marked_expected_output`s that can immediately be done with, you can see them in the diff to the second commit.  Added an extra test to highlight a fix to precisely what's mentioned here in this thread.

While playing around with this, I noticed that a lot more output differences, about 4-5 or so, could also be purged from the fixtures if we were to fix a mildly annoying bug where the `marked` output doesn't have `<p>` tags around the `<span >`s corresponding to equations.  While this would still leave annoying differences in some cases, I think ditching the naive strings approach has another benefit.

When you take the DOM elements and serialize them, this HTML does not necessarily equal the HTML string that was used to create the element in the first place.  This is a good thing.  You can then diff these strings instead of diffing the original strings.  The result is that your diff has no "noise" in it.  Only relevant differences will be evident; something like using `&quot;` over `\"` will not show up.

Combined with a pretty diff tool, which I also have prototyped as well (I can combine them and show that here too if you'd like to give it a look) then I imagine it could make adding markdown features and seeing what the current bugs are a much more pleasant experience (I can attest to the nightmarish difficulty of dealing with a large 1200-character single-line`tex` equation output in the fixtures when trying to fix a bug or change anything at the moment).

**Greg Price** · 2017-11-29 23:26 UTC

One quick summary from one of my commit messages:

    From just my experience attempting this change, I've been impressed
    with the very fast turnaround in CircleCI for a change -- from `git
    push` to the build starting is usually just a couple of seconds.
    
    It also looks like we get much clearer control over the caching
    system, and the setup of the environment via a Docker image of our
    choice, which can help avoid most of the several minutes Travis takes
    to set up our environment before it actually starts running the tests
    themselves.
    
    Plus it supports fine-grained parallelism, e.g. by test file:
    https://circleci.com/docs/2.0/parallelism-faster-jobs/
    
    So we can probably get much faster builds by making this switch.

**Greg Price** · 2017-11-29 23:27 UTC

For debugging and developing the build, you'll want to set up CircleCI for your GitHub fork -- should be easy to do on circleci.com

Back at the end of August I got it all the way through setup to actually running the tests, and most of them passed but there were a few failures. **Tim Abbott** · 2017-03-24 06:16 UTC

We managed to get several files to 100% backend test coverage in the few days, which is pretty exciting.  There's now probably <10 major files that are primarily business logic that aren't are 100% backend test coverage (the holy grail of this party is `zerver/lib/actions.py`, with about 100 lines uncovered).  

In addition to those, there are a few subsystems that we're basically not testing at all via the Django suite:
* The Tornado event delivery system
* Our queue processors (this could easily be changed with some tweaks to how we test things)
* Large sections of zerver/lib/export.py
(Those actually account for the majority of our uncovered lines)

**Steve Howell** · 2017-03-24 13:54 UTC

Just some up-front advice about getting tests up to 100% coverage:
* For modules that have big gaps, often it's just a matter of writing lots of straightforward tests to improve the coverage.
* For modules that are more like 95% covered, expect the remaining tests to involve some subtleties.  Often, the uncovered lines will require more advanced testing techniques, like stubbing.  Also, for those lines, you will want to be extra alert to bugs, as often the uncovered lines of code will deal with edge cases that we haven't properly tested before (obviously, we won't have covered them with automated tests, but we may have also never properly manually tested them or given them the right level of code review).

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-03-24 18:06 UTC

https://github.com/zulip/zulip/issues/999 has some tracking data on the missing actions.py coverage.  Some of these conditionals may be tricky to figure out how to get into; I'd start by focusing on the ones where it's clear how to get there

Thanks @Steve Howell. Problem solved! 
The problem was that `allow_message_deleting` was added in `property_types` of `Realm` model. So when api request was made it was updated with all other `property_types`. And that's why the condition was not satisfying(cause it was already updated in above lines) to for `108` line.

## bugdown tests

*2017-03-31 to 2017-03-31 · 7 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/43-automated-testing/topic/bugdown.20tests/with/182528)*

**Yago González** · 2017-03-31 18:10 UTC

During my work in the TeX math feature, I found out a small problem with bugdown tests: if HTML attributes had a different sorting in the frontend than in the backend, the tests would fail (even though semantically both strings were identical).

**Yago González** · 2017-03-31 18:11 UTC

We [discussed](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/near/174639/stream/general/topic/tex.20math.20support.20.232056) this, and a very nice suggestion made by Steve was to add something like a `backend_expected_output` field to the bugdown fixtures.

**Yago González** · 2017-03-31 18:13 UTC

This way, we could do something like:

~~~py
if sorted(output.js) != sorted(expected.python):
    raise Exception('Your expected JS output differs non-trivially from your expected Python output!')
~~~

**Yago González** · 2017-03-31 18:15 UTC

I was thinking... for the moment, is it okay to compare only the attribute-sorted versions of both strings, or do we want something a bit more complex, like fuzzy string matching or something similar?

In the sort term I believe this would only benefit TeX tests, although maybe in the process we discover that other fixtures with the `bugdown_matches_marked` flag set to "false" can be turned to "true" if we admit some other variations.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-03-31 18:19 UTC

I think starting with attribute-sorting is a good idea, as I fear that too "fuzzy" a match will let real problems slip through, although we may eventually find we need that too.

**Yago González** · 2017-03-31 18:29 UTC

Sounds good!

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-03-31 19:12 UTC

I was actually thinking of adding a `marked_expected_output` as the name, since the default is the backend syntax with how the `bugdown_matches_marked` works

**Andrea  Longo** · 2017-04-18 21:41 UTC

@Tim Abbott I see lots of uses of `with self.settings` to set single attributes and then execute code. How would that work for creating a user? If I put the call to `self.register` inside a `with self.settings` block does it then vanish after?

**Andrea  Longo** · 2017-04-18 21:41 UTC

I'm confused how that works, I would think creating a user would have tons of side-effects to deal with.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-04-18 21:57 UTC

Most of the side-effects of tests are database updates, but those all get rolled back.  Also, lots of our code updates memcached, but we use a new way of generating keys for each test, so that effectively gets rolled back.  So, it's actually the less common things that bite us, such as clumsily updating settings directly rather than using the test helper.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-04-18 22:11 UTC

Right, database changes are automatically rolled-back, but changes to the global settings are not

**Steve Howell** · 2017-04-18 22:15 UTC

When you call `self.settings(...)`, you're calling a Python context manager, which is Python's mechanism for allowing things to change only for a certain scope.  It's similar to how we mock functions--that also usually happens via a context manager, so that a single test can temporarily change the definition of a function, but then it gets set back to its original implementation.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-04-18 22:16 UTC

Whenever you see the Python keyword `with`, a context manager gets invoked.

**Andrea  Longo** · 2017-04-18 22:33 UTC

Ok, that makes more sense. Thanks!

**Joshua Pan** · 2017-06-02 04:00 UTC

**Steve Howell** · 2017-06-02 04:00 UTC

This is more "overriding" than "stubbing", since "stubs" generally don't invoke real code.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-06-02 04:00 UTC

It's actually more in the realm of "monkeypatching".

**Steve Howell** · 2017-06-02 04:01 UTC

Generally:
* mocks == replace with object that records stuff and does nothing else interesting
* stubs == just do nothing so that your code can get to the "interesting" parts
* monkeypatch = replace with some other function that is more predictable

**Steve Howell** · 2017-06-03 21:34 UTC

Another tricky thing from your PRs is that you were trying to test util.strcmp() when Intl.Collator was not present (or threw some kind of error--that part you can simulate either way).   What's happening here is that util.strcmp is actually the evaluation of an anonymous function that would be appropriately called util.make_strcmp if we extracted it.  We should go ahead and extract that, and then say `util.strcmp = exports.make_strcmp()` to actually make it, within the module.  Then, within the test,  you can first test the collating version of `util.strcmp`, then you can say something like this in the tests:

~~~ js
Intl.Collator = undefined;
var stcmp = util.make_strcmp();
// test "dumb" strcmp

~~~js
function select_on_focus(field_id) {
    // A select event appears to trigger a focus event under certain
    // conditions in Chrome so we need to protect against infinite
    // recursion.
    var in_handler = false;
    $("#" + field_id).focus(function () {
        if (in_handler) {
            return;
        }
        in_handler = true;
        $("#" + field_id).select().one('mouseup', function (e) {

        });
        in_handler = false;

~~~

**Steve Howell** · 2017-06-12 12:33 UTC

It's reachable in theory, because the inner function can re-bind in_handler to true in the scope of the outer function.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-06-12 12:37 UTC

Here is a simplified version you can study:

~~~ js
function yo(obj) {
    var in_handler = false;

    obj.func1 = function () {
        if (in_handler) {
            console.log('already in func1!!!');
            return;
        }

        in_handler = true;

        obj.func2();

        in_handler = false;
    };  
}

var foo = {}; 

foo.func2 = function () {
    // simulate buggy behavior that could lead
    // to infinite multiple recursion
    foo.func1();
};

yo(foo);

foo.func1();

~~~

~~~js

241

`q` is going to be the same content we put in `query`, because we are using zjquery and hence there is no cursor to split at.

Meanwhile, let's take a closer look at `tokenize_compose_str`:

~~~js
exports.tokenize_compose_str = function (s) {
    // This basically finds a token like "@alic" or
    // "#Veron" as close to the end of the string as it
    // can find it.  It wants to find white space or
    // punctuation before the token, unless it's at the
    // beginning of the line.  It doesn't matter what comes
    // after the first character.
~~~

The comment says it all! There's a while loop that starts "eating" the string `s` from the very end until it finds a token, e.g. an `@`.

One thing to consider is that the loop has a limit:

~~~js
var min_i = s.length - 25;
    if (min_i < 0) {
        min_i = 0;
    }
 
    while (i > min_i) {
~~~

So, `tokenize_compose_str` will only search in the last 25 characters. Anything before that point is too far,

**Yago González** · 2017-06-21 16:45 UTC

and it will return an empty string (as if nothing was found). Since we want `current_token[0]` to be `@` in order to take the if path, we don't want that to happen. We need to put an @-mention in the query **in the last 25 characters**.

**Steve Howell** · 2019-02-02 14:07 UTC

For folks using  **zjquery** in **node** tests, it's sometimes necessary to test this kind of code:

~~~
$(...).on(..., function() {
    var widget = $(e.target);
    // ...

**Steve Howell** · 2019-02-02 14:08 UTC

The question is how do you stub `e` so that `target` can be wrapped by `$` into a zjquery stub?

**Steve Howell** · 2019-02-02 14:09 UTC

The answer is **`to_$`**. Here is the idiom:

~~~
    var textarea = $.create('target-stub');

    var ev = {
        preventDefault: noop,
        target: {
            to_$: () => textarea,
        },
    };

    var handler = $("body").get_on_handler("click", ".video_link");

    handler(ev);

**Steve Howell** · 2019-02-02 14:11 UTC

Because `ev.target` has the attribute `to_$`, when zjquery does `$(ev.target)`, it will just dispatch that function and return `textarea` here.  (And then it depends on your code how you want to set up `textarea`--in this case I just made it a boring stub.)

**Steve Howell** · 2019-02-02 14:13 UTC

You can find real-life examples by doing `git grep 'to_\$'`.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-07-24 01:47 UTC

I don’t necessarily agree with the suggestion that writing new tests for poorly-covered code will always add more value than improving existing tests for well-covered code. The existing tests are themselves code, after all—code that we need to run and update and maintain.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-07-24 01:54 UTC

If not for the Node tests, we would have been able to convert all our code to ES6 modules in a weekend and we’d be done or well on our way to converting it to TypeScript by now. This isn’t to say that the Node tests are bad or that we’d be better off without them, but it is an illustration of the point that work spent improving them could have major benefits.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-07-24 01:58 UTC

A good thing to prototype might be testing `list_render` with actual jQuery.  The current tests actually don't use zjquery, but they stub the jQuery layer in a similar fashion.  https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/master/frontend_tests/node_tests/list_render.js

**Steve Howell** · 2020-07-24 02:01 UTC

Another candidate is the compose tests.  Those are probably the lowest quality node tests we have, partly because `compose.js` is a bit of a beast.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-07-24 02:04 UTC

But I also think it's completely sane to focus on the stuff where we've proven that neither node, casper, or puppeteer hit the sweet spot.  Which is our settings system.  Which has always been buggy.  And which doesn't get as much eyeball testing for free on czo as the main page stuff.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-07-24 02:10 UTC

`settings_emoji.js` might be an interesting experiment.  Right now it literally only tests that we call the upload_widget with the intended jQuery fields.  We could have it do a deeper test using the actual upload widget.

~~~ js
set_global("$", global.make_zjquery());
set_global("upload_widget", {});
zrequire("settings_emoji");

run_test("build_emoji_upload_widget", () => {
    let build_widget_stub = false;
    upload_widget.build_widget = function (
        get_file_input,
        file_name_field,
        input_error,
        clear_button,
        upload_button,
    ) {
        assert.deepEqual(get_file_input(), $("#emoji_file_input"));
        assert.deepEqual(file_name_field, $("#emoji-file-name"));
        assert.deepEqual(input_error, $("#emoji_file_input_error"));
        assert.deepEqual(clear_button, $("#emoji_image_clear_button"));
        assert.deepEqual(upload_button, $("#emoji_upload_button"));
        build_widget_stub = true;
    };
    settings_emoji.build_emoji_upload_widget();
    assert(build_widget_stub);
});
~~~

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-07-24 05:23 UTC

Interesting, I would not have guessed that Electron had fast enough startup.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-07-30 21:24 UTC

Does anyone have action items here?  We clearly had some recent regressions that weren’t caught with our current automated testing methodology.  OTOH all the recent bugs that I know of were shallow in nature, quickly identified on czo, and quickly fixed.

## overrides

*2017-06-19 to 2017-06-19 · 14 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/43-automated-testing/topic/overrides/with/231769)*

**Cory Lynch** · 2017-06-19 21:08 UTC

Quick question for node tests. What is the advantage to using `with_overrides` over just `set_global`?

**Cory Lynch** · 2017-06-19 21:14 UTC

Well, I guess it makes it easier to set individual functions in a module that may/may not exist.

**Joshua Pan** · 2017-06-19 21:16 UTC

Just wondering, is `with_overrides` just specifying what you override first and then running tests?

**Cory Lynch** · 2017-06-19 21:18 UTC

Yeah, like
```javascript
with_overrides(function (override) {
    override('module.function', some_function);
    function_that_uses_override();
});
```

**Steve Howell** · 2017-06-19 21:26 UTC

I only use `with_overrides` in test modules where I'm paranoid about leaking monkey patches.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-06-19 21:27 UTC

The two modules where you want to be very rigorous with stubs are `dispatch.js` and `hotkeys.js`, because almost all that we test there is stubbed out, so you don't want to leak a stub.

**Joshua Pan** · 2017-06-19 21:28 UTC

(which seems to be where all the instances of `with_overrides` are)

**Steve Howell** · 2017-06-19 21:28 UTC

In most other modules I just directly patch functions:

~~~ js
set_global('stream_data', {});

stream_data.get_name = function () { return 'stub-stream-name'; }
~~~

**Steve Howell** · 2017-06-19 21:30 UTC

The way that `with_overrides` works is that it actually restores the old value after the function exits.  Whereas the `set_global` stuff only gets cleared after the entire module is run.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-06-19 21:30 UTC

~~~ js
 54 exports.with_overrides = function (test_function) {
 55     // This function calls test_function() and passes in
 56     // a way to override the namespace temporarily.
 57 
 58     var clobber_callbacks = [];
 59 
 60     var override = function (name, f) {
 61         var parts = name.split('.');
 62         var module = parts[0];
 63         var func_name = parts[1];
 64 
 65         if (!_.has(global, module)) {
 66             set_global(module, {});
 67         }
 68 
 69         global[module][func_name] = f;
 70 
 71         clobber_callbacks.push(function () {
 72             // If you get a failure from this, you probably just
 73             // need to have your test do its own overrides and
 74             // not cherry-pick off of the prior test's setup.
 75             global[module][func_name] =
 76                 'ATTEMPTED TO REUSE OVERRIDDEN VALUE FROM PRIOR TEST';
 77         });
 78     };
 79 
 80     test_function(override);
 81 
 82     _.each(clobber_callbacks, function (f) {
 83         f();
 84     });
 85 };
~~~

**Steve Howell** · 2017-06-19 21:31 UTC

`frontend_tests/zjsunit/namespace.js` is where all the complicated stubbing helpers live

**Cory Lynch** · 2017-06-19 21:31 UTC

Hm, I see.

**Cory Lynch** · 2017-06-19 21:31 UTC

Thanks!

**Steve Howell** · 2017-06-19 21:33 UTC

Then in `index.js` you can see how we restore stuff after file is run:

~~~ js
 49 files.forEach(function (file) {
 50     global.patch_builtin('setTimeout', noop);
 51     global.patch_builtin('setInterval', noop);
 52 
 53     console.info('running tests for ' + file.name);
 54     render.init();
 55     require(file.full_name);
 56     namespace.restore();
 57 });
~~~

**Steve Howell** · 2017-06-28 12:17 UTC

My conclusion from this is that we don't need to worry about Handlebars slowing down the execution time of the tests, so we can base our testing strategy on other factors.  The pros of using Handlebars is that we could catch bugs in the templates themselves.  The con of using Handlebars is that the tests get a little too coupled to the templates, when it's really higher level interactions we want  to test.  I think the pros outweigh the cons for things like error messages, but for bigger widgets you want to stub out templates.render.

Ohk, @Vishnu Ks effort for #5500 brought this issue to light.
This is in reference to issue: `i18n`error out as not being defined, though we recently added a minimal lib version of it for tests in global scope.
So what is happening is that once the module is put in global scope by doing, `global.i18n = require(./i18n.js')` from inside of `index.js` in zjsunit, this module should stick around for every test run. What happens is that if a module with same name is added  using add_dependency from inside of any test file, this module comes under the namespace. Now at every test run, at end `index.js` performs a namespace cleanup leading to `i18n` being lost. This is what happens at end of `i18n.js`(Test file inside node tests) resulting in stubbed version of `i18n` no longer available in any of the further test files.
I am purposing to use a hacky approach here and just put in `i18n.js` module in global scope from `index.js` after every namespace cleanup or maybe conditionally if the global doesn't already has a `i18n`.
Would like your views.

**Greg Price** · 2017-07-24 20:29 UTC

Hi @Vaibhav Singhal !

> I am trying to write backend tests for a function which takes a Response object as input. I tried to pass another object and it works but it gives mypy error.

Yep -- when a function is annotated to say it takes a certain type of object, then mypy will check callers to be sure that that's actually what they pass to it. That's the key thing that makes it possible for you to believe the annotations when you read them :)

> I also tried to initialize actual Response object and set it's _content, but again I am getting mypy error that Response object has no _content attribute. content attribute couldn't be set either.

This means that the interface defined for the Response object doesn't allow for that. In general in Python the convention is that an attribute whose name starts with a single underscore is "private" -- it's not part of the interface, and code that isn't part of that class's own implementation isn't supposed to use it. So it's natural that `_content` isn't available in the interface.

**Aditya Bansal** · 2017-07-24 21:51 UTC

a private object makes sense. Thanks Greg for explanation.

**Vaibhav Singhal** · 2017-07-25 03:12 UTC

@Greg Price thanks.

    # ensures we'll still check JSON files for whitespace.
```
I don't think the comment is valid anymore, since we check for whitespace by appending `+ whitespace_rules` to a linting list.
When I did that, there were ~600 tab-based whitespace and ~200 trailing whitespace issues, mostly in fixture files. Since we probably only want to remove the trailing whitespaces, should we add the trailing whitespace rule to `json_rules` and remove all issues?

## linter pep8

*2017-08-16 to 2017-08-17 · 17 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/43-automated-testing/topic/linter.20pep8/with/268631)*

**Robert Hönig** · 2017-08-16 12:00 UTC

Travis CI runs `tools/lint --pep8` by default. Running `tools/lint` doesn't catch some of the errors Travis complains about when the PR is up. Should we rename the option to `--nopep8` / completely remove it?

**Steve Howell** · 2017-08-16 12:31 UTC

The pep8 checks are really slow, which is pretty annoying when you're working on JS code (and with JS, you're frequently linting, since JS is more persnickety about syntax).

**Steve Howell** · 2017-08-16 12:32 UTC

So my vote is to leave it "as is," but if other people have gotten burned by the pep8 thing, I'd consider the "--nopep8" option.

**Harshit Bansal** · 2017-08-16 21:42 UTC

I am in favor of `--nopep8` option since when I run `./tools/lint` I expect it to report all the lint errors by default. Specifying the `--nopep8` option to limit the checking to javascript only seems more natural to me.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-08-16 21:51 UTC

If we can get one more person to chime in on preferring `--nopep8`, we can start debating the name for that option.   Something like `--fast` might be better.

**Tommy Ip** · 2017-08-17 12:54 UTC

Maybe we could try to speed up pycodestyle by running it in parallel? eg spawning a few threads and distribute source files to it

**Steve Howell** · 2017-08-17 13:10 UTC

The problem with that approach is that we are already running several linters in parallel.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-08-17 13:15 UTC

For me:
* lint: 10s
* lint w/pep8: 20s

I could imagine threading pep8 bringing the second time down to 15s or so, which would still be pretty unacceptable for me.

**Tommy Ip** · 2017-08-17 13:16 UTC

ok yeah

**Steve Howell** · 2017-08-17 13:22 UTC

For me the best fix here would be:

* lint --py: exclude eslint
* lint --js: exclude pyflakes and pycodestyle

**Robert Hönig** · 2017-08-17 14:29 UTC

**Steve Howell** · 2017-08-17 14:32 UTC

yep, I think that would be fine

**Robert Hönig** · 2017-08-17 14:46 UTC

For both options, do we only want to exclude the things you mentioned, or rather any file not belonging to that language?

**Steve Howell** · 2017-08-17 15:00 UTC

Just the things I mentioned for now, and get some measurements with `time` to see the savings.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-08-17 15:02 UTC

For the JS case, it's often the case that I know there's no Python, but there might be a bit of random CSS/HTML.

This is the right output. CircleCI doesn't support caching the entire image. It only caches the docker image layers. [1]

> Error response from daemon: error parsing HTTP 404 response body: invalid character 'p' after top-level value: "404 page not found\n"

and 

> Error response from daemon: unauthorized: authentication required

**Greg Price** · 2018-11-26 20:02 UTC

Yeah, I think what this message is saying:
```
 image cache not found on this host, downloading gregprice/circleci:xenial-python-4.test
```
is that the host that build got assigned to run on didn't happen to have a cache of our Docker image lying around, so it had to fetch it over the network.

Which is normal in CircleCI. A more optimized CI system would have some locality so that builds typically ran on a host that had their Docker images cached (and similarly any other caches), but Circle isn't designed with that optimization.

```
error parsing HTTP 404 response body: invalid character 'p' after top-level value: "404 page not found\n"
```

## unused imports

*2017-10-16 to 2017-10-17 · 11 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/43-automated-testing/topic/unused.20imports/with/298881)*

**Robert Hönig** · 2017-10-16 09:08 UTC

After stumbling over a few unused imports in `registration.py`, I came to wonder why we don't lint for this sort of thing. Seeing that we do run `pyflakes`, but ignore its `unused import` statements, I noticed that most of the times, `pyflakes` would give false positives on unused imports due to our heavy use of mypy comment annotations. There seems to be no action to be taken by pyflakes (https://gitlab.com/pycqa/flake8/issues/342) and other linters like `pylint ` face the same problem. 
I wonder if it would make sense for us to build some custom linting function here that simply checks for the occurrence of an imported statement in the rest of the file. This would greatly reduce the number of false positives. For the few remaining special cases, like in [wsgi.py](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/master/zproject/wsgi.py#L30), we could add ignore annotations.

**Tommy Ip** · 2017-10-16 10:09 UTC

I think the false positives from mypy comments would go away when we migrate to the PEP 484 & 526 syntax

**Robert Hönig** · 2017-10-16 10:16 UTC

Yeah, that'd be ideal. I guess though that the couple thousand lines that'd need to be updated to fully migrate make this a fairly large project. If we decide to to that, some half-automated tooling might help as well?

**Tommy Ip** · 2017-10-16 10:19 UTC

I believe @Rein Zustand is working on this? see #6791

**Robert Hönig** · 2017-10-16 10:20 UTC

Cool, good to know!

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-10-16 16:50 UTC

I should add that even if we didn't have the mypy problem, historically, we've generally been happier with purging unused imports on a quarterly basis rather than requiring them to be removed on every commit, and we might want some exclude rules.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-10-16 16:51 UTC

The reason being that you can often end up with an import being added/removed/added again as one works on a part of the codebase in a series of commits, and so unused-import errors can sometimes result in what feels like makework.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-10-16 16:51 UTC

We can play around with options for how to do it, but obviously we need to handle the imports required for mypy first :)

**Umair Khan** · 2017-10-17 04:46 UTC

Mypy import problem should be fixed once we move to Python 3.5.

**Greg Price** · 2017-10-17 22:30 UTC

This has nothing to do with Python 3.5 -- it's a matter of switching to the `def f(x: int) -> None:` syntax. Which works in all Python 3.x versions that mypy works for at all, i.e. 3.3+.

**Greg Price** · 2017-10-17 22:31 UTC

(For the lint issue specifically, it's possible to hack up the linters to understand type comments -- and that's what Dropbox has done -- but it's kind of a tricky hack, and there's no need for us to do it because we can just migrate to the new-style syntax.)

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-11-16 16:42 UTC

So, the way this works is a bit complicated, so I'll explain it (maybe should put this in the docs):
* We have a `zulip_test_template` database that is generated by running migrations, and only is rebuild when the migrations change.
* For most of these tools, they just check if the template is current (if it isn't, rebuild it), and then copy the template to `zulip_test`.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-11-16 16:42 UTC

So you'll only see the migrations run when they actually change.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-04-18 12:07 UTC

There are a couple missions going forward:
* As always, we encourage folks to add/maintain tests for new features, and there's a learning curve for new folks, so help on code reviews and similar things are appreciated.
* We want to move toward **ES6** idioms.
* We want to improve **documentation** of the system.
* We want to get almost-100%-covered modules to fully **100% line coverage**.
* We want to cover **difficult modules** that require more advanced knowledge of stubbing (typically UI-heavy modules).

## StubBotHandler

*2017-12-15 to 2017-12-18 · 8 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/43-automated-testing/topic/StubBotHandler/with/390673)*

**Nikhil Kumar Mishra** · 2017-12-15 22:06 UTC

Since we recently modified out `StubBotTestCase` to` BotTestCase` , I want to know why didn't we modify `StubBotHandler` to simple `BotHandler` ? Is it just that we missed it or is there some important reason behind it?
If we simply missed it, then I would like to clear this from all `test_lib.py` and other tests.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-12-15 22:11 UTC

We really only have one class like `BotTestCase`, whereas we have multiple variations of `FooBotHandler`.  So let's leave it alone for now.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-12-15 22:12 UTC

One possible renaming is `StubBotHandler` -> `TestBotHandler`, but I view that as low priority for now.

**Nikhil Kumar Mishra** · 2017-12-15 22:13 UTC

ohh I see, thanks.

**Neil Pilgrim (neiljp)** · 2017-12-17 01:14 UTC

@Steve Howell I've also read a little about using terminology for stubs (vs fakes/mocks) - but I'm not sure if that was part of your decision?

**Steve Howell** · 2017-12-17 13:44 UTC

I think the lines are blurry when you talks fakes vs. stubs vs. mocks, but it's arguable that "StubBotHandler" is more of a "fake" than a "stub."  I'm wary to change names now, though, as I think the distinction will mostly be lost on people and just cause more code churn.

**Neil Pilgrim (neiljp)** · 2017-12-17 19:02 UTC

To be clear, I wasn't suggesting changing names between fakes and stubs, it was more whether having a prefix in the first place was intentional, or just to avoid conflict with the pre-existing class names (eg. with `StubBotTestCase`). Leaving those names in there could potentially be a learning opportunity, if the former?

**Steve Howell** · 2017-12-18 12:51 UTC

@Neil Pilgrim For `StubBotHandler`, the prefix is very necessary for disambiguation (because of `ExternalBotHandler` and friends).  For `StubBotTestCase`, there are no longer any ambiguity concerns, so it's a tradeoff between a concise name (`BotTestCase`) and a more descriptive name (`StubBotTestCase`) that can also have the side effect of being a learning opportunity.

I probably would have left it as `StubBotTestCase`, but when somebody submitted the PR to shorten the name, I was enough on the fence that I just merged it (because I do see the value in short names).

## broken links

*2018-01-10 to 2018-01-11 · 10 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/43-automated-testing/topic/broken.20links/with/438129)*

**Steve Howell** · 2018-01-10 13:56 UTC

We seem to have doc links break about once a month, for reasons beyond our control (the other sites move stuff around), and it tends to invalidate our builds for hours at a time, even up to a day.  It's kind of a nuisance when these things cause delays on important features, whereas broken links in docs aren't really user-facing, since most of those links are for devs that can figure out how to google around those kind of issues.

@Greg Price @Vishnu Ks I'm wondering if as part of #7748, we could split out the doc tests to their own build.  Another possibility would be to make `test-documentation' only run if one of the last N commits changes doc-related files (which I think we could identify with reasonable confidence/acceptable risk of missing changes).

**Greg Price** · 2018-01-10 21:06 UTC

Yeah. I'd make it separate from #7748, but it would be pretty reasonable to separate the links check out, and not always run it or not have it fail the build (just warn somehow out-of-line) if it fails.

**Greg Price** · 2018-01-10 21:06 UTC

Note that `test-documentation` does more than that -- it also tries building the docs in the first place, which is not flaky and is good for finding syntax errors, etc.

**Greg Price** · 2018-01-10 21:09 UTC

Also see 1a83b32da, which I wrote/merged yesterday -- I added a flag `test-documentation --skip-check-links`, and had us pass that in CircleCI for now. So we can control this by passing that flag.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-01-10 21:48 UTC

I'd be happy to just run with `--skip-check-links` for a while, and if the pendulum starts swinging the other way (we start having more carelessness on the Zulip side than sites breaking originally valid links), we can revisit.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-01-10 22:15 UTC

@Steve Howell it might make sense to do something a bit more nuanced; we really do want to fail the build for any broken links in our our sites (e.g. ReadTheDocs, etc.).

**Steve Howell** · 2018-01-10 22:29 UTC

Do you know off the top of your head if there is there an easy way to distinguish external broken links from internal broken links?  (Obviously, the latter are both more avoidable and more embarrassing if we were to let them pass.)

**Steve Howell** · 2018-01-10 22:30 UTC

I suppose "internal" may be tough to specify if you consider "internal" anything within's Zulip reach (so, repo, rtd, zulipchat.com, etc.)

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-01-10 23:46 UTC

I think we could probably just have a whitelist for the "internal" links.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-01-11 00:21 UTC

For some reason I was thinking our documentation crawler was opaque to us, but after poking around I bit I see that we have our own code that customizes scrapy, including `EXCLUDED_URLS` in `tools/documentation_crawler/documentation_crawler/spiders/common/spiders.py`.  I'll poke around some more tomorrow to try out a whitelist approach.

Is `queries_captured` context manager in `zerver/tests/test_helpers.py` count the no of queries performed on database during particular operation/function? :thinking_face: 

```python
@contextmanager
def queries_captured(include_savepoints: Optional[bool]=False) -> Generator[
        List[Dict[str, Union[str, bytes]]], None, None]:
    '''
    Allow a user to capture just the queries executed during
    the with statement.
    '''

    queries = []  # type: List[Dict[str, Union[str, bytes]]]

    def wrapper_execute(self: TimeTrackingCursor,
                        action: Callable[[NonBinaryStr, Iterable[Any]], None],
                        sql: NonBinaryStr,
                        params: Iterable[Any]=()) -> None:
        cache = get_cache_backend(None)
        cache.clear()
        start = time.time()
        try:
            return action(sql, params)
        finally:
            stop = time.time()
            duration = stop - start
            if include_savepoints or ('SAVEPOINT' not in sql):
                queries.append({
                    'sql': self.mogrify(sql, params).decode('utf-8'),
                    'time': "%.3f" % duration,
                })

    old_execute = TimeTrackingCursor.execute
    old_executemany = TimeTrackingCursor.executemany

    def cursor_execute(self: TimeTrackingCursor, sql: NonBinaryStr,
                       params: Iterable[Any]=()) -> None:
        return wrapper_execute(self, super(TimeTrackingCursor, self).execute, sql, params)  # type: ignore # https://github.com/JukkaL/mypy/issues/1167
    TimeTrackingCursor.execute = cursor_execute  # type: ignore # https://github.com/JukkaL/mypy/issues/1167

```

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-01-29 17:28 UTC

@Yashashvi Dave technically, it also logs them to the `queries` list, so you could actually inspect them individually, but yes, the main thing we use it for is counting for tests.

**Yashashvi Dave** · 2018-01-29 17:34 UTC

``` 
Are those no's are asserted after manually checking out that how many queries we performed? I have changed backend code which changes the no of events and queries. So no's are failing.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-01-29 17:38 UTC

If the number is expected to have changed (i.e. we added a query obviously), increase the number.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-01-29 17:39 UTC

The purpose is to prevent accidental increases in the number of database queries when refactoring, not to prevent adding new features that require, by their nature, more database queries.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-01-29 17:39 UTC

But I would be thoughtful when reviewing about whether an existing query could get the data we need.

**Yashashvi Dave** · 2018-01-29 17:42 UTC

**Dinesh Ch** · 2020-06-07 19:17 UTC

@Tim Abbott The tests passed for the PR. It's ready for review.

So the reason we think it's failing is puppeteer is doing a reload with `await page.goto(this.realm_url);` in log_out() as soon as it submits login form. So it's ending up in login page instead of getting logged in. The commit I linked to waits for navigation until `DOMContentLoaded`. That way the selector is appeared for sure before logging out even if there's a refresh since the the user is already logged in.

**Neil Pilgrim (neiljp)** · 2020-09-16 01:45 UTC

Isn't the premise that one only bumps the release instead? I suppose in the worst case if you don't have a substitute you might consider removing it, but it seems better to push a point release, admitting the problem?

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-09-16 03:35 UTC

Yes of course that’s what you should do. For whatever reason, it’s not what this maintainer did, as [happens](https://pydist.com/blog/never-delete-a-release) from time to time. This maintainer realizes now that the decision was a mistake. So it’s reasonable to ask if PyPI could do a better job of emphasizing to maintainers that removing a package is a last resort for extreme cases (e.g. the package was infected with malware, or its distribution is illegal) and will break downstream projects relying on the package.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-09-16 17:51 UTC

Yeah, exactly, that's the sort of warning that I had in mind -- helping maintainers realize it's going to be a mistake before they do it by just documenting clearly what the impact is.

For folks new to the project, this is one reason that it's important to make sure that the test changes are in the same commit as the code changes that require them. **Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-03-12 17:17 UTC

The fix may be as simple as
```diff
--- a/static/js/ready.js
+++ b/static/js/ready.js
@@ -1,3 +1,5 @@
 import $ from "jquery";
 
-$("#app-loading").addClass("loaded");
+$(() => {
+    $("#app-loading").addClass("loaded");
+});
```
not because the DOM isn’t ready here (we’re in a `<script defer>`), but because we want to wait until after all the other callbacks that wait for the DOM to be ready.

**Riken Shah** · 2021-05-03 13:40 UTC

Phew, Finally found a solution that works :tada:,
If we wait for 100ms after we type each character (`ot`) and wait until filtering is completed.
```typescript
- await common.fill_form(page, "form#stream_creation_form", {user_list_filter: "ot"});
+ await common.fill_form(page, "form#stream_creation_form", {user_list_filter: "ot"}, 100);
await page.waitForSelector("#user-checkboxes", {visible: true});
await page.waitForSelector(cordelia_checkbox, {hidden: true});
await page.waitForSelector(othello_checkbox, {visible: true});
+ // Wait until filtering is successfully completed.
+ await page.waitForFunction(() => $("#user-checkboxes label").first().attr("id") === "user_checkbox_12");
+ await page.waitForFunction(() => $("#user-checkboxes label").last().attr("id") === "user_checkbox_12");
```
[Link to the commit](https://github.com/Riken-Shah/zulip/commit/b9667646012bc65004133b32e1fb5b91fc53418f#diff-e4c59dc1f9818f8ab747e86d179d57648e6e2ebb846a633839737c87ae4b95df).
[Link to the CI](https://github.com/Riken-Shah/zulip/runs/2491348899).

Better version of the above changes,
```typescript
diff --git a/frontend_tests/puppeteer_tests/subscriptions.ts b/frontend_tests/puppeteer_tests/subscriptions.ts
index 93cb190f13..46b4a10593 100644
--- a/frontend_tests/puppeteer_tests/subscriptions.ts
+++ b/frontend_tests/puppeteer_tests/subscriptions.ts
@@ -129,16 +129,19 @@ async function test_user_filter_ui(
     // Desdemona should be checked by default
     await wait_for_checked(page, "desdemona", true);
 
-    await common.fill_form(page, "form#stream_creation_form", {user_list_filter: "ot"});
+    await page.type(`form#stream_creation_form [name="user_list_filter"]`, "ot", {delay: 100});
     await page.waitForSelector("#user-checkboxes", {visible: true});
     await page.waitForSelector(cordelia_checkbox, {hidden: true});
     await page.waitForSelector(othello_checkbox, {visible: true});
+    // Wait until filtering is successfully completed.
+    await page.waitForFunction(() => $("#user-checkboxes label").length === 1);
```



It also works if we click with jQuery after we wait for filtering to complete. 
[Link to the CI](https://github.com/Riken-Shah/zulip/runs/2491381941).

P.S: You may find some containers in the CI that are yet not finished (i.e: Still running or stopped after 6 hours limit ), this means it has already run successfully 100 times and running again. 
(I have noticed this many times now.)

**Riken Shah** · 2021-05-03 16:31 UTC

I think so it's because of the scrolling before it clicks.

From [documentation](https://devdocs.io/puppeteer/index#frameclickselector-options),
> This method fetches an element with selector, scrolls it into view if needed, and then uses page.mouse to click in the center of the element. If there's no element matching selector, the method throws an error.

Puppeteer [click method source code](https://github.com/puppeteer/puppeteer/blob/8816645c719e58621a36c9628ddcb78befcd5b2e/src/common/JSHandle.ts#L494
),
```typescript
  async click(options: ClickOptions = {}): Promise<void> {
  -> await this._scrollIntoViewIfNeeded(); <-
    const { x, y } = await this._clickablePoint();
    await this._page.mouse.click(x, y, options);
  }
```

It was a race where `page.waitForSelector` scrolls the page and `page.click` calculates the `Set All` button position before/while scrolling.

**Riken Shah** · 2021-05-04 18:33 UTC

I think so there are two possible solutions for this, 
- Wait until scrolling is completed.
- [Click using jQuery instead of `page.click`](https://github.com/Riken-Shah/zulip/commit/6e18d561cc794edb52083331094bd9a1a525ef55#diff-e597faefed54bacef341319c76078bc7ec61fcf051518d3e33649044c2eaa36d).

For the first option, 
I think so we can get the `top` of the form before we scroll and after it `call focus` and `list is filtered` we can check if  `current top`  is not equal to `previous top`. 

```typescript
diff --git a/frontend_tests/puppeteer_tests/subscriptions.ts b/frontend_tests/puppeteer_tests/subscriptions.ts
 
+async function wait_for_stream_creation_form_scroll(page: Page): Promise<void> {
+    await page.waitForFunction(() => {
+        if (
+            zulip_test.top_of_form &&
+            $("#stream_creation_form").position().top !== zulip_test.top_of_form
+        ) {
+            zulip_test.top_of_form = $("#stream_creation_form").position().top;
+            return true;
+        }
+        return false;
+    });
+}
+
...
+    // Set the top of the form so that we can later check if it's scrolled.
+    await page.evaluate(() => {
+        zulip_test.top_of_form = $("#stream_creation_form").position()?.top;
+        return;
+    });
+
     await common.fill_form(page, "form#stream_creation_form", {user_list_filter: "ot"});
+    // Wait until we have scrolled.
+    await wait_for_stream_creation_form_scroll(page);
+    // We are wrapping the next scroll event wait call in the try-catch block because it can
+    // be possible that both the scroll event was checked in the first wait call.
+    // It happens very rarely.
+    try {
+        await wait_for_stream_creation_form_scroll(page);
+    } catch {} // eslint-disable-line no-empty
```
I have tested the above changes on the [CI](https://github.com/Riken-Shah/zulip/runs/2501934576), where it successfully ran 100 times.


So which option should we go with or Any suggestion about the approach?

> Hmm, could we instead just do a manual scroll down the page in the test before the automatic scroll happens?

I tried that earlier but calling,
```javascript
await page.evaluate(() => document.querySelector("#stream_creation_form").scrollIntoView());
```
Just initiate the scroll event, it doesn't wait until the page is scrolled.

Even if we wait until it is scrolled. 

Typing `ot` will produce two scrolling event ([reason](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/stream/43-automated-testing/topic/master.20failing/near/1173996)). 
And it can be possible that while we wait for scroll after typing `ot`, the first scrolling event (`focus`) will take that check.
And second scroll event will cause the same flake!

**Sumanth Rao** · 2021-05-12 01:29 UTC

(replying to Riken Shah (Riken-Shah))
> > And I can see that realm-playground.ts uses a timeout of 4 secs instead of default 3 secs? I also don't think it's necessary to update the default 30sec timeout limit to 4secs. Is there any specific reason to do this @Sumanth Rao?
That timeout actually waits for a previous alert to disappear. We set the fadeaway time for those alerts as 3 seconds (see `admin-playground-form` in `settings_playground.js`). In theory, we could set the disappear timeout to 3 seconds, but that might again cause races.

**Riken Shah** · 2021-05-12 05:29 UTC

Yeah, but if you don't specify `timeout`, it will be by default set to **30 seconds**.
So there is no need to specify `4 seconds timeout`.

And It is also possible that in a slower PC, due to lag it takes more than 4 seconds to disappear.

**Riken Shah** · 2021-06-09 06:34 UTC

The failure is because of the changes in this commit only [7b4039ade6a](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/commit/7b4039ade6add81b8035e72982ff58b6c376a547) (@Ganesh Pawar (ganpa3)  FYI). 

The reason for the failure is it didn't click on the `Confirm` button it clicked on `.modal-backdrop.in` div. 

This happed because we have removed the `fade` property from the deactivate user's confirm dialog box and with it [`pointer-events: all` property was also removed](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/d905eb61315610d161b6d6704856ba3872efa2d0/static/styles/settings.css#L1545).  And  `pointer-events: none` property was inherited from [`div.overlay.show`](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/d905eb61315610d161b6d6704856ba3872efa2d0/static/js/overlays.js#L53). Hence, it caused click event to not work.

Maybe a fix for this is the move the [`.in`](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/d905eb61315610d161b6d6704856ba3872efa2d0/static/styles/settings.css#L1545) block outside of [`.fade`](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/d905eb61315610d161b6d6704856ba3872efa2d0/static/styles/settings.css#L1539) block.

**Riken Shah** · 2021-06-13 05:14 UTC

(replying to Dinesh Ch)
> Why's there no artefacts tab for this? :thinking:

Yeah, it happens that you couldn't see the artifacts download button if the URL has `check_suite_focus=true`.

You can just remove that and you'd see the artifacts download button.

For example, You will not see the download button here https://github.com/zulip/zulip/runs/2807683934?check_suite_focus=true but you will see it now https://github.com/zulip/zulip/runs/2807683934.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-06-13 07:49 UTC

(replying to Anders Kaseorg)
> Bisection shows this was introduced by https://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/git/git.git/commit/?id=v2.25.0-rc0~144^2~1.

[Reported to upstream](https://lore.kernel.org/git/148044c89c194a82aa15ab0ca016669d@oc11expo7.exchange.mit.edu/T/), who quickly replied pointing out that it actually goes back further (https://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/git/git.git/commit/?id=v2.18.0-rc0~2^2~20). This suggests `git -c merge.directoryRenames=false cherry-pick` as a workaround, if you need one. They’re working on a fix.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-02-16 19:00 UTC

The way things work is this:
* the real code calls "on"
* "on" in zjquery populates `on_functions` and `child_on_functions`, which are both a `Dict` (so it has set/get)
* you can call `get_on_handlers` in your tests to get at the internal dicts and then get the handlers
