**Greg Price** · 2018-03-01 20:44 UTC

(BTW a bit of context on my thinking, just to make it explicit for everyone:
* False failures in PR builds, i.e. failures that aren't actually caused by the change, are bad -- they waste people's time, and/or undermine their confidence in the test suite.
* False failures in master mostly don't matter as much, but they are easier to spot, because almost every failure in master is a false one. And the causes of false failures apply in pretty much the same way to master and PR builds, so the ones in master should be representative of what's happening in PR builds. Hence, scanning through failures in master.
* Also on the infrequent occasions there are non-false failures in master, those are extra bad because they usually cause false failures in several PR builds before they're fixed.

)

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-03-28 19:56 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-03-29 18:43 UTC

OK, so the most mysterious one has been the `test_stream_error_pm_to_bot_owner` issue, and I just traced that down.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-03-29 18:43 UTC

We rate-limit those notices to once per 5 minutes using the `last_reminder` field.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-03-29 18:44 UTC

However, that field is initialized to the current time when a user account is created.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-03-29 18:44 UTC

So if one runs the tests within 5 minutes of creating the DB, it fails.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-03-29 18:44 UTC

Hence the flakiness; apparently it's nondeterministic whether or not there are 5 minutes between populate_db and that test running.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-03-29 18:45 UTC

The fix is that `last_reminder` should have a default value of `None` (all the code that interacts with it uses that default).

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-03-29 18:48 UTC

@Eeshan Garg FYI, since this mystery was probably bothering you :)

**Eeshan Garg** · 2018-03-29 18:49 UTC

@Tim Abbott: Ooh, nice, I don't think I would have been able to track this down! Thanks so much, Tim! :)

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-03-29 18:53 UTC

Fixed in 4570936ac2f33ded53d48a03e36e43182982d954

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-03-29 18:54 UTC

Tracking this down just required a bit of luck and then some print-debugging and code-reading; I'd noticed this weird pattern where the test would fail sometimes, and consistently, when running the full test suite locally, and then stop failing.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-03-29 18:54 UTC

Didn't know why, but that caused me to be quick to add print statements and rerun just the one test the next time I saw it fail locally.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-03-29 18:55 UTC

And then those print statements showed the message in question was simply not being sent.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-03-29 18:55 UTC

If you go read the code the `send_pm_if_empty_stream`, there's only really one reason it would not be sent that seems variable, the `last_reminder` stuff.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-03-29 18:55 UTC

So it's just a matter of being systematic and seizing opportunities when something reproduces.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-03-29 18:56 UTC

That all said, I sorta wonder if we should make the error output better for this situation; might help with future debugging.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-03-29 18:56 UTC

Anyway, that flake was by far the most common; the two that remain are:

* A long-open rare flake with `add_missing_messages` in the Soft Deactivation tests.

**Aditya Bansal** · 2018-04-09 17:29 UTC

I think what you are talking about is actually database migrations. https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/2.0/topics/migrations/
Basically migrations are a way of adding changes to our DB on the database layer. Lets say there was a table for user profile and you decided to add a new column to this table called phone number. We will essentially add the variable in the model class of user profile. Then we will write a migration for database (for simple changes like adding a column these migrations can be automatically generated as well).
You can look take a look at some of Zulip's migrations which are located under the directory `zerver/migrations` :)
@Ben Reeves 

As far as testing goes I don't think migrations are particularly used in backend testing apart from actually running them upon the test database so that our unit tests are testing the db with latest schema. Though maybe I don't get your question about migrations and backend testing :confused:

## Coverage vs. Correctness

*2018-04-09 to 2018-04-09 · 16 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/43-automated-testing/topic/Coverage.20vs.2E.20Correctness/with/556833)*

**Ben Reeves** · 2018-04-09 17:19 UTC

The testing efforts for zulip, as far as I can tell, are currently centered around coverage. Having test coverage is good, but I've learned in class that having it as a goal can lead to perverse incentives for test writers ("All I have to do is make this line of code run, I don't need to think about correctness"). I am curious if the zulip team takes this into consideration and, if so, what strategies you have employed to combat coverage over correctness.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-04-09 17:27 UTC

@Ben Reeves yeah, this is a topic I've thought about a lot.  Coverage is a good baseline metric (you at least know which code is completely untested!), but it's mostly good for that.  But when you're adding tests, you need to read the tests for whether they actually test what you care about.  

We do try to design important functions (E.g. security checks) so that each case has its own conditional, which means that test coverage can easily tell you whether you have tests for all the cases that function checks.

**Ben Reeves** · 2018-04-09 17:28 UTC

On that note, do you test branch coverage as well?

**Ben Reeves** · 2018-04-09 17:28 UTC

Oh wait, I think I see what you're saying. Rather than trying to use branch coverage, you give each possible case its own unique conditional

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-04-09 17:29 UTC

When reviewing code, I generally look pretty carefully at the tests and whether they cover all the corner cases that are important for verifying the correctness of the feature (ideally, one doesn't want to have to do any manual testing of the backend).

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-04-09 17:29 UTC

Right, exactly.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-04-09 17:29 UTC

We do have the tooling available for branch coverage, but I think it's only slightly better than line coverage.  Fundamentally, these metrics just tell you what is tested, not whether the tests are any good.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-04-09 17:29 UTC

E.g. a common bad test failure mode is folks writing a test that just runs the code, but doesn't assert anything about what happened

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-04-09 17:30 UTC

So your endpoint returns an graceful error rather than success, and the test happily passes

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-04-09 17:30 UTC

It's sorta hard to prevent that with tooling; you need to actually read the code.

**Steve Howell (test)** · 2018-04-09 20:10 UTC

The most important c for me, above coverage and correctness, that a testing style can produce is clarity.

**Steve Howell (test)** · 2018-04-09 20:12 UTC

Coverage percentage is really just a tactical goal to get a baseline where new features at least get minimal coverage, which is all fine and good but not a guarantee of much else.

**Steve Howell (test)** · 2018-04-09 20:13 UTC

Correctness is obviously a great goal for the overall process but people I think overestimate a bit how much testing contributes to that.

**Steve Howell (test)** · 2018-04-09 20:16 UTC

I think the best thing you get from testing is that it can clarify how you think the software should work and it can sometimes push you to write clear, simple code if you write tests as part of the process and not as a qa process or similar afterthought.

**Steve Howell (test)** · 2018-04-09 20:28 UTC

One sort of counterintuitive thing about getting a module to 100% coverage isn’t so much the positive feeling that you think you have 100% correctness.  It’s more that a subsequent change with poor coverage is very easily identified by tooling.  So in some ways the high bar of 100% coverage just helps us keep a low bar of some testing for additive changes.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-04-09 20:48 UTC

The other thing is that having high test coverage does mean that certain classes of bugs can't happen (generally in the "this code crashes always" category).  While that's a pretty narrow range of bugs, it does actually save time as a developer to be able to reason with that in mind.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-04-24 21:51 UTC

Sounds like an ordering-dependent test issue!

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-04-24 21:51 UTC

Those can be tricky to debug.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-04-24 21:52 UTC

One strategy that I've used successfully that isn't just reading the code is to generate a `test-backend --processes=1`  command that runs the tests in roughly the same order that they ran in with the parallel testing

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-04-24 21:52 UTC

(Often listing half the files in the project)

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-04-24 21:53 UTC

Once you've got that, you can start removing half the files from the list in a binary search method to try to get a minimal reproducer

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-04-24 21:54 UTC

It can take an hour of doing the manual binary search (often you can do other work that won't break backend tests in the meantime), but it's a way to get down to a reproducer that's just running 2-3 individual tests in a particular order.  At that point, the bug becomes shallow.

**Shubham Dhama** · 2018-04-24 21:58 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-04-25 17:07 UTC

Yeah, that's another thing worth knowing -- the track traces for `--processes=1` are often a little cleaner.  We use `--processes=1` always when testing a single file/class/etc., so usually you get this for free when you just rerun the test that failed.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-05-15 10:29 UTC

@Tim Abbott @Joshua Pan I created #9394 for my initial work on replacing jQuery with cheerio to parse html from templates.  I'm probably still leaning toward just removing those tests, but you can see my due diligence there.  I'm still somewhat tempted to keep the tests, especially if I'm just at a small bump with cheerio.  One thing about cheerio is that it's a little more finicky about semantic correctness--like you have to surround tr's with table rows or it won't recognize them in selectors.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-05-15 13:18 UTC

One of the quirks of cheerio is that they don't support ':first' selectors, which we use extensively.  That was an easy search/replace for some, but then their model of drilling down through multiple selectors isn't obvious, and they're like jQuery in supporting 5 different ways to do the same thing, so going through their docs is kind of painful.

      1 lxml

**Eeshan Garg** · 2018-06-04 21:30 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-06-04 21:32 UTC

So to clean this up:
* I don't see why we're declaring `requests` in these; it's included in the dependencies of the framework, so it doesn't do anything anyway.  We should remove those useless entries (and maybe also the empty `requirements` files that a lot of the bots have, too?).
* I think a few things that are reusable, like `lxml`, `BeautifulSoup4`, and `html2text` we should include in the base `zulip_bots` distribution. 
* `tools/provision` is the place where that code to install all the `requirements` files belongs, since you do want them all for development/unit tests.
* All the other stuff (python-chess, wit, apiai, tweepy, etc.) should not be included in the `zulip_bots` package dependencies; we just need a good error message for if the requirements for a given bot are missing when you try to run it

## self-executing functions

*2018-07-12 to 2018-07-12 · 5 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/43-automated-testing/topic/self-executing.20functions/with/611274)*

**Joshua Pan** · 2018-07-12 05:48 UTC

In a node test (or any javascript file), if you had the following two self-executing anonymous function, which one is run first? Or are they run simultaneously?

```js
(function a() {
     console.log("hi1");
}());

(function b() {
     console.log("hi2");
}());
```

**Rohitt Vashishtha** · 2018-07-12 06:34 UTC

The first one.

**Rohitt Vashishtha** · 2018-07-12 06:34 UTC

BTW, we recently moved from IIFEs to named tests in our node_tests.

**Joshua Pan** · 2018-07-12 07:00 UTC

Ah, ok; so in order? Not exactly. We still use IIFEs inside our `run_test` functions.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-07-12 11:33 UTC

Yes, in order.  It's sort of like Python in that sense--when you import a Python module, code gets executed in order, although "defining" a function just adds a function to a namespace, it doesn't run it till you invoke it.  Likewise for JS, everything gets executed in order, and since we're invoking the functions immediately, those events happen in order too.

## test flake pitfalls

*2018-08-08 to 2018-08-08 · 9 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/43-automated-testing/topic/test.20flake.20pitfalls/with/627731)*

**Steve Howell** · 2018-08-08 21:14 UTC

It's worth reminding people of two common test-flake patterns.  I use the word "remind", because I think most people are aware of these to some degree, but it's human nature that we may sometimes be rushing when we write tests and forget some pitfalls:

* sorting (or, really, lake thereof)
* dates

**Steve Howell** · 2018-08-08 21:15 UTC

I think the most common test pitfall in a codebase like the Zulip backend is that you're often comparing a complex List of Dicts to some expected value, and the "real code" doesn't always return the list in some deterministic sort.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-08-08 21:16 UTC

Occasionally this is a problem in the real code that is just being reflected in the test, and the answer is to fix the "real code" to have a deterministic sort or to explicitly return a non-ordered data structure like a Set.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-08-08 21:16 UTC

Other times it's just something you work around in the test by converting the results of a "real code" function into a sorted list or a set.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-08-08 21:17 UTC

The other common pitfall is times and dates.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-08-08 21:18 UTC

I'm not gonna elaborate on  all the ways that time-sensitive code can pass tests in July and fail in December.  Hopefully the overall pitfall is obvious.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-08-08 21:19 UTC

I'll instead give a more subtle example of how tests can fail in `test-backend`.  Even though you often construct most of your data within the tests themselves, some of our test data is pre-populated via `populate_db`, and that data causes messages and other data elements to "age" over time.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-08-08 21:20 UTC

Often you can fix this by doing fairly big-hammer stuff like `Message.objects.all().update(pub_date=timezone_now())` at the top of your tests or in `setUp` methods.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-08-08 21:21 UTC

Am I leaving out any other common pitfalls?  (Another category of pitfall is caches leaking between tests, but we are pretty aggressive about preventing that in the test runner.)

## python coverage

*2018-08-14 to 2018-08-15 · 6 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/43-automated-testing/topic/python.20coverage/with/630464)*

**Steve Howell** · 2018-08-14 13:36 UTC

I am definitely seeing strange cases where `pass` and `continue` are not given credit for having run in coverage reports.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-08-14 13:40 UTC

The bug supposedly comes from Python's peephole optimizer.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-08-14 13:42 UTC

There are often cases where `pass` and `continue` are code smells:

* pass - often used for complicated boolean logic that can be extracted to a function
* continue - often more clumsy than just pre-filtering a list before a loop

Unfortunately, the places where I'm hitting this aren't lending themselves to super obvious refactorings.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-08-14 13:42 UTC

Here's the bug report that I think may be relevant here:

https://bugs.python.org/issue2506

**Steve Howell** · 2018-09-06 19:39 UTC

It occurs to me that `test-api` doesn't really use web assets at all.  It just uses server endpoints, and it has no notion of CSS or JS.  So, technically, it could just run off a server that doesn't serve up an asset pipeline, and presumably it would run faster, not waiting for webpack to build stuff.  I'm throwing that out there as food for thought, although I'd be wary to muck with it for several reasons:
* it's extra cognitive complexity to have yet another server configuration
* I believe `test-help-documentation` does use web assets (although maybe not from webpack?), so if you're running `test-all`, then  you're not really saving time by streamlining `test-api`
* the failure here was in the Django startup, so you'd have to fix Django to deal with a "null" configuration

*2018-11-02 to 2018-11-05 · 20 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/43-automated-testing/topic/mypy.20runtime.20costs/with/657764)*

**Steve Howell** · 2018-11-02 15:39 UTC

@Tim Abbott @Greg Price As part of profiling the import program, I'm seeing non-negligible costs of executing Python annotations for `MutableSequence` in `fenced_code.py`.  Part of the problem is that we use inner classes there, which is probably bad performance-wise for ordinary Python, but the `MutableSequence.__getitem__` calls seems to dwarf everything in that module in the profile results.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-11-02 15:42 UTC

~~~
 47     45174    0.803    0.000    5.808    0.000 typing.py:989(__getitem__)
 48     37682    0.708    0.000    4.785    0.000 {built-in method builtins.__build_class__}
 49     45174    0.619    0.000    3.547    0.000 abc.py:132(__new__)
 50    135522    0.614    0.000    0.614    0.000 _weakrefset.py:36(__init__)
 51   1166013    0.606    0.000    0.606    0.000 {built-in method builtins.getattr}

**Steve Howell** · 2018-11-02 15:43 UTC

I can fix this for `fenced_code.py`, but I wonder if this contributes to slow startup for Django.

**Greg Price** · 2018-11-02 17:43 UTC

Hmm interesting.

Would you paste the header for those columns? It's been a few months at the least since I've looked at a Python profile :wink:

**Greg Price** · 2018-11-02 17:44 UTC

And what's the denominator here -- how much in relative terms does this end up contributing to the total runtime? I'm also curious about what workload that's for; I don't know what "the import program" is.

**Greg Price** · 2018-11-02 17:49 UTC

I know there's been some work recently on reducing the runtime cost of type annotations -- fundamentally there's no good reason for them to have any runtime cost, beyond perhaps keeping a bit more metadata about the code in memory. The Instagram/FB folks have been especially keen on driving that work :smile: 

Some of that work is in PEPs that require language change, so we'll get the results in maybe 3.8 (not sure of the status).

I think some of it is also in the typing module itself. Which, on Python 3.5+, comes from the stdlib. What Python version did you use for this profile?

**Steve Howell** · 2018-11-02 17:57 UTC

The 5.8s is total time, and I  confirmed the difference with `time` when I fixed the inner classes.  Granted this is for a few thousand messages, and there were a couple inner classes getting reinterpreted on every message.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-11-02 17:57 UTC

I'm only on 3.5.2

**Steve Howell** · 2018-11-02 17:59 UTC

The import program renders every single message using the markdown processor, and then part of that parsing is `zerver/lib/bugdown/fenced_code.py`, which is very recursive.  The recursive nature of the parser drove the decision to use inner classes, but it wasn't a huge thing to fix, so the proximal issue is solved.  I'm more concerned about big picture stuff, like loading the app, where we possibly have death by a thousand cuts.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-11-02 18:02 UTC

The 6s overhead of mypy was in the context of about a 30s-90s overall workload.  (I have been fixing bigger issues with the import program--mostly unnecessary queries--so as I resolved those the mypy thing became a more obvious bottleneck.)

**Greg Price** · 2018-11-02 18:11 UTC

Ah I see, "import" as in importing data for a realm.

**Greg Price** · 2018-11-02 18:13 UTC

All of this is good reason to use an up-to-date version of Python, I think.

**Greg Price** · 2018-11-02 18:19 UTC

OK, and specifically we can get the benefit of the complete solution starting in Python 3.7, by writing
```
from __future__ import annotations
```
See [PEP 563](https://www.python.org/dev/peps/pep-0563/).

**Greg Price** · 2018-11-02 18:22 UTC

I think Python 3.6 and/or 3.7 also have improvements to `typing` that make things like `MutableSequence[str]` a lot faster, as they should be anyway.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-11-02 18:40 UTC

Do you happen to know which version we're running in  prod?

**Greg Price** · 2018-11-02 18:42 UTC

We use the system Python, so on Xenial it looks like that's 3.5.1.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-11-02 18:59 UTC

Anders did some testing a while back and determined overall Python 3.6/3.7 is even slower than 3.5 for another metric we care about (Python startup time, which impacts downtime when we do a server restart)

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-11-02 18:59 UTC

Let's open an issue for "Upgrade to Python 3.7" and make a note about this as a potential benefit/thing to do there, and then get back to optimizing the database perf stuff :)

**Neil Pilgrim (neiljp)** · 2018-11-04 00:02 UTC

This is interesting, as my recent reading of general changes in 3.7 seemed to suggest that startup time was improved - though of course each case is different...

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-11-05 02:35 UTC

Well, it might be that 3.6 was worse and 3.7 was better than 3.6 but still slower than 3.5; we just compared 3.5 to 3.7 for importing Zulip...

I found the linting for zerver templates to be kind of annoying while trying to edit them. After doing a bit of digging around in the zulip issues, I found that they're being linted by some custom code for indentation which was failing lint tests without being very descriptive. After a bit of digging in the zulip issues and code I found that they're being linted by something called pretty_print which actually pretty prints the file and then checks against it line by line to see if they match. I then found a tool called ```pretty_print_html``` which actually does exactly what I had in mind but wasn't documented anywhere!

Would be nice if -
a) This linting was more standardized so the rules were expressly documented somewhere.
b) There was an extension that could run ```pretty_print_html``` on save in the IDE. I found [Run on Save](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=emeraldwalk.RunOnSave) that could pretty print the file every time its saved. Just jotting a note here for future reference.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-12-18 15:30 UTC

The linting rules basically come down to using four-space indents.  If you do reasonable things in your editor like convert-tabs-to-spaces and set the tab width to 4, you will almost never encounter these errors.  The Zulip-based pretty-printer has some flexibility about whether you indent tags inside of things like `{#if}` blocks and respects the designer's choices there.  I think we generally do **not** indent there, but it depends on how big the code blocks are and individual preferences.

## Testing strategy for typescript

*2019-02-08 to 2019-02-11 · 12 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/43-automated-testing/topic/Testing.20strategy.20for.20typescript/with/696597)*

**Tommy Ip** · 2019-02-08 14:20 UTC

Given that most JS run time errors would have been caught by the Typescript compiler, a lot of tests can be removed once the migration is done. However, during the transition phase where we have both JS and TS, I am wondering how we should approach the testing of typescript modules.
Consider the following methods of the new `Dict` typescript class:
```typescript
    private _munge(key: string): string {
        if (this._opts.fold_case) {
            key = key.toLowerCase();
        }
        return ':' + key;
    }

    has(key: string): boolean {
        return this._items.hasOwnProperty(this._munge(key));
    }
```
and the test case
```javascript
assert.equal(dict.has(undefined), false);
```
This test case is obviously not needed if it was type-checked (it wouldn't even compile), but it isn't, along with every usage of `.has()` in the codebase. The test currently outputs
```
TypeError: Cannot read property 'toLowerCase' of undefined
    at Dict._munge (/srv/zulip/static/ts/dict.ts:59:23)
```
since the `undefined` check of the original implementation is not present/wouldn't make sense in the TS version.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-02-08 15:37 UTC

Hmm, interesting problem.  There must be a standard solution to this problem, if we can figure out how to google for it.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-02-08 15:38 UTC

Is the undefined check really invalid in the TS version?  Like, what happens if we just leave that useless check in?

**Tommy Ip** · 2019-02-09 04:35 UTC

I can add undefined as a possible return type of _munge, but then the functions that takes its value wouldn't accept it since I have `strictNullCheck` enabled in the TS compiler. I guess we could make TSC less strict, but then we really lose all the benefits of having it in the first place.
[Screenshot-from-2019-02-09-12-25-18.png](https://chat.zulip.org/user_uploads/2/20/uyl6wAQPCmGauyzlK1j0rN5K/Screenshot-from-2019-02-09-12-25-18.png)

**Steve Howell** · 2019-02-09 18:29 UTC

@Tommy Ip For `Dict` I think there are several different levels of checking:
* checking keys and values is very hard to do statically (even if you swept the entire codebase, a lot of keys for dicts come from server data, so we need defensive checks at runtime)
* seeing that something actually **is** a `Dict` seems a lot easier to do statically
* given that something **is** a `Dict`, it seems easy to statically check that it's calling `set` and `get` and not `updateWidget`

**Steve Howell** · 2019-02-09 18:32 UTC

I think your explorations also suggest we might be ready for a `FoldedDict` helper function.  It could still be a `Dict` under the hood in the sort term, but we could eventually try to statically determine when folks are passing `int` values into `FoldedDict` (illegal) vs. normal `Dict` (legal).

**Steve Howell** · 2019-02-10 04:36 UTC

Do we have any recent JS-related commits that fixed a type error?  Maybe that could inform where we place our focus.

**Tommy Ip** · 2019-02-10 14:53 UTC

Ok so I have updated Dict to check keys at run time and opened #11513.

**Tommy Ip** · 2019-02-10 15:17 UTC

Why would passing an int into `FoldedDict` be illegal?

**Steve Howell** · 2019-02-10 15:20 UTC

> Why would passing an int into `FoldedDict` be illegal?
 The idea behind `FoldedDict` is that it always works with strings where we don't care about case (we "fold" case to something canonical like lowercase).  Whereas other dicts typically use int keys.

**Steve Howell** · 2019-02-10 15:21 UTC

I wouldn't worry too much about that right away.  I think the most useful thing to know is when we're using any kind of `Dict` vs. a raw JS object.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-02-11 22:07 UTC

@Tommy Ip can we do a conditional exclude to StrictNullCheck for just that line?

## code coverage reduction

*2019-02-26 to 2019-02-27 · 12 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/43-automated-testing/topic/code.20coverage.20reduction/with/708271)*

**Rohitt Vashishtha** · 2019-02-26 19:42 UTC

[This commit](https://codecov.io/gh/zulip/zulip/commit/c6da0d13cd79c6338d5a4ace8b19425dd9aa95ce) by @Anders Kaseorg dropped code coverage by 5% despite being a simple docs related commit. Why did this happen?

Commit: c6da0d13cd79c6338d5a4ace8b19425dd9aa95ce

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-02-26 20:08 UTC

@Rohitt Vashishtha what source tells you it dropped coverage by 5%?

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-02-26 20:08 UTC

Codecov's handling of coverage coming from multiple suites (frontend and backend) is really buggy, and sometimes drops the frontend suite data, which often results in in inaccurately reporting coverage drops/gains due to that.

**Rohitt Vashishtha** · 2019-02-26 20:09 UTC

[pasted image](https://chat.zulip.org/user_uploads/2/3b/mLvBYYtXRgwqOVbT8vRd8Z4R/pasted_image.png) 

This is the codecov link above.

**Rohitt Vashishtha** · 2019-02-26 20:10 UTC

I think we should prevent codecov from being able to display a build failing sign on github then?

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-02-26 22:30 UTC

Codecov doesn't seem to support doing that and actuall running, as best I could tell last I looked.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-02-26 22:31 UTC

That said, I think there is a thing we can do here.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-02-26 22:31 UTC

Because we now run both backend and frontend tests in the same suite with the circleci integration.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-02-26 22:31 UTC

So we could convert our codecov integration to do a single post, rather than their "multiple codebases" coverage feature (can't remember what they call it off the top of my head)

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-02-26 22:32 UTC

@Vishnu Ks actually, possibly all we need to do is only run the `upload_coverage_report` step on the Trusty plan (i.e. the one that runs frontend as well as backend tests)?  Do you remember why you have us uploading coverage data from all 3 builds?

**Vishnu KS** · 2019-02-27 06:25 UTC

hmm. I dont remember any specific reason for uploading the report from all three. Will just make it upload from trusty.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-02-27 16:53 UTC

Great :)

@Tim Abbott That seems like a mypy issue. However, is the fix you introduced going to now be unchecked too? Assuming we're not using django type hints yet, then `.id` is likely an `Any`?

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-03-19 17:37 UTC

@Neil Pilgrim it shouldn't be -- we have type annotations on the classes, so as long as it knows that e.g. `user` is a UserProfile, then it knows `user.realm` is a `Realm`, etc.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-03-19 17:37 UTC

The key thing is that we're fetching the UserProfile object using a function that is properly annotated.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-03-19 17:38 UTC

Django type hints would make `UserProfile.objects.get()` type functions not return an Any but instead return the actual types.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-03-19 17:38 UTC

But because we in most places fetch model objects using dedicated functions, it's not as big a problem as it would otherwise be.

Sorry if I conflated two issues:

b) All the non-automatic types have explicit `# type: Foo` annotations (given pre-python-3.6), but `.id` is an automatic field, so it probably isn't picked up as an int by mypy?

**Neil Pilgrim (neiljp)** · 2019-03-19 17:46 UTC

I agree that the wrappers are good for converting types nicely.

I believe it would help new contributors would be to introduce them to the word "stub" in case they aren't familiar, and also show the error that would imply that they're trying to call a function that hasn't been stubbed (and so that that they know they'll have to stub it themselves) an example of this is that if I didn't have:

TypeError: search_string_display.append is not a function

## test-backend parallelization

*2019-05-02 to 2019-05-23 · 89 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/43-automated-testing/topic/test-backend.20parallelization/with/738633)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-05-02 17:57 UTC

test-backend now runs using the number of CPUs detected on your system, which will hopefully make it a lot faster with folks who have a lot of CPUs on their system (the previous default was 4).

Thanks to @Wyatt Hoodes for the work on this.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-05-02 18:03 UTC

There are a few things everyone should be on the lookout for:
* OOM kills for folks who have a lot of CPUs but not much RAM
* New nondeterministic test failures due to state leakage with running at high levels of parallelism.  I definitely have seen a few weird ones related to i18n that I haven't tracked down.

Also, it's probably worth a few folks experimenting with comparing `time ./tools/test-backend` vs. `time ./tools/test-backend --parallel=4` to see the impact and post results here, to check if this causes issues for anyone or if it's uniformly an improvement.

In theory, that shouldn't be possible with well-behaved code, since Django runs each test case inside a transaction, and rolls back the transaction after every test.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-05-03 20:43 UTC

`test-backend test_bugdown zerver.tests.test_events.EventsRegisterTest.test_add_attachment` fails!

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-05-03 20:44 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-05-03 20:44 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-05-03 20:45 UTC

Reading that test class, we find that it only has one test function that works with realm patterns, and we can see that
`test-backend zerver.tests.test_bugdown.BugdownTest.test_realm_patterns zerver.tests.test_events.EventsRegisterTest.test_add_attachment` still fails!

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-05-03 20:47 UTC

Aha!  Reading the code of for how we fetch realm filters in `zerver/lib/events.py`, I notice this code:
```
# We have a per-process cache to avoid doing 1000 remote cache queries during page load              
per_request_realm_filters_cache = {}  # type: Dict[int, List[Tuple[str, str, int]]]                  
                                                                                                     
def realm_in_local_realm_filters_cache(realm_id: int) -> bool:                                       
    return realm_id in per_request_realm_filters_cache                                               
                                                                                                     
def realm_filters_for_realm(realm_id: int) -> List[Tuple[str, str, int]]:                            
    if not realm_in_local_realm_filters_cache(realm_id):                                             
        per_request_realm_filters_cache[realm_id] = realm_filters_for_realm_remote_cache(realm_id)   
    return per_request_realm_filters_cache[realm_id]                                                 
```

So what's almost certainly happening here is that the `BugdownTest.test_realm_patterns` code is accessing Bugdown with some realm filters configured, which puts things into that cache, but the cache isn't cleaned up at the end of the test.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-05-03 20:48 UTC

Generally, in-process caches can be a source of this sort of bug, because in theory they should be cleared at the end of each test.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-05-03 20:49 UTC

Indeed, the other similar caches we have are cleaned up in the standard `ZulipTestCase` code:
```
class ZulipTestCase(TestCase):                                                                       
    # Ensure that the test system just shows us diffs                                                
    maxDiff = None  # type: Optional[int]                                                            
                                                                                                     
    def tearDown(self) -> None:                                                                      
        super().tearDown()                                                                           
        # Important: we need to clear event queues to avoid leaking data to future tests.            
        clear_client_event_queues_for_testing()                                                      
        clear_supported_auth_backends_cache()                                                        
```

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-05-03 20:49 UTC

But this one isn't.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-05-03 20:49 UTC

We do have a function, `flush_per_request_caches`, that is designed to flush these caches.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-05-03 20:49 UTC

```
def flush_per_request_caches() -> None:                                                              
    global per_request_display_recipient_cache                                                       
    per_request_display_recipient_cache = {}                                                         
    global per_request_realm_filters_cache                                                           
    per_request_realm_filters_cache = {}                                                             
```

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-05-03 20:50 UTC

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2019-05-23 09:35 UTC

Okay, I think I know the issue:

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2019-05-23 09:42 UTC

First `` move_expired_messages_to_archive(realm) `` is called and then `` move_expired_user_messages_to_archive ``. They simply run custom SQL queries, in order:
```sql
    INSERT INTO zerver_archivedmessage ({dst_fields}, archive_timestamp)
    SELECT {src_fields}, '{archive_timestamp}'
    FROM zerver_message
    INNER JOIN zerver_userprofile ON zerver_message.sender_id = zerver_userprofile.id
    LEFT JOIN zerver_archivedmessage ON zerver_archivedmessage.id = zerver_message.id
    WHERE zerver_userprofile.realm_id = {realm_id}
          AND  zerver_message.pub_date < '{check_date}'
          AND zerver_archivedmessage.id is NULL
```
then
```sql
    INSERT INTO zerver_archivedusermessage ({dst_fields}, archive_timestamp)
    SELECT {src_fields}, '{archive_timestamp}'
    FROM zerver_usermessage
    INNER JOIN zerver_userprofile ON zerver_usermessage.user_profile_id = zerver_userprofile.id
    INNER JOIN zerver_archivedmessage ON zerver_archivedmessage.id = zerver_usermessage.message_id
    LEFT JOIN zerver_archivedusermessage ON zerver_archivedusermessage.id = zerver_usermessage.id
    LEFT JOIN zerver_message ON zerver_usermessage.message_id = zerver_message.id
    WHERE zerver_userprofile.realm_id = {realm_id}
        AND  zerver_message.pub_date < '{check_date}'
        AND zerver_archivedusermessage.id is NULL
```

When we have a crossrealm message(from realm A to B), and the iteration over realms for archiving first goes to realm B, what happens:

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2019-05-23 09:45 UTC

First query has `` INNER JOIN zerver_userprofile ON zerver_message.sender_id = zerver_userprofile.id `` as well as `` WHERE zerver_userprofile.realm_id = {realm_id} ``,  so zerver_userprofile.realm_id in each row returned by this select, is the sender's realm (which is A). So this message won't be archived by this query. It'll get archived later, when the iteration starts archiving realm B.

Now, the second query (which archives usermessages for realm B) has `` INNER JOIN zerver_archivedmessage ON zerver_archivedmessage.id = zerver_usermessage.message_id ``. So the Message corresponding to the UserMessage has to already be in the archive, for the given UserMessage to be returned by this select query.  But the first query didn't archive the Message, so the recipient's UserMessage gets lost.

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2019-05-23 09:47 UTC

I hope this reasoning makes sense. Now to figure out a solution to this :thinking:

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2019-05-23 10:48 UTC

Correction (can't edit anymore): Of course I meant " zerver_userprofile.realm_id in each row returned by this select, is the sender's realm (which is A **for this cross realm message**). So this message won't be archived by this query. It'll get archived later, when the iteration starts archiving realm **A**."

## nondeterminsitic test failures

*2019-05-03 to 2019-05-10 · 4 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/43-automated-testing/topic/nondeterminsitic.20test.20failures/with/738934)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-05-03 19:02 UTC

Now that @Mateusz Mandera fixed our Bionic issue, we should try to fix the others.  
* There are a couple casper failures we see occasionally; the main one is https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/stream/43-automated-testing/topic/Casper.20tests.20failing.20inconsistently/near/737488.  Theoretically, the way we're supposed to debug these is using the screenshots that Casper captures when it gets an error (to see what the screen looked like in the failure case).  I think when we migrated the frontend test suite from Travis CI to CircleCI, we lost that.
* We have a few `test-backend` failures as well.  The main one is that is some sort of i18n bug that causes `test-backend` with high levels of parallelism to fail sometimes (e.g. 6, for me).  My best idea for how to debug this is to add code to the `setUp` and `tearDown` methods of `ZulipTestCase` to print out the language, and see .  There may also be one in `add_missing_messages` that seems to be related to provision generating a different number of users; we should just find a traceback for it and add a print statement just before the error so we can see what's different.
* We should work on moving our `production` test suite, which tests `build-release-tarball` and the production installer, to CircleCI; Travis CI is just a much more flaky platform.  While we're at it, we likely will want to migrate the platform from `trusty` to `bionic`.  @Vishnu Ks has useful experience from the original CircleCI port that may help with this project.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-05-03 19:08 UTC

I think it's be really valuable for these projects to happen; the backend piece might be a good project for you @Mateusz Mandera since you just got a bunch of experience with debugging this sort of thing.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-05-03 19:09 UTC

These nondeterministic failures are all over a year old; if we can clear them out, we'd get back into the really happy state where CI always passes if your code is correct, which has a subtle but huge impact on productivity.  (Greg and I actually led the project at Dropbox to solve this problem there)

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-05-10 16:40 UTC

So, I think we've done pretty good work on clearing out the `test-backend` nondeterministic failures.  The next big things that we should do are:
* Fix our nondeterministic casper test failures.  
* Migrate our `production` suite to test the installer experience on Ubuntu Bionic in CircleCI (probably higher priority because we also want to EOL Trusty support, and we can't do that until this happens)

Is anyone interested in these projects?  Both will likely require some disciplined work over a few weeks, but they're also really important to the project.

(zulip-py3-venv) tabbott@coset:~/zulip$ git grep make_import_output_dir

zerver/tests/test_mattermost_importer.py:        output_dir = self.make_import_output_dir("mattermost")
zerver/tests/test_mattermost_importer.py:        output_dir = self.make_import_output_dir("mattermost")

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-05-03 20:11 UTC

Which computes a path determined entirely by the argument:
```
    def make_import_output_dir(self, exported_from: str) -> str:                                     
        output_dir = "var/test-{}-import".format(exported_from)                                      
        self.rm_tree(output_dir)                                                                     
        os.makedirs(output_dir, exist_ok=True)                                                       
        return output_dir                                                                            
```

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-05-03 20:11 UTC

So that obviously is going to be the same path, and if the right two tests are running simultaneously, is going to crash in the way we saw.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-05-03 20:11 UTC

## test_email_mirror.py and high parallelism?

*2019-05-10 to 2019-05-10 · 3 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/43-automated-testing/topic/test_email_mirror.2Epy.20and.20high.20parallelism.3F/with/740948)*

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2019-05-10 12:01 UTC

I'm wondering if there could be a risk of race conditions with the way those tests are made, that could perhaps demonstrate if we increase parallelism?

The general scheme there is that in each test, we do:
```python
user_profile = ...  # get a user_profile subscribed to stream Denmark
incoming_valid_message = ....   # make an email object
process_message(incoming_valid_message)  # pass it into the email mirror, it gets posted to stream Denmark
message = most_recent_message(user_profile)  # we assume this should be this message from above
# assert stuff about "message"
```

if a bunch of these tests are run simultaneously, couldn't things get mixed up, and a test, when grabbing most_recent_message will obtain a message passed into the mirror by another test, thus leading to a fail when it starts asserting its own assumptions about it?

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-05-10 16:20 UTC

@Mateusz Mandera good question!  The way Django's test runner works is that it runs each test case within a database transaction, and rolls back the transaction at the end of the test.  Because things you do inside a transaction are not visible to other processes until the transaction completes, effectively, this should mean that stuff done in the database can't impact other processes.

Additionally, we've setup the parallel test runner so that each process has its own copy of the database; this is what this block of output is about (Which we should probably suppress or something since it's kinda spammy):
```

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-05-10 16:24 UTC

Because we have similar generic solutions for access to memcached and other services, our sources of nondeterministic test failures are generally limited to places where tests or code they are testing are storing data in a place other than those, e.g.:
* In-process memory (can impact how later tests work), e.g. an in-memory cache.  This was the cause of two of the bugs we fixed this week.
* The filesystem (can impact other test threads or later tests), which was why our data export tests had parallelism failures (a few tests always used the same path for their export).
* Parts of the database that do change even when you roll back a transaction (e.g. hardcoding the ID of a message) -- because while rows get removed when you roll back a transaction, sequences (i.e. the the internal structure used to generate the next message ID) do not get reset.

**Vinit Singh** · 2019-06-13 23:42 UTC

I'm sure this has already been noticed. Travis CI has a flake and the CI fails with the following message:
`The command "mispipe "tools/ci/setup-$TEST_SUITE" ts" failed and exited with 1 during .`

[[1]](https://travis-ci.org/zulip/zulip/builds/545506494?utm_source=github_status&utm_medium=notification) [[2]](https://travis-ci.org/zulip/zulip/builds/545482506?utm_source=github_status&utm_medium=notification)

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-06-14 05:09 UTC

Yeah, I think it's actually not a flake, it's just failing in master.  https://travis-ci.org/zulip/zulip.  I pinged @Puneeth Chaganti since from reading the output I think 86840adda5120be318ee3edd49d1709040cf7226 is the root cause; hopefully someone can debug as I need to go to bed.

**Puneeth Chaganti** · 2019-06-14 06:12 UTC

I've a fix at #12574. The problem turned out to be that Travis does a shallow clone, and `git describe --tags` fails with the shallow clone.

**Puneeth Chaganti** · 2019-06-14 06:17 UTC

I'm not sure why the [original PR](https://travis-ci.org/zulip/zulip/builds/542696651) didn't fail, though.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-06-14 17:04 UTC

Yeah, that's what surprises me -- I would have expected this to fail everywhere.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-06-14 17:04 UTC

Oh, maybe it's some detail having to do with how shallow the clone was happening to result in a reasonable `git describe` result or not, or something.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-06-14 17:04 UTC

Still not what I'd have expected.

**Puneeth Chaganti** · 2019-06-15 02:00 UTC

I think the fact that 2.0.4 tag was incorrect on upstream, meant that git describe worked for that commit, but stopped working a few commits later. Travis gets a shallow clone with last 50 commits.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-06-16 23:45 UTC

Ahh, yes, that makes sense, great.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-06-16 23:46 UTC

@Puneeth Chaganti as a sidenote, I've discovered a problem with our code for caching the Git version when using `upgrade-zulip-from-git`; we don't use a `git fetch` command version in `upgrade-zulip-from-git` that will actually get tags....

**Puneeth Chaganti** · 2019-06-17 02:50 UTC

## Delete `future` dependecy altogether

*2019-10-10 to 2019-10-14 · 10 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/43-automated-testing/topic/Delete.20.60future.60.20dependecy.20altogether/with/791009)*

**Rafid Aslam** · 2019-10-10 01:57 UTC

Currently we're commenting `future` dependency in requirements.txt files with `tools/update-locked-requirements` so it won't be installed, but we have to upgrade the version number and the hashes by running `tools/update-locked-requirements` every time `future` got a version bump from its developers. I think deleting the line for `future` in requirements.txt files with `tools/update-locked-requirements` altogether instead of just commenting it would be nice?

It's breaking the circleCI tests now.. https://circleci.com/gh/refeed/zulip/9?utm_campaign=vcs-integration-link&utm_medium=referral&utm_source=github-build-link

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-10-10 21:21 UTC

@Rafid Aslam hmm, yeah, I'd be fine with migrating that.

**Rafid Aslam** · 2019-10-11 00:56 UTC

So, I think we want to create a  ticket for that? I can work on this

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-10-11 01:00 UTC

@Rafid Aslam yeah, go for it.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-10-11 01:00 UTC

I fixed it temporarily by just updating values.

**Rafid Aslam** · 2019-10-11 02:00 UTC

alright, I will create the ticket later

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2019-10-11 20:15 UTC

Why don’t we just include `future` uncommented? I’m having a hard time figuring out why it was excluded in the first place. The original comment was “pip-tools bug; future, futures are obsolete in python3”, which is wrong on both counts. It’s not a pip-tools bug that pip-compile included the dependencies that packages specify. And while `futures` (the concurrency primitive) doesn’t work on Python 3, `future` (the version compatibility layer) is designed to work on 2 and 3. It happens that the packages we have that declare a `future` dependency use it in such a way that it’s not needed on Python 3, and I think they all have pending commits to drop it or include it conditionally on Python 2, but it wouldn’t harm anything just by being there.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-10-11 21:12 UTC

Yeah, that's definitely better; I'd missed that the history was it was the original 8aaf34d06d7c73123ad88755dc59edb76f409a94.

**Rafid Aslam** · 2019-10-13 02:04 UTC

oh okay, I actually thought that it's better to remove it altogether since it will save a bit of work in the future (not in the `future` package ;)) like changing the `future` version (they don't update their package quite frequently though), bumping up the provision version, etc, but I was late to come here to say that and it's a bit ..trivial.. anyway yes, it won't harm anything

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2019-10-14 01:55 UTC

No it's definitely less work to treat it like all our other requirements than to keep around special code to remove this one specific requirement for no reason in particular. We update our locked requirements on our own terms.

## nondeterministic failure

*2019-10-28 to 2019-10-30 · 13 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/43-automated-testing/topic/nondeterministic.20failure/with/794598)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-10-28 23:22 UTC

Just saw this failure in CI, our first backend nondeterministic failure in a while:
https://circleci.com/gh/zulip/zulip/31965

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2019-10-29 00:18 UTC

So it's in this block, that processes 5 pre-generated incoming email mirror messages, with rate limiting settings to accept 2 messages per 10 seconds - so it should accept 2 messages:
```
        with simulated_queue_client(lambda: fake_client):
            start_time = time.time()
            with patch('time.time', return_value=start_time):
                worker = queue_processors.MirrorWorker()
                worker.setup()
                worker.start()
                # Of the first 5 messages, only 2 should be processed
                # (the rest being rate-limited):
                self.assertEqual(mock_mirror_email.call_count, 2)
```

```
** Test is TOO slow: zerver.tests.test_queue_worker.WorkerTest.test_mirror_worker_rate_limiting (21.159 s)
```
With this (very strange) long runtime of the test it looks as if 2 emails got accepted, then things were going so slow that 10 seconds passed and another 2-message batch ended up going through. But I don't know if that's actually what happened, because with the ``time.time`` mocking, it shouldn't matter how much time is actually passing during the test. Strange.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2019-10-29 00:21 UTC

Are we actually polling `time.time` somewhere, or is there a `time.sleep` or similar that it’s racing against?

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2019-10-29 00:24 UTC

``time.time()`` is what the main rate-limiting login in ``lib/rate_limiter.py`` uses to check the current time and decide if the limits have been hit.

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2019-10-29 00:25 UTC

the rate limiting gets called in MIrrorWorker's ``consume``:
```
@assign_queue('email_mirror')
class MirrorWorker(QueueProcessingWorker):
    def consume(self, event: Mapping[str, Any]) -> None:
        rcpt_to = event['rcpt_to']
        if not is_missed_message_address(rcpt_to):
            # Missed message addresses are one-time use, so we don't need
            # to worry about emails to them resulting in message spam.
            recipient_realm = extract_and_validate(rcpt_to)[0].realm
            try:
                rate_limit_mirror_by_realm(recipient_realm)
            except RateLimited:
                msg = email.message_from_string(event["message"])
                logger.warning("MirrorWorker: Rejecting an email from: %s "
                               "to realm: %s - rate limited."
                               % (msg['From'], recipient_realm.name))
                return

        mirror_email(email.message_from_string(event["message"]),
                     rcpt_to=rcpt_to, pre_checked=True)
```

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-10-29 19:07 UTC

Ahh, OK, and I see that test oddly ran for like 21s.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-10-29 19:07 UTC

So I think the fix here is we need to mock `time.time()` like we do in other tests.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-10-29 19:08 UTC

(Obviously there's something wrong with the server this was running on that caused this relatively small bit of code to take 20s of latency, but it's still a bug in our test)

**Ray Kraesig** · 2019-10-29 20:16 UTC

> So I think the fix here is we need to mock `time.time()` like we do in other tests.
Unless things have changed in the last few years, I have to strongly suggest *not* doing this, here or elsewhere. I recall an issue at Dropbox that resulted from exactly this: there are (or were) Python-stdlib-internal (and/or test-harness-internal) things which depend on `time.time`, and which can express their displeasure in obscure and pernicious ways if it's mocked out directly.

**Ray Kraesig** · 2019-10-29 20:22 UTC

(IIRC, the fix in most cases was to change `import time` to something like `import time as get_time from time` in the module being tested, and then mock out `relevant.module.get_time` rather than `time.time` itself.)

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-10-29 22:38 UTC

I think we can mock time via `mock.patch(zerver.lib.foo.time)`, i.e. only mocking references to time called from that module.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2019-10-30 03:53 UTC

Only if you replace the entire `time` module that way. If you replace the `time` function with `mock.patch('zerver.lib.foo.time.time')`, that’s just another name for `mock.patch('time.time')`.

**Steve Howell** · 2019-10-30 18:49 UTC

One thing that sometimes makes sense is to extract a function in the real code that hides most of the time logic.  Something like `secs_since_last_event` or something.  And then you can mock the helper function, rather than `time.time`.  (Or sometimes just add a one-liner `get_time = ...` for pure testing expediency.)

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2019-12-09 22:06 UTC

I try to use Black everywhere I can, but its [failure to preserve the semantics of mypy `# type: ignore` comments](https://github.com/psf/black/issues/195) complicates applying it to Zulip directly. There are manual workarounds we could use, like putting them in Black `# fmt: off` blocks if necessary. I would like to do this eventually.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-12-10 00:23 UTC

My view is that we spend fairly little time at this point on Python formatting (in part because our linters do a decent job of teaching it to new contributors), so it's not worth dealing with issues like that mypy bug to get the potential benefits of something like Black (because they're small for our project).

I also expect that eventually we'll switch to Black or something similar, but I don't feel any hurry to do so (i.e. I guess we're largely hoping someone else fixes Black's mypy-related bugs).

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-07-07 18:12 UTC

Personally I find hanging indents a lot more readable and convenient to deal with for certain classes of cases (often where one only gets to 2 lines and not using them with Black's algorithm leads to it exploding to 6 lines), and I am to use them only for cases where they achieve that.  

The problem is that concept where there are judgement calls is not really compatible with the algorithm-based approach.  I think it's possible one could refine an algorithm to define when "using hanging indents makes things nicer" and do so in those cases, but it's not something Black has invested in (or that I particularly expect them to).

> What I’ve literally been doing is running Black on the file, copying the reformatted signature out, undoing Black, pasting the reformatted signature back in, and moving on.

I suspected this!  Several of your recent refactoring PRs have had obviously Black style changes, which I decided not to complain about since it was only in a few places and we're having this discussion anyway. :)

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-07-07 18:17 UTC

I feel like I would be reasonably happy to adopt something like black conceptually; and it may be that the benefits outweigh the downsides of making a bunch of 1-2 line blocks of code that were pretty readable in their original form (often list comprehensions) into giant 7-line things that I find harder to process because they take up so much vertical real estate.

I wonder if we should do an experiment looking at how often in those cases a bit of pre-refactoring to extract named variables or whatnot can improve the readability and avoid corner cases where the Black formatting ends up not being happy.  Because if the answer is that usually one can "work around" cases of the automated formatting being non-ideal by doing something that would improve the code regardless of formatting, that would make me feel a lot better than if in most cases that sort of "work around" would be making the codebase worse in the name of happier autoformatting.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-07-07 18:19 UTC

The other experiment that I was thinking we might want to try is integrating running black on subsets of the codebase, like `scripts/` and `tools/,` that largely don't have many complex expressions and so there's unlikely to be things we want to rethink.

(BTW have we compared its performance to our other linters?  I'd imagine it should be fine but we should check off that consideration)

* We verify we're happy with performance and the zulint integration etc. with running it against `scripts/` and `tools/`; that's also the codebase we backport the most to so the best to migrate first.
* We look at examples, consider settings (E.g. is 100 characters right?) over the rest of this week in parallel with the last batch of pre-release bug fixing.
* If we decide to go with Black, we merge that change as soon before the release as we feel is appropriate for QA on a "whitespace-only" change so we don't make every backport a merge conflict.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-07-08 22:22 UTC

One thing I'd be sad about with moving to Black is that it doesn't allow configuring blank lines between functions.  I suppose that'd be an easy fork to make.

The PEP-8 rule is that within a class, you do 1 blank line between methods, but it wants 2 blank lines between module-level functions.  This rule works great if a lot of your code is in classes, but almost none of Zulip's is, and the result is that the PEP-8 style wastes a lot of vertical space.  YAPF makes this configurable, and I'd certainly want to set that option with black if we could.

## node tests cruft

*2020-02-08 to 2020-02-08 · 3 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/43-automated-testing/topic/node.20tests.20cruft/with/815539)*

**Steve Howell** · 2020-02-08 13:03 UTC

@Anders Kaseorg This might be something in your wheelhouse.  The node tests undoubtedly have some cruft with `set_global` or `zrequire` statements that aren't actually needed by tests.  Some of them were probably cargo-culted and never needed in the first place, and others may have never been cleaned up after code cleanups to the real code.  We could probably script something brute-force that just tries to remove one at a time and complain if the test still passes.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-02-08 13:08 UTC

Some stats:
* tests take 21s to run
* there are 116 JS files
* average JS file takes 180ms
* there are 513 zrequire statements we could possibly eliminate
* In theory we could test all 513 eliminations in 92s

Realistically the script would probably take longer than 92s to run, unless we could consolidate all the node startup overhead up front.  But even if you assumed 2s overhead per trial, I think the whole script would run in about twenty minutes.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-02-08 13:20 UTC

There are probably some edge cases where multiple unnecessary zrequires in the same file don't get sniffed out with a naive remove-one-at-a-time approach, but I would guess we'd catch a lot of things.

*2020-02-17 to 2020-02-18 · 13 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/43-automated-testing/topic/.2Ecoverage.2Exxxxx.20file.20not.20getting.20cleaned.20up/with/817557)*

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2020-02-17 15:43 UTC

Lately I've noticed that ``test-backend --coverage`` leaves behind a file like ``.coverage.001e00969316.136794.312744`` and doesn't clean it up. The biggest issue with it is that it somehow pollutes future runs and I've gotten false claims of full coverage after changing code and to get correct result I have to delete this leftover file

**Steve Howell** · 2020-02-17 15:47 UTC

Interesting!  I was noticing it too and thought the remedy was to simply add it to `.gitignore`.  I'm surprised it's actually polluting results.  We should obviously fix that.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-02-17 15:48 UTC

I am guessing the correct solution is this:
* add it to `.gitignore`
* remove it at the **beginning** of running `./tools/test-backend` (so we don't have to worry about previous runs failing to clean it up)

**Steve Howell** · 2020-02-17 15:49 UTC

I guess I would actually try to remove it at both the beginning and end of running the tests.  (And I'd still add it to gitignore, since it just seems like something we'd never check in, even if we make the tool better about cleaning up after itself.)

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-03-17 22:34 UTC

I ran a local `test-run-dev` loop and reproduced a hang. The reason I observed was that `run-dev` exited but `process_queue` did not. Killing `process_queue` allowed `test-run-dev` to continue (“successfully”, even).

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-03-17 23:33 UTC

Hmm, do we know why `process_queue` was hanging rather than exiting properly?

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-03-17 23:59 UTC

One possible explanation is that `test-run-dev` sent `SIGINT` to `run-dev` before `run-dev` installed the janky signal handler that sends `SIGTERM` to the process group on exit. That scenario leaves everything running, not just `process_queue`. It is a clear bug, though.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-03-18 00:25 UTC

There must be some period at startup during which `process_queue` ignores `SIGTERM`.

```
2020-03-18 00:21:26 thumbor:WARNING Caught signal: 15. Shutting down server.
2020-03-18 00:21:26.932 INFO [process_queue] 17 queue worker threads were launched
```

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-03-18 00:27 UTC

`process_queue.py` does setup signal handlers; it doesn't seem like it does much beyond importing things before that though.

tools/stop-run-dev:    os.killpg(pid, signal.SIGTERM)
zerver/management/commands/process_queue.py:            signal.signal(signal.SIGTERM, signal_handler)
zerver/tornado/event_queue.py:        signal.signal(signal.SIGTERM, lambda signum, stack: sys.exit(1))
```

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-03-18 00:38 UTC

`manage.py` forks itself within `django.core.management.execute_from_command_line` to add `--traceback` to its `argv`. I bet the `killpg` is racing with that.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-03-18 00:43 UTC

Ooh, interesting.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-03-18 00:57 UTC

No, not within `execute_from_command_line`. But it’s forking somewhere.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-03-18 01:01 UTC

Within `django.utils.autoreloader.run_with_reloader`.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-03-18 01:02 UTC

Which also installs a ridiculous `SIGTERM` handler.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-03-18 03:33 UTC

Well, that's consistent with the Django 2.x upgrade being responsible, since they rewrote `django.utils.autoreloader` in there.

## Faster Casper Testing

*2020-03-01 to 2020-03-31 · 9 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/43-automated-testing/topic/Faster.20Casper.20Testing/with/824407)*

**Rohitt Vashishtha** · 2020-03-01 19:33 UTC

We recently added support for interactively running casper tests without having to restart the test server again. This makes the feedback cycle on casper tests significantly faster in the dev environment.

You can try it out using `tools/test-js-with-casper --interactive <list of tests to run>`. After that, once the server has been started, each time you press 'Return' on the input prompt, the specified tests will be run without shutting down the server at the end of each run.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-03-01 19:36 UTC

This will be really helpful!  And I think we can easily use the same code for any solution that replaces Casper, too.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-03-31 15:05 UTC

We now call the option `--loop` here.  So you can say something like `./tools/test-js-with-casper --loop 5 04 07` to run the 04/07 tests five times in a loop.  Each loop will terminate immediately if you encounter a failure.  And then after each loop of tests, you can start a new loop with a new count.  An example session might be something like this:

- launch with `--loop 10` to try to reproduce a test flake (or verify that it doesn't flake for you)
- get coffee
- come back and see that the test failed
- modify the test code
- say "3" when it asks you how many loops to run
- see it fairly quickly confirm your fix works three times
- refactor your test code a bit
- say "10" to run 10 loops
- get more coffee
- etc.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-03-31 15:08 UTC

@Rohitt Vashishtha Can you confirm the following?
* after each loop, you can modify the Casper tests themselves (including the `common` library), and the next loop will use your updated code
* the database will **not** be reset between runs (fortunately, most Casper tests don't rely on a completely clean database)

If you modify the app itself, I don't remember off the top of my head whether the server will reflect those changes.

**Rohitt Vashishtha** · 2020-03-31 15:29 UTC

After each loop-set we can modify the code in case of success.

**Rohitt Vashishtha** · 2020-03-31 15:31 UTC

An easy natural way to stop the loop would be to give obviously incorrect code and then reach the 'Press "q" to quit or enter number of loops:' prompt. We *could* intercept CTRL-C in our python script and stop the currently running test loop but I don't think this should cause too many issues.

**Rohitt Vashishtha** · 2020-03-31 15:32 UTC

And yes, the database will not reset between runs.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-03-31 15:39 UTC

I don't think it would be too difficult to insert some code between loops to at least reset the database fixtures.  I thought about adding control-c handling while I was working on this, but I think we mainly have the removed the need for it.
- if it fails on trial 3 / 10 or whatever, the loop just immediately stops
- if you expect it to succeed and just want to look at the output, just run 1 loop
- if you want to verify it doesn't flake, just let it run 10 loops or whatever (and it will still fail fast)

**Steve Howell** · 2020-03-31 15:39 UTC

I guess the only other thing you might want to do between loops is change the list of tests to run, which seems feasible enough to implement.

## RUNNING_INSIDE_TORNADO hack in TestCommandsCanStart

*2020-03-09 to 2020-03-11 · 4 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/43-automated-testing/topic/RUNNING_INSIDE_TORNADO.20hack.20in.20TestCommandsCanStart/with/828923)*

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2020-03-09 13:48 UTC

Old discussion about this, for context: https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/stream/43-automated-testing/topic/test.20flake/near/151711
Due to the issue discussed at the link above, we have the hack at the bottom of this test:
```
    @slow("Aggregate of runs dozens of individual --help tests")
    def test_management_commands_show_help(self) -> None:
        with stdout_suppressed():
            for command in self.commands:
                with self.subTest(management_command=command):
                    with self.assertRaises(SystemExit):
                        call_command(command, '--help')
        # zerver/management/commands/runtornado.py sets this to True;
        # we need to reset it here.  See #3685 for details.
        settings.RUNNING_INSIDE_TORNADO = False
```

My question is, in `runtornado.py`, do we have to set ``RUNNING_INSIDE_TORNADO = True`` at command startup? Can't we move that (and perhaps the imports if necessary) into the ``handle()`` function and thus avoid the test triggering that code, and allowing us to remove this hack?

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-03-09 20:47 UTC

@Mateusz Mandera yes, I think we can make that change; it likely was not possible before in that I'm guessing previous versions of the code accessed RUNNING_INSIDE_TORNADO at import time.  Though see this block comment:
```
# We must call zerver.tornado.ioloop_logging.instrument_tornado_ioloop                               
# before we import anything else from our project in order for our                                   
# Tornado load logging to work; otherwise we might accidentally import                               
# zerver.lib.queue (which will instantiate the Tornado ioloop) before                                
# this.                                                                                              
from zerver.tornado.ioloop_logging import instrument_tornado_ioloop                                  
                                                                                                     
settings.RUNNING_INSIDE_TORNADO = True                                                               
instrument_tornado_ioloop()                                                                          
```

I think it's likely we'd want to move `instrument_tornado_ioloop` as well and just confirm that other changes mean that we're no longer starting the Tornado event loop at import time in `zerver.lib.queue`.

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2020-03-11 13:41 UTC

Though all it does is
```
def instrument_tornado_ioloop() -> None:
    IOLoop.configure(InstrumentedPollIOLoop)
```
so I'm not sure why we'd need `RUNNING_INSIDE_TORNADO=True` for it?

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-03-11 20:08 UTC

Right, I don't think it does.  But that whole section of code, intended to run some things early, may be able to be moved into the `handle` method; we should try doing that and see if the idle logging still works (likely will require a small config tweak since it doesn't print in development by default).

## conditionals in tests

*2020-03-19 to 2020-03-19 · 11 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/43-automated-testing/topic/conditionals.20in.20tests/with/834054)*

**Steve Howell** · 2020-03-19 13:50 UTC

Here is a little testing anti-pattern that comes up now and then:

~~~ py
for user in result.json()['members']:
    if user['email'] == user_profile.email:
        self.assertEqual(
            user['avatar_url'],
            avatar_url(user_profile),
        )

~~~

Any time you use a loop or a conditional in a test (or, in this case, both at the same time), you are vulnerable to having your test silently succeed.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-03-19 13:57 UTC

For example, the above test **should** fail if we changed which email we sent back in the `members` payload, but instead it would just silently succeed.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-03-19 13:59 UTC

A better way to write the test code is as follows (note that both assertions run unconditionally):

~~~ py
matches = [
    user for user in result.json()['members']
    if user['email'] == user_profile.email
]

self.assertEqual(len(matches), 1)
my_user = matches[0]

self.assertEqual(
    my_user['avatar_url'],
    avatar_url(user_profile),
)
~~~

**Steve Howell** · 2020-03-19 14:00 UTC

The above pattern is a bit tedious, though, so I'm gonna write a helper for this in `ZulipTestCase`.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-03-19 14:25 UTC

Ok, here's the version with the helper:

~~~ py
my_user = self.findOne(
    result.json()['members'],
    lambda user: user['email'] == hamlet.email,
    'member for Hamlet'
)

self.assertEqual(
    my_user['avatar_url'],
    avatar_url(hamlet),
)
~~~

**Steve Howell** · 2020-03-19 14:35 UTC

Ok, just pushed https://github.com/zulip/zulip/commit/80acbb9fdff8ab1000a5c4d3d4d74ee494ad6239

**Steve Howell** · 2020-03-19 14:35 UTC

So now `findOne` is available for backend tests.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-03-19 15:39 UTC

renamed to `find_one` (we generally prefer snake_case in our Python code, even though the unit test library has javaCase)

**Abinash Maharana** · 2020-03-19 16:14 UTC

yay! All tests are passing on both the PRs now

**Steve Howell** · 2020-03-19 16:22 UTC

It turns out `find_one` is good at exposing bugs.  I went looking for easy places to add it, and found a bug with duplicate events being sent when we create new bots.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-03-19 20:44 UTC

**Steve Howell** · 2020-03-26 11:51 UTC

So my example before of adding `_finalize_payload` was just an untested, rough sketch of the idea.  Note that `_finalize_payload` doesn't return anything.  Make sure that you're actually dealing with the correct copy of these things throughout the codepath.

**Udit Krishna Chaudhary** · 2020-03-26 11:51 UTC

The changes done by `finalize_payload`on the object  are not reflected back the original object which causes the test to fail

**Steve Howell** · 2020-03-26 11:51 UTC

Right, you need to change the calling patterns so that instead of expecting mutation, you return new copies of the object to callers.

**Udit Krishna Chaudhary** · 2020-03-26 11:52 UTC

Okay
So, now each time `finalize_payload` is called, it should return a new object?

**Steve Howell** · 2020-03-26 11:54 UTC

Basically the paradigm now (on master) is this:  The caller gives `finalize_payload` an object, then `finalize_payload` mutates it in place.

The new paradigm should be this: I hand you an unfinalized object, you give me back a new, finalized object.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-03-26 11:54 UTC

(replying to Udit Krishna Chaudhary)
> Okay So, now each time `finalize_payload` is called, it should return a new object?
Correct.

**Udit Krishna Chaudhary** · 2020-03-26 11:54 UTC

**Steve Howell** · 2020-03-26 11:54 UTC

:thumbs_up:

**Steve Howell** · 2020-03-26 11:56 UTC

I think what's still gonna happen on the inside is that `_finalize_payload` itself will mutate objects (for internal performance reasons).

**Steve Howell** · 2020-03-26 11:57 UTC

So it's gonna look something like this, ideally:

~~~
def finalize_payload(unfinal_msg):
   msg = copy(unfinal_msg)
   _finalize_payload_in_place(msg)
  return msg
~~~

I think `_finalize_payload_in_place` might actually be a better name here.  It's a bit less confusing and describes what's different about it.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-03-30 11:54 UTC

Here are docs for Django tests: https://zulip.readthedocs.io/en/latest/testing/testing-with-django.html

I am kinda surprised we don't have a troubleshooting section there that mentions do-destroy, to be honest.  It's not a super common thing to need to do, since we automatically rebuild the test database any time the schema changes.  Also, when these flakes happen, it's always a problem with the test itself--the tests should never make assumptions about the date the database was created, and any test that is timing-sensitive should just explicitly set dates.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-03-30 11:56 UTC

To give an example of a timing-based test, let's say you're testing our logic that you can only edit a topic within a day of creating a message.  A flaky test might just find the last message, assume it's current, and then assert that you can edit it.  But what if the DB was created more than 24 hours ago?  You should really set the date explicitly.   (This is just a contrived example--we do this correctly in most tests, but there are still some places we overlooked in the past.)
