## blueslip (node)

*2020-04-03 to 2020-04-20 · 26 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/43-automated-testing/topic/blueslip.20.28node.29/with/846931)*

**Steve Howell** · 2020-04-03 17:00 UTC

I just pushed a couple changes to the node tests.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-04-03 17:01 UTC

You **no longer** need to do the following:

~~~
set_global('blueslip', global.make_zblueslip());
~~~

Now you can just rely on `blueslip` being in your namespace with the stubbed API.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-04-03 17:02 UTC

Also, the new API is **expect** and **reset**:

~~~
 61     blueslip.expect('error', 'Unknown user ID in presence data: 999');
 62     presence.set_info(presences, now);
 63     blueslip.reset();

**Steve Howell** · 2020-04-03 17:03 UTC

If you have open PRs, now is a good time to fetch the latest copy of master and rebase your PR.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-04-03 17:04 UTC

I also recommend running this command locally after you do the rebase:

~~~
./tools/lint --groups=frontend --skip=gitlint && ./tools/test-js-with-node --coverage

**Steve Howell** · 2020-04-03 17:06 UTC

To summarize the changes:
* make_zblueslip -> *automatic*
* set_test_data -> **expect()**
* clear_test_data -> **reset()**

**Steve Howell** · 2020-04-03 17:08 UTC

The test runner will also complain now if you say `blueslip.expect('error', 'Some error')` but then don't call any functions that lead to that error.  The goal here is to prevent misleading test code.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-04-03 17:58 UTC

Great, thanks for doing this!

**Rohitt Vashishtha** · 2020-04-08 02:35 UTC

Nice! This also makes a lot of our `assert.equal(blueslip.get_test_logs('warn').length, 1);` type assertions redundant to some extent.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-04-08 02:37 UTC

Yeah we could probably clean up a few more things here

**Rohitt Vashishtha** · 2020-04-08 02:39 UTC

Maybe.... `blueslip.expect = (type, message, count=1) => {...}`so that most of the cases where we are asserting for a single error would be easier to read.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-04-08 02:42 UTC

Isn’t this [`assert.throws`](https://nodejs.org/api/assert.html#assert_assert_throws_fn_error_message)?

**Rohitt Vashishtha** · 2020-04-08 02:55 UTC

That wouldn't work for `blueslip.warn`calls. Only `.error` and `.fatal` throw errors.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-04-08 03:05 UTC

How does *this* deal with `.fatal`? It looks like the mocked `blueslip.fatal` actually just saves the error and returns normally to caller, which the caller by definition is not expecting?

**Rohitt Vashishtha** · 2020-04-08 03:08 UTC

Right. That should be fixed as well.

**Rohitt Vashishtha** · 2020-04-08 03:10 UTC

The idea here was to have something like this for the testing flow:

```js
blueslip.expect(something);
code_to_test();
blueslip.reset();
```

I think we made the tradeoff that even if we don't stop execution on fatal, it wouldn't matter much since we aren't asserting anything on the output afterwards.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-04-08 03:19 UTC

Such a flow can’t possibly work. Imagine we’re testing `outer_function` which calls `inner_function` which checks some invariant and calls `blueslip.fatal`. Now `blueslip.fatal` returns to `inner_function`, which at best returns some garbage value to `outer_function`, and what is `outer_function` supposed to do with that? We can’t write all our code under the assumption that we might get garbage values from any function.

**Rohitt Vashishtha** · 2020-04-08 03:28 UTC

So, we'd have to switch to something like this eventually?

```diff
diff --git frontend_tests/node_tests/message_list_data.js frontend_tests/node_tests/message_list_data.js
index 04a747c660..25d14553dc 100644
--- frontend_tests/node_tests/message_list_data.js
+++ frontend_tests/node_tests/message_list_data.js
@@ -207,7 +207,9 @@ run_test('errors', () => {
     assert.equal(mld.get('bogus-id'), undefined);
 
     blueslip.expect('fatal', 'Bad message id');
-    mld._add_to_hash(['asdf']);
+    blueslip.test(() => {
+        mld._add_to_hash(['asdf'])
+    });
     assert.equal(blueslip.get_test_logs('fatal').length, 1);
```

**Rohitt Vashishtha** · 2020-04-08 03:29 UTC

Or simply using assert.throws without any wrapper for additional assertions?

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-04-08 03:33 UTC

Yeah I think we want to use plain `assert.throws` where it’s appropriate.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-04-08 13:54 UTC

I feel like `blueslip.fatal` is a somewhat unnecessary API, since we already have the ability to catch exceptions.  Doing something like `throw blueslip.FatalError('expected valid stream')` would make it more clear to the human that you're not gonna proceed further in the code.  In one place we put in the unreachable `return;`, but that unfortunately breaks line coverage if you use `assert.throws()` in the tests and change `zblueslip` to throw errors in its `blueslip.fatal` stub.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-04-08 14:05 UTC

@Rohitt Vashishtha [said](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/stream/43-automated-testing/topic/blueslip.20(node)/near/849457):
> Maybe.... `blueslip.expect = (type, message, count=1) => {...}`so that most of the cases where we are asserting for a single error would be easier to read.

Yes, I would much prefer that API for `warn` and `error`.  (Note that `error` only throws exceptions in debug mode.  Most functions try to recover gracefully, and changing our error stubs to throw exceptions would not only be less representative of production; it would also be a nuisance for line coverage.)

**Steve Howell** · 2020-04-08 15:40 UTC

I just merged a couple commits related to `fatal` and `get_test_logs(...).length`.  I think with a bit more work we could eliminate `reset`.

**Puneeth Chaganti** · 2020-04-11 17:17 UTC

```diff
diff --git a/tools/webpack.config.ts b/tools/webpack.config.ts
index 91fb671d0e..75cad3d322 100644
--- a/tools/webpack.config.ts
+++ b/tools/webpack.config.ts
@@ -50,7 +50,7 @@ export default (env?: string): webpack.Configuration[] => {
                         resolve(__dirname, '../static/shared/js'),
                         resolve(__dirname, '../static/js'),
                     ],
-                    loader: 'babel-loader',
+                    use: [cacheLoader, 'babel-loader'],
                 },
                 // Uses script-loader on minified files so we don't change global variables in them.
                 // Also has the effect of making processing these files fast
```

This seems to cut down the time for webpack in about half. 

The babel loader also comes with it's own caching, which is turned off by default. But, I guess we can just use the `cacheLoader`, instead of configuring the `babel-loader` to cache by itself?

**Steve Howell** · 2020-04-21 11:39 UTC

If folks are interested in a little challenge here, it would be nice to get it so that we can run all of our individual Casper tests in a loop, so that it's easier to track down flakes.    @Rohitt Vashishtha This might be good for you to either try or to help somebody out with.

The main options here are probably below:

* Improve **--loop**: If we can pretty quickly clear the test database between each loop through our tests in `--loop` mode, that might be the way to do.
* Make tests **idempotent** -- Some of our tests either always add new data that doesn't collide with previous data, or they clean up after themselves (i.e. test an "add" feature, then immediately test a "remove" feature), but `00-realm-creation` is an example of a test that can only run once, since you can't create the same realm twice.  A workaround here is to randomize the name of the new realm somehow.

I'm not crazy about the latter option, since you still have scenarios where the 2nd, 3rd, 4th runs aren't really dealing with pristine data, so you can still end up chasing down sort of irrelevant anomalies.  But it might be more expedient than the other option.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-04-21 11:40 UTC

BTW even though we're hoping to move away from Casper soon, I think the above work would apply equally well to puppeteer.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-04-21 11:42 UTC

(The context here is Tim's message about a page up here.  We're getting flakes with the `00` test, but I can't reproduce the flake, and it's a pain to run it in a loop, since it will always fail on the second loop for known reasons, and it's painful to loop it from a shell script, since the startup for running Casper is a long time, due to webpack and other things.)

## Circle CI production package leak

*2020-04-22 to 2020-04-24 · 51 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/43-automated-testing/topic/Circle.20CI.20production.20package.20leak/with/860134)*

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2020-04-22 15:11 UTC

Currently, we run production install after running provision on the OS in CI, this leaks installed packages from provision install to production install. 

For example suppose if I install Package `X` via provision in the OS, then this package will also be available in production install even if the production install script doesn't install it.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-04-22 15:19 UTC

That's unfortunate.  I don't know much about Circle, but is the remedy here to just run the production install in its own test instance (or whatever the proper terminology is)?

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2020-04-22 15:20 UTC

We can share files across builds via https://circleci.com/docs/2.0/workflows/#using-workspaces-to-share-data-among-jobs

**Steve Howell** · 2020-04-22 15:21 UTC

We want the opposite, though, don't we?  We want more isolation?

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2020-04-22 15:21 UTC

We are already testing after running provision in the first CI build, we can add the `build-release-tarball` script to it and save the tarball. Then in the second build we  simply run the tarball.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-04-22 15:23 UTC

Ah, make sense.  I assume building the tarball takes a significant amount of time, correct?  (I assume the actual tarring takes negligible time, but we have to do lots of more expensive steps beforehand.)

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2020-04-22 15:25 UTC

Yes.

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2020-04-22 15:26 UTC

To save time, it would be better to run the `build-release-tarball` in a separate job since the first CI build also runs tests which take a LOT of time.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-04-22 15:26 UTC

Seems like a sensible plan to me, then.  Does this require some admin powers to try it out?

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2020-04-22 15:28 UTC

I don't think so, It should be pretty simple to implement. Let me do a PR for this if the change looks fine to you?

**Steve Howell** · 2020-04-22 15:28 UTC

Yep, I think this is the best plan.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-04-22 16:20 UTC

@Aman Agrawal yeah, that would be a nice improvement.

**Arpit Sharma** · 2020-04-22 17:35 UTC

(replying to Aman Agrawal)
> We are already testing after running provision in the first CI build, we can add the `build-release-tarball` script to it and save the tarball. Then in the second build we simply run the tarball.
Yes, this would be effective.

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2020-04-22 17:36 UTC

(replying to Aman Agrawal)
> To save time, it would be better to run the `build-release-tarball` in a separate job since the first CI build also runs tests which take a LOT of time.
This is the final plan btw.

**Arpit Sharma** · 2020-04-22 17:42 UTC

Do ``` build-release-tarball``` takes that much time? I mean to add a new job for it, is justified?

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2020-04-22 17:43 UTC

The first CI also runs tests, which takes a lot of time. This is the primary reason for doing it in a different job.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-04-22 18:13 UTC

I think also since CircleCI doesn't have a ton of overhead for a minimal job, the real question is what extra work we'd do with `build-release-tarball` in a separate job than `scripts/setup/install`

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-04-22 18:14 UTC

In theory, the production job could just run `scripts/setup/install` from Git, rather than going through `build-release-tarball`.  But then we wouldn't notice if we had a bug where the release tarballs were missing some key file.

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2020-04-23 07:49 UTC

I don't think we can run anything else on the build tarball job since it would delay the production install job which also takes a significant amount of time.

It won't address the fact that we do linter checks first and abort if they fail (I think managing the output for multiple suites failing is harder), but it would make `test-backend` output more useful given that we did all the test setup work for it.

All the failed tests will be printed at the bottom.

Oh! Then I support `test-backend --nonfatal-errors`.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-07-30 23:22 UTC

Today I switched the `test-backend` default to the previous `--nonfatal-errors` behavior: f84703bc48d29f75cd5f35a727c71056880a72bf.  One can run it to fail after the first errors with  `--stop` or `-x` if desired.  

This is something I'd made a TODO note of as a response to feedback about our testing system that we should change, but I don't actually remember when that conversation was.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-07-30 23:22 UTC

This does make us match the default behavior of most test runner software (pytest, etc.).

**Dinesh Ch** · 2021-08-01 10:27 UTC

Does this mean our CI failures for `test-backend` will show all failed tests? I think that'll be helpful but it'd be nice if CI would report failure soon after first test failure rather than waiting to complete running all tests. Not sure if that's possible.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-08-01 14:39 UTC

Yes it will now show all errors. This means it'll run all tests before reporting failure; but given that the provisioning time exceeds the runtime anyway, this may not be a big deal.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-12-09 00:28 UTC

One thing I've been reminded of that I think is a major regression with this change is that if you run `test-backend`, and `stdout` from failed tests ends up very far up in the scrollback, and well separated from the traceback associated with that test.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-12-09 00:29 UTC

This isn't that big a deal for me, since I know about this, but it seems like a substantial regression in the debugging experience for folks new to the project, because you run `test-backend` and you're missing half the debugging output (and may not know about `test-backend --rerun` to rerun just the failing tests)

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-12-09 00:29 UTC

I'm not sure I have a good solution to this problem other than flipping the default back and getting the other set of downsides, but figured I'd mention it in case anyone else has a clever idea here.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-12-09 00:30 UTC

**Steve Howell** · 2021-12-09 01:17 UTC

I definitely prefer the old workflow.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-12-09 01:51 UTC

Yeah, I do too; when running tests locally, I'd generally prefer to start working on fixing the first failure than get the full set.

**Greg Price** · 2021-12-09 19:08 UTC

(replying to Tim Abbott)
> `stdout` from failed tests ends up very far up in the scrollback, and well separated from the traceback associated with that test.

I'd take that as a bug (or arguably a missing feature, but an important feature in a test runner) and say that the way to solve the problem is to fix it.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-12-09 19:09 UTC

I suppose that specific issue might not be hard to fix; clearly the test runner is already doing something to reorder the traceback output to the end.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-12-09 19:11 UTC

But I suspect doing so may require overriding various parts of the built-in Django test runner.  Let me see if they have an option for this.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-12-09 19:13 UTC

I think there's a strong tradition for this anti-pattern.  I feel like other test runners I've worked with also do this annoying buffering of stdout.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-12-09 19:14 UTC

https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/3.2/topics/testing/advanced/#defining-a-test-runner sadly doesn't do that for us.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-12-17 00:37 UTC

I prefer `--nonfatal-errors` because I don’t want to wait several minutes to find the second failure, but I do get annoyed at this disconnect between a failing test’s stdout and its exception. This is likely another thing that pytest-django would solve.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-12-17 00:41 UTC

One thing that would help me (I like to deal with one failure at a time) is a cousin to the `--rerun` option that is `--resume`.  Basically, it would look at the last test that ever failed for me, and then re-order the tests so that the failed test is at the top, and then all the recently-passing tests are at the bottom.  So if test 7 fails out of ten tests, the next run would 7,8,9,10,1,2,3,4,5,6.  I know our parallelization slightly complicates that.  (I've wanted this for both backend tests and node tests.)

**Steve Howell** · 2021-12-17 00:43 UTC

Another thing that I've been meaning to add for about five years now is a `--broaden` option.  Basically, if you do `--rerun` to fix one test, it's pretty common that there will be other tests in that same module with similar failures.  So `--broaden` would run one level out, either broadening from a single test to a single class, or from a single class to the entire module.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-12-17 00:50 UTC

On a recent code sweep my workflow caused a lot of inefficiency, but I often work out of my kitchen, so I was able to do things like brew coffee, microwave food, and clean dishes while I waited for the tests.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-12-17 01:47 UTC

Pytest has `--lf/--last-failed` and `--ff/--failed-first` ([docs](https://docs.pytest.org/en/latest/how-to/cache.html)).

*2020-05-11 to 2020-05-13 · 16 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/43-automated-testing/topic/CircleCI.202.2E1/with/873747)*

**Arpit Sharma** · 2020-05-11 16:32 UTC

This is in context of
`"Fixing Zulip's CircleCI integration and adding configuration for posting to this stream whenever CI fails in master"`
Currently, we are using CircleCI version 2.0 and [commit](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/commit/e3b48833860ebcd8375ffff0c305b10fb439a4cd) is the reason why we can't update to 2.1. 

Since notify only works till CircleCI 2.0 (Although they have completely removed it from the documentation and is unstable but it works somehow [issue](https://github.com/circleci/circleci-docs/issues/3145) ), our CircleCI integration can't work on CircleCI 2.1. CircleCI recommends using orbs to receive notification (requires 2.1) and apparently there is already an [orb](https://circleci.com/orbs/registry/orb/ponylang/zulip) for Zulip it uses our `/api/v1/messages` API to send alerts. 

So to add support for CircleCI integration in version 2.1 either we have to create a new orb or modify this one.  But still even while creating an orb we will have to `POST` to our CircleCI webhook URL. So I think this hacky [PR](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/14940) can enable posting to this stream if CI fails in master.

@Aman Agrawal @Anders Kaseorg - Drew, Brendon, and I thought it might be valuable for Zulip + Semgrep folks to regularly sync about Semgrep bugs, your friction points, and our roadmap. Does a recurring meeting sound valuable? We've been doing this with some other projects and so far it has been productive for all involved.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-05-26 21:37 UTC

From my perspective, aside from bugs I’ve already filed:

* [#830](https://github.com/returntocorp/semgrep/issues/830) semgrep 0.8.0 --version reports 0.8.1.dev0+gb3c2930.d20200521 (we can work around this),
* [#831](https://github.com/returntocorp/semgrep/issues/831) --lang fails to set input file language (we probably can’t work around this),

the major issue that discourages me from doing more with semgrep is speed. Our regex-based `custom_py` linter takes ~10 seconds to check 50 rules, while semgrep spends more time checking 6 rules. So I’m concerned about what would happen to our linting time if we migrated many more rules to semgrep.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-05-26 21:39 UTC

And, having not tried to migrate many more rules to semgrep, I’m skeptical we have enough feedback to justify a recurring meeting.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-05-26 22:17 UTC

# Fixed
Performance optimizations in deep statement matching
Disable normalization of != ==> !(==)
Support empty variable declaration in javasript
Support "print expr," in Python 2.X
Support "async" keyword on inner arrow functions for ECMAScript 7+
Support optional catch bindings for ECMAScript 2019+
Support non-ASCII Unicode whitespace code points as lexical whitespace in JavaScript code
Support assignment expressions in Python 3.8
Emtpty block in if will only match empty blocks

For this rule:

> "Avoid using null on string-based fields such as CharField and TextField. If a string-based field
has null=True, that means it has two possible values for "no data": NULL, and the empty string. In
most cases, it's redundant to have two possible values for "no data;" the Django convention is to
use the empty string, not NULL."

I think at least some of these are things I'd want to change.

> Looks like you are only accessing first element of an ordered QuerySet. Use `latest()` or `earliest()` instead. See https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/3.0/ref/models/querysets/#django.db.models.query.QuerySet.latest

These could be small code cleanups; haven't look at them all but I think they're mostly things I'd merge if someone did the change since I think it's a readability improvement.  

> This is a last resort. You should be careful when using QuerySet.extra due to SQLi https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/3.0/ref/models/querysets/#django.db.models.query.QuerySet.extra

If there was a way we could make this note fire on cases where the input to `extra` is a literal, possibly by changing our code to make this clear, I'd be happier.  Right now, it's just telling you not to use a feature that's usually a better choice than the alternative (a full raw SQL query).  I'm not sure how the rule works here.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-06-04 21:09 UTC

I meant to post this yesterday, but got distracted;  we are now running `puppeteer` tests via `test-js-with-puppeteer` in CI!  These are intended to replace the old `casper` suite, using a more modern, maintained framework.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-06-04 21:10 UTC

Please report and nondeterministic failures you see here; we expect there to not be many as we've run the tests in a loop, and there's essentially only a single test thus far, but we'll of course be porting more tests over with time.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-06-04 21:11 UTC

One thing we should probably do a bit of planning on is deciding exactly what tests we actually want here.  Many of the older Casper tests had been stagnant for a long time, so we will want to think carefully on what things are worth having a slow end-to-end test for; it's likely to be somewhat different from the suite of tests we happened to have written, largely in 2014, and maintained over the years.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-06-04 21:12 UTC

Thanks to @Priyank Patel and @Dinesh Ch and I think several others for making this happen :)

**Steve Howell** · 2020-06-04 21:14 UTC

My view is that `puppeteer` should largely focus on settings-related features.  I don't feel that the Casper tests ever found bugs on the main page that wouldn't have been caught pretty quickly on czo.  And we have better node coverage on things like the left sidebar, unread counts, messages, and the buddy list than we do on settings.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-06-04 21:40 UTC

The Node tests are mock-heavy unit tests; that’s not to say they’re bad, but they shouldn’t be considered a substitute for end-to-end tests with a real browser, DOM, jQuery, backend, etc.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-06-04 21:42 UTC

Yeah, of course.  I just mean that there's more risk mitigation for the modules that are node-tested.  And I think the node tests occasionally increase the quality of the code under test (which doesn't prevent regressions directly, but more subtly).

**Steve Howell** · 2020-06-04 21:44 UTC

I would say the same sort of thing about human QA.  It's good that on the main page bugs are a lot less likely to go undetected, but there's still room for puppeteer to catch things even before czo.  It's just that settings have basically **nothing** now--less minute-to-minute usage on czo and less node tests.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-06-04 21:49 UTC

I guess login/signup has similar forces--we don't get much eyeballs on those from our actual devs on czo, and we don't have great node coverage on them that I'm aware of.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-06-04 22:03 UTC

Yeah, the things I'd want prioritize are 2 types of things:
* Basic tests for the most important flows: Signup, login, sending a message, editing a message, etc.  These are intended to catch issues before they get deployed to chat.zulip.org, even if we think we'd catch them there.
* Tests for things that we thing will be hard to properly test using Node tests.  Copy/paste might be a good example of this.

Settings I think are probably relatively low-value, since there's a ton of them, and I think node tests will be less work to do a nice version than puppeteer tests, and then be valuable for longer.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-06-04 22:06 UTC

Well, another reason to put full-end stack on settings stuff is that they tend to be very full-stack in nature.  @Tim Abbott You may be jaded by the Casper tests, but I think most settings tests in puppeteer could be set up pretty nicely to do full-stack checks.  They're all pretty simple in nature:
* click some widget
* enter some value
* hit send
* wait for server response
* validate server response
* validate live update

And I think there's a reason we haven't pushed hard on node test coverage for settings--I just don't think that's in node's wheelhouse.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-06-04 22:21 UTC

Yeah, I think for that it'll depend a bit on whether we do the investment to make a test like that <5 lines of code in the common case.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-06-04 22:33 UTC

I think we can do that.

Yes, you can run have dev server running in vagrant and run the test in host. You just need to make the following change and run `node frontend_tests/puppeteer_tests/03-compose.js` to see what's happening in that test.
```diff
diff --git a/frontend_tests/puppeteer_lib/common.js b/frontend_tests/puppeteer_lib/common.js
index de52e1d336..fa720aa18c 100644
--- a/frontend_tests/puppeteer_lib/common.js
+++ b/frontend_tests/puppeteer_lib/common.js
@@ -9,7 +9,7 @@ class CommonUtils {
     constructor() {
         this.browser = null;
         this.screenshot_id = 0;
-        this.realm_url = "http://zulip.zulipdev.com:9981/";
+        this.realm_url = "http://zulip.zulipdev.com:9991/";
         this.pm_recipient = {
             async set(page, recipient) {
                 await page.type("#private_message_recipient", recipient);
@@ -35,7 +35,7 @@ class CommonUtils {
             this.browser = await puppeteer.launch({
                 args: ["--window-size=1400,1024", "--no-sandbox", "--disable-setuid-sandbox"],
                 defaultViewport: {width: 1280, height: 1024},
-                headless: true,
+                headless: false,
             });
         }
     }
```
(We might have to increase window size height as a part of it isn't visible though both viewport and window heights are same)

https://dev.to/retyui/how-debugging-github-actions-with-ssh-273n has interesting piece of code for it.
```yaml
# .github/workflows/my-build.yml
name: Debugging with SSH
on: push
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
     - uses: actions/checkout@v1

     - name: Try Build
       run: ./not-exist-file.sh it bloke build

     - name: Start SSH via Ngrok
       if: ${{ failure() }}
       run: curl -sL https://gist.githubusercontent.com/retyui/7115bb6acf151351a143ec8f96a7c561/raw/7099b9db76729dc5761da72aa8525f632d8875c9/debug-github-actions.sh | bash
       env:
        # After sign up on the https://ngrok.com/
        # You can find this token here: https://dashboard.ngrok.com/get-started/setup
        # NGROK_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.NGROK_TOKEN }}
        NGROK_TOKEN: 1cu2nQXxljrX4mNGxz4z9N1QSfm_3JDS7Ek4Rti6oTwov43Sx

        # This password you will use when authorizing via SSH 
        # USER_PASS: ${{ secrets.USER_PASS }}
        USER_PASS: murAmur

     - name: Don't kill instace
       if: ${{ failure() }}
       run: sleep 1h # Prevent to killing instance after failure
```

## semgrep

*2020-06-11 to 2021-09-13 · 11 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/43-automated-testing/topic/semgrep/with/902150)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-06-11 23:27 UTC

semgrep when running with `lint --fix` prints this output: `semgrep-py| Successfully modified 0 file.`, which feels like spam to me.

**Luke O'Malley** · 2020-06-12 15:04 UTC

(replying to Tim Abbott)
> semgrep when running with `lint --fix` prints this output: `semgrep-py| Successfully modified 0 file.`, which feels like spam to me.
Does Semgrep's specific output feel like spam or the way it's integrated with Zulint? On the Semgrep side, when no files are modified, what kind of output would you expect or want to see?

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-06-12 21:23 UTC

We run 18 different linters in parallel, so we only want output from the ones that failed and/or fixed anything. (Our current parallel implementation of `lint --fix` is [broken](https://github.com/zulip/zulint/issues/7) and we need to change it to serial, but still.)

**Isaac Evans** · 2021-09-13 20:49 UTC

hey folks, I'm one of the developers of Semgrep which Zulip uses as part of its lint flow. I was chatting with @Tim Abbott about some changes we're considering to Semgrep and he suggested I post them here for feedback.

We are planning to eventually merge our Semgrep CI wrapper, semgrep-action, into the main Semgrep codebase. As part of this we need to figure out how to manage the metrics that semgrep-action collects (https://github.com/returntocorp/semgrep-action/blob/develop/PRIVACY.md).

Our current thinking is a new "auto" mode for metrics:
* default-enable Semgrep metrics for runs that fetch rules from the Registry  (https://semgrep.dev/r) (e.g., —config=p/ci, —config=p/xss, —config=“p/dgryski.semgrep-go”). We’d use the same metrics as before with one addition: we’d transmit the organization name (probably extracted from the git origin URL) to simplify setup for first-time users.
* runs that use non-Registry rules in a local file, or a local expression with -e/--pattern, will have metrics default-disabled.

Looking at https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/main/tools/semgrep.yml Zulip does not use any remote rules (eg from https://semgrep.dev/r) right now, so it would not affect your current usage at all.

Still, if you add rules from the registry later, I'm curious: if the CLI was forthright about sending this data when running with a remote-based config, would this impact your use of Semgrep? Might it impact how/whether you recommend Semgrep to others?

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-09-13 21:26 UTC

@Isaac Evans One thing I'd be looking for is it being impossible to miss in the documentation for enabling a remote-based configuration that doing so results in metrics being sent, with a clear link to documentation that tells you how to turn it off and verify it's disabled, and clear details on exactly what is included (E.g. is your code sent?  Or just stats on the number of failures of what types of rules?).

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-09-13 21:27 UTC

If that's the case, and a local configuration like ours doesn't make any network requests, I think that'd be a privacy model one would be OK with.  Fundamentally when one puts a `semgrep.dev` URL in your configuration, you're going to be making some sort of network request to download the rule, which I imagine will end up in webserver logs if nothing else.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-09-13 21:28 UTC

I do think that the Help Center articles on this should be sure to explain clearly the exposure; e.g. potentially it could be a risk for a business if you got hacked and a state-sponsored hacker now knows that Customer X of yours has 500 SQL injection vulnerabilities in their codebase.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-09-13 21:28 UTC

(Since that could help the attacker figure out what to prioritize in trying to break into your codebase)

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-09-13 21:29 UTC

So I can certainly imagine many organizations wanting to disable any sort of metrics that send back data computed from the code (vs. just data about which rules are enabled).

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-09-13 21:29 UTC

Others may have more subtle thoughts; those are just my first reactions.

**Isaac Evans** · 2021-09-13 22:44 UTC

Thanks Tim, helpful feedback! No code is sent, ever; the stats are on things like # bytes of code by file extension, # of and hash of id for rules fired, etc. (we do this for users who set up an action that integrated with our online system and document it here: https://github.com/returntocorp/semgrep-action/blob/develop/PRIVACY.md)

Even if the proposal matches expectations, the details of messaging, documenting, and broadcasting it will require a lot of care. We do plan to add output to the default CLI text that explains, when fetching from central registry, that metrics will be transmitted.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-07-01 05:28 UTC

**Steve Howell** · 2020-07-01 05:43 UTC

I think the clutter factor here is death by a thousand cuts.  It's how cruft works.  It's insidious.  Every time somebody runs tests, they see what is signal 1% of the time but noise 99% the other time.  And then when Anders is trying to streamline our test runner code, he has to deal with this.

It's not 100% cruft--that would be an easy decision.  But it's cruft.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-07-01 06:04 UTC

Yeah, let's remove this.  We have several nice features in our test runner, but this one is probably more complexity than it's worth for what it achieves.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-07-01 06:06 UTC

Another area we should talk about is the various types of coverage logic that we added back in 2016 to try to get to the goal of "not having totally untested pages".

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-07-01 06:07 UTC

We have 2 things that do something fairly similar:
* The "test every template" logic, which confirms that the test suite actually rendered every backend HTML template in the product.
* The "URL coverage" logic, which aims to check that we used every item in `urls.py` during the tests.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-07-01 06:08 UTC

I think the combination of 100% code coverage for views files and the "test every template" logic subsume the goals of the "URL coverage" logic, and we can probably remove the latter.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-07-01 06:09 UTC

Because we have an assertion that all of the Python code for our views was tested (which is very close to implying that every API URL is tested) plus the assertion that every HTML template (i.e. all the Jinja2 code) was run and tested at least in the very basic level that URL coverage would verify.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-07-01 06:09 UTC

The only type of thing we'd miss by removing it is if there were multiple `urls.py` entries pointing to the same view function.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-07-01 06:11 UTC

Maybe I'm missing something, but I think that's right; my recollection is that both pieces of tooling were invaluable for helping us track down these gaps in testing (which in turn back in 2016 led to frustrating bugs where a page just didn't compile happening a few times), but the investments in overall backend testing in 2017 and 2018 make this no longer a problem.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-07-01 06:14 UTC

(replying to Tim Abbott)

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-07-08 22:34 UTC

My conclusions overall on the formatting after doing this:
* I wish Black had the magic commas feature for function calls.  This one may be hopelessly annoying for a number of files such that we end up having to turn Black off or move data to live somewhere else; not sure (part of the problem is that Black today will destroy the magic commas, so running it later won't turn things back if they add the feature).  It's too bad this isn't fixed upstream yet.
* I wish Black handled lists being passed to functions without putting the `[` / `]` on its own line in many places (more generally larger structures like we have with schema checkers in `test_events.py` end up weird; most especially the `(` on a line by itself in example 5 for the `message` tuple).
* I like hanging indents in a subset of cases but it's perhaps too heuristic to have a tool do it right so I think the concept requires we live with losing them.
* I don't like lines with just `):` on them; with function definitions there's the type definition which makes it sorta OK, but it's annoying for `with` statements or similar
* I really wish Black let us configure the blank lines between top-level objects to be 1 rather than 2.
* Beyond that, I think everything else feels like things that are rare, unavoidable, or where we can transform the code in a way that doesn't make it worse and makes Black not do something weird.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-07-08 22:39 UTC

> (part of the problem is that Black today will destroy the magic commas,

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-07-08 22:40 UTC

No, but we have existing code that intentionally puts things on a line by themselves for readability (E.g. those enum-like things or the Nagios check defaultdicts), which is what the magic commas feature looks for.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-07-08 22:48 UTC

I need to break for lunch and then I should really focus on more directly release-critical work for a bit.  But I'm currently feeling like if we had a `black` fork that did magic commas for function calls (or wanted to tag the ~50 places where we'd really want that feature with `nofmt` comment), it'd on balance by worth doing a `black` migration now despite the flexibility downsides of using a highly opinionated formatter, with a focused effort at cleaning up or skipping patterns where it behaves badly.  

Without those things, I'm leaning more towards "we should probably punt until a later release or think more or try `yapf` which does allow configuring style details we like or something", though I worry yapf may have much worse performance that would make it not super viable.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-07-17 22:30 UTC

```sh
#!/bin/sh
set -eux
git fetch https://github.com/andersk/zulip.git prettier-prep
git rebase FETCH_HEAD
FILTER_BRANCH_SQUELCH_WARNING=1 \
    git filter-branch --force \
    --tree-filter '/srv/zulip/node_modules/.bin/prettier --write "**/*.{js,ts}" tools/check-openapi' \
    --commit-filter 'git_commit_non_empty_tree "$@"' \
    "FETCH_HEAD^..HEAD"
```

``` python3
class _AssertLogsContext(_BaseTestCaseContext):                                                      
    """A context manager used to implement TestCase.assertLogs()."""                                 
                                                                                                     
    LOGGING_FORMAT = "%(levelname)s:%(name)s:%(message)s"                                            
                                                                                                     
    def __init__(self, test_case, logger_name, level):                                               
        _BaseTestCaseContext.__init__(self, test_case)                                               
        self.logger_name = logger_name                                                               
        if level:                                                                                    
            self.level = logging._nameToLevel.get(level, level)                                      
        else:                                                                                        
            self.level = logging.INFO                                                                
        self.msg = None                                                                              
                                                                                                     
    def __enter__(self):                                                                             
        if isinstance(self.logger_name, logging.Logger):                                             
            logger = self.logger = self.logger_name                                                  
        else:                                                                                        
            logger = self.logger = logging.getLogger(self.logger_name)                               
        formatter = logging.Formatter(self.LOGGING_FORMAT)                                           
        handler = _CapturingHandler()                                                                
        handler.setFormatter(formatter)                                                              
        self.watcher = handler.watcher                                                               
        self.old_handlers = logger.handlers[:]                                                       
        self.old_level = logger.level                                                                
        self.old_propagate = logger.propagate                                                        
        logger.handlers = [handler]                                                                  
        logger.setLevel(self.level)                                                                  
        logger.propagate = False                                                                     
        return handler.watcher                                                                       
                                                                                                     
    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc_value, tb):                                                     
        self.logger.handlers = self.old_handlers                                                     
        self.logger.propagate = self.old_propagate                                                   
        self.logger.setLevel(self.old_level)                                                         
        if exc_type is not None:                                                                     
            # let unexpected exceptions pass through                                                 
            return False                                                                             
        if len(self.watcher.records) == 0:                                                           
            self._raiseFailure(                                                                      
                "no logs of level {} or higher triggered on {}"                                      
                .format(logging.getLevelName(self.level), self.logger.name))                         
```

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-07-23 18:56 UTC

``` py
    def assertLogs(self, logger=None, level=None):                                                   
        """Fail unless a log message of level *level* or higher is emitted                           
        on *logger_name* or its children.  If omitted, *level* defaults to                           
        INFO and *logger* defaults to the root logger.                                               
                                                                                                     
        This method must be used as a context manager, and will yield                                
        a recording object with two attributes: `output` and `records`.                              
        At the end of the context manager, the `output` attribute will                               
        be a list of the matching formatted log messages and the                                     
        `records` attribute will be a list of the corresponding LogRecord                            
        objects.                                                                                     
                                                                                                     
        Example::                                                                                    
                                                                                                     
            with self.assertLogs('foo', level='INFO') as cm:                                         
                logging.getLogger('foo').info('first message')                                       
                logging.getLogger('foo.bar').error('second message')                                 
            self.assertEqual(cm.output, ['INFO:foo:first message',                                   
                                         'ERROR:foo.bar:second message'])                            
        """                                                                                          
        return _AssertLogsContext(self, logger, level)

import unittest

class TestAssertLogs(unittest.TestCase):

if __name__ == '__main__':
    unittest.main()
```

```python3
class TeeStderr():
    def __enter__(self, spam_finder):
        self.stderr_stream = sys.stderr
        sys.stderr = self
        
        # object to find spam have my spam finding logic
        self.spam_finder = spam_finder

    def __exit__(self):
        sys.stderr = stderr_stream

    def write(self, data):
        self.spam_finder.find_spam(data)
        self.stderr_stream.write(data)

    def writelines(self, data):
        lines= ""
        for line in data:
            lines += line
        self.spam_finder.find_spam(lines)
        self.stderr_stream.writelines(data)

    def flush(self):
        self.stderr_stream.flush()

```

So as a result of merging the migration from `ujson` to `orjson`, I expect folks will get this error:

> You need to run test-backend inside a Zulip dev environment

when you try to run Zulip tools after rebasing from 61d0417e75a09075d9a61ac0ddd959efd6934478 to something older than it.  The fix is to just run `provision`.

Details here: https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/16063/files#r468762199

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-08-11 17:59 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-08-11 18:00 UTC

I think the only downside is that folks who've done `pip install django` and `pip install zulip` on their host machine will not get the handy "You're not in the Vagrant environment" error.

## event_schema.py

*2020-09-28 to 2020-09-28 · 8 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/43-automated-testing/topic/event_schema.2Epy/with/1026755)*

**Steve Howell** · 2020-09-28 18:37 UTC

For any folks who have added full-stack features to our app, it's likely that you have had to deal with the challenge of writing tests in `test_events.py`.  If you don't know what `test_events.py` is, then you can probably ignore this topic.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-09-28 18:38 UTC

One of the things that we do in `test_events` tests is to validate the data types of the events that come back from exercising the actions in `verify_action`.  We usually refer to this as "schema checking."

**Steve Howell** · 2020-09-28 18:39 UTC

Now, on master, we now define all these schemas in `event_schema.py`.  So if you write new tests in `test_events`, you will want to look at the existing tests to see the new code patterns.  Essentially, all tests have some `check_foo` step.  It used to be the case that the implementations of the `check_foo` helpers were inside of `test_events.py`; going forward, we want them to be in `event_schema.py`.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-09-28 18:41 UTC

The reason that we have moved the actual schemas to `event_schema.py` is that it's easier for tooling to leverage the schemas for other things.  We now have a slightly misnamed tool called `check-node-fixtures` that checks two things against those schemas:
* our tests data for node tests should abide by the schemas
* our OpenAPI documentation should be equivalent to the schemas

**Steve Howell** · 2020-09-28 18:41 UTC

I have PR https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/16429 (still building) to update the docs on this.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-09-28 18:42 UTC

https://zulip.readthedocs.io/en/latest/subsystems/events-system.html#testing provides more context.  (It will be fleshed out by my PR, but the current docs should be accurate.)

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-09-28 23:40 UTC

Thanks for doing those documentation updates!  They are often a really important capstone of this sort of major refactoring project.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-09-28 23:46 UTC

Thanks for your edits, too...I feel like the docs are pretty complete now.

## test-backend cruft

*2020-10-15 to 2020-10-15 · 12 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/43-automated-testing/topic/test-backend.20cruft/with/1038369)*

**Steve Howell** · 2020-10-15 15:46 UTC

I get messages like this:

~~~
Coverage.py warning: Data file '/home/zulipdev/zulip/var/.coverage.showell.zulipdev.org.2752.309364' doesn't seem to be a coverage data file: 'NoneType' object is not iterable

**Steve Howell** · 2020-10-15 15:46 UTC

I can try to debug this later, but does anybody know why we're getting these?  It seems like some kind of race, because these files go away eventually.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-10-15 21:55 UTC

Yeah, I've seen those as well.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-10-15 21:56 UTC

I believe the core problem is an upstream bug in `coverage` that prevents us from just writing coverage data to a controlled path (so it instead goes to those random paths), and then I suspect if you do a `Ctrl+C` at the right time they'll get leaked.  But I haven't verified that last bit.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-10-15 22:03 UTC

They leak for me without control c

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-10-15 22:22 UTC

OK, good to know.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-10-15 22:23 UTC

We should try to figure out if there's a way to control the path they get written to.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-10-15 22:29 UTC

We do (`data_file=var/.coverage` in `tools/coveragerc`). They have to have random suffixes because they’re written from multiple processes. Can we just `cov.erase()` before `cov.start()` in `test-backend`?

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-10-15 22:36 UTC

That's probably OK.  We want to support running multiple `test-backend` in parallel, but we're not trying to achieve that with the coverage option on both.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-10-15 22:36 UTC

Not multiple `test-backend`s, multiple processes in a single `test-backend` (from `multiprocessing`).

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-10-15 22:37 UTC

Yeah, I understand that -- the only potential downside for doing the erase would be if we were running multiple `test-backends`, since that happens pre-fork, right?

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-10-15 22:38 UTC

In any case, that seems reasonable to try adding such an `erase`; I'm not convinced it'll solve this problem though.

## queries_captured

*2020-11-04 to 2020-11-05 · 17 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/43-automated-testing/topic/queries_captured/with/1056374)*

**Steve Howell** · 2020-11-04 00:13 UTC

I discovered a slightly annoying thing about our `queries_captured` decorator today.  Instead of just clearing the cache before the entire operation inside the `with`, it instead clears the cache right before it executes any query, which, of course, is too late.  This means it exempts the first query from the query count (if it's already in cache, which is a fairly common case, since we often get UserProfile first).  And then it also over-penalizes certain actions as SQL abusers, when they are really, in fact, merely cache slammers.

I'll have more details tomorrow.  It should be an easy thing to fix, and it might expose some places where we might be able to remove some cache traffic by either using in-memory caches or, better yet, just organize code better so that we pass data around internally.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-11-04 00:17 UTC

Hmm, interesting.  I think ideally we want to support asking either question: "How many queries with cold cache"  and "How many queries with hot cache".

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-11-04 00:18 UTC

But I guess if we're doing the hot cache case, we potentially don't want to clear the cache at all.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-11-04 00:28 UTC

Yeah, in my use case I may introduce a `hot_cache` flag.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-11-04 00:28 UTC

The way I discovered it is this...

**Steve Howell** · 2020-11-04 00:28 UTC

You know I'm working on making digest emails work in bulk.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-11-04 00:30 UTC

We have a test where we send othello a digest email, and it takes 9 queries.  I wanted to make a loop with aaron, desdemona, and prospero thrown into the test, and I expected them to each also take 9 queries.  (And then presumably my bulk operation would cut the total from 36 down to something smaller by sharing work.)

**Steve Howell** · 2020-11-04 00:31 UTC

I had othello at 9, and then when I added aaron, I expected it to either stay at 9, but aaron went up to 10.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-11-04 00:31 UTC

Othello was on a mostly cold cache; Aaron was on a completely cold cache.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-11-04 00:32 UTC

And Aaron's cache was actually cold from Othello's turn through the loop.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-11-04 00:34 UTC

I think what we want is just count queries and cache hits for expensive operations.  The worst, worst case SQL-wise is a cache that is completely worthless, so that even as you're trying to add cache entries in your own operation, they don't make it to the cache.  That's what our current tests test (but off by one), but that scenario is overly pessimistic.  What's more interesting to me is just a cold cache.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-11-04 00:39 UTC

Well, I think we do care about cases where the cache being empty means we do 500 queries, but then after that everything is nice.  But maybe that's unlikely code to be written anyway.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-11-04 00:46 UTC

For any places where that happens, in my sweep tomorrow, I am gonna count how many cache hits we have.  And, obviously, if there are any egregious offenders, I will try to call them out explicitly.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-11-04 00:47 UTC

I expect most places to just be off by one or two.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-11-04 16:17 UTC

https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/16704

**Steve Howell** · 2020-11-04 16:21 UTC

Fixing queries_captured() didn't reveal anything too major.  I made a couple tests now check for cache hits.  Some of the reasons we hit the cache are kinda annoying:

* we hit the cache to get the id of the welcome bot whenever we send a PM
* we hit the cache to get the id of the "Internal" client when we generate internal messages

Both of the above are values that would never change, so you could put them in something like settings.py, but I doubt it's worth fussing with.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-11-05 18:31 UTC

Yeah, and both of those are dynamic data that may vary between different Zulip servers.

def clean_file(orig_fn: str) -> str:                                                                                                          
    fn = orig_fn                                                                                                                              
    if not fn.endswith(".js"):                                                                                                                
        fn += ".js"                                                                                                                           
    if "frontend_tests/" not in fn:                                                                                                           
        fn = os.path.join(ROOT_DIR, "frontend_tests", "node_tests", fn)                                                                       
    fn = os.path.abspath(fn)                                                                                                                  
    if not os.path.exists(fn):                                                                                                                
        print(f"Cannot find {orig_fn} ({fn})")                                                                                                
        sys.exit(1)                                                                                                                           
    return fn                                                                                                                                 
```

hello @Aman Agrawal (possibly of interest to @Tim Abbott), I'm working on a PR that may change some of the Semgrep output in minor ways. Specifically, printing a ---------- separator between matches to make it more obvious where multiline matches start and end. As part of that, I might make the default that a max of ten lines or so are printed per finding before truncation. So if you have a pattern like logger.info(...) that could match multiple lines, you'll now see separators between matches eg: 

```

~/test-repos/zulip/analytics/lib/counts.py
130:        logger.info("DONE %s (%dms)" % (stat.property, (end-start)*1000))

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
193:        logger.info("%s RealmCount aggregation (%dms/%sr)" % (
194:            stat.property, (end - start) * 1000, cursor.rowcount))
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
...
```
Would love comments here or at https://github.com/returntocorp/semgrep/pull/2082 on whether this will affect anything with the zulint flow.

## dependency inspection

*2020-12-28 to 2021-01-07 · 12 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/43-automated-testing/topic/dependency.20inspection/with/1088841)*

**Isaac Evans** · 2020-12-28 19:46 UTC

I’ve been working on hardening some of my open-source projects by automating dependency upgrade audits and shared some of what I've been up to with @Tim Abbott, who thought it might be a topic of broader interest to the Zulip dev team.

Screenshot attached; I built an internal Github bot that comments on PRs with yarn/pipenv lockfile changes uses Semgrep to summarize the “permissions” in the modules and whether they changed. Permissions are coarse but roughly fall into does it use exec/equivalent (code execution), does it have any network functionality, IO functionality, use crypto libraries, etc.

How well does it work? I did a sampled assessment on 938,381 Javascript packages and had a 4.6% success rate with finding new or previously reported malicious/vulnerable packages. So best case, 19 out of 20 times the comment will lead you to a “this is fine” conclusion in exchange for “hmm, malicious?” the other 1 time.

My thought is that this might be useful for PRs touching lockfiles like https://github.com/zulip/zulip/commit/6c989550ba2f9f54effd6768721e40939479dfee for which Github currently just says "large diff..can't be rendered by default." Tim suggested it might be more useful for considering new dependencies. I would love thoughts on what the team's threat model is and if this side project can be helpful!

[Screen-Shot-2020-12-17-at-2.22.53-PM.png](https://chat.zulip.org/user_uploads/2/ab/lu02miOvpxtS6WkNh645jhJT/Screen-Shot-2020-12-17-at-2.22.53-PM.png)

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-12-28 20:45 UTC

> I did a sampled assessment on 938,381 Javascript packages and had a 4.6% success rate with finding new or previously reported malicious/vulnerable packages. So best case, 19 out of 20 times the comment will lead you to a “this is fine” conclusion in exchange for “hmm, malicious?” the other 1 time.

I’m confused by the statistics here—does this mean that 4.6% of flagged packages were malicious, or that 4.6% of malicious packages were flagged?

**Isaac Evans** · 2020-12-28 22:05 UTC

sorry -- the former, 4.6% of flagged were malicious /vulnerable

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-12-28 22:43 UTC

Seems like it might be an interesting experiment. Does it work on `requirements.txt` files (since we don’t use Pipenv)? See #16857 for an example.

**Jonathan Rudenberg** · 2020-12-28 23:38 UTC

This is awesome! Is it an open source repo? I'd like to explore using this for my projects.

**Isaac Evans** · 2020-12-29 20:00 UTC

@Anders Kaseorg it does not currently, but that's just because I figured the only people who would be interested in this are those who are paranoid enough to be using lockfiles so I only supported Pipfile.lock and yarn.lock. TIL that requirements.txt can have pinned hashes as well!

**Isaac Evans** · 2020-12-29 20:01 UTC

@Jonathan Rudenberg I hope to release it as OSS if there's enough interest!

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-12-29 21:24 UTC

Yeah, we compile hashed `requirements.txt` files from `.in` files with [pip-tools](https://github.com/jazzband/pip-tools) and consume them with `pip install --require-hashes`. Other tools to consider (not used in Zulip, but in general): Poetry’s poetry.lock, NPM’s package-lock.json = npm-shrinkwrap.json.

**Isaac Evans** · 2020-12-30 14:24 UTC

@Anders Kaseorg thanks for explaining the process; I'm curious, if you were starting from scratch, would you do it that way or use Pipenv/Poetry? I added support for package-lock/npm-shrinkwrap already in addition to yarn.lock. Pipenv.lock is nice because it's just JSON

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-12-31 00:54 UTC

Oh I would definitely be in favor of burning our custom venv system to the ground and replacing it with something reasonable. This may yet happen.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-12-31 00:54 UTC

We’ve also talked about using Conda so we don’t need to rely on the system Python, although Conda has its own env file format that doesn’t seem to support hashes.

**Isaac Evans** · 2021-01-07 18:05 UTC

I had a little more time to work on productizing this, though I haven't done the requirements.txt hash support yet. Here's a preview of what it currently does on Zulip: https://github.com/ievans/zulip/pull/1. I need to add more documentation, but I'm pretty happy with the current level of assurance: for every hash specified in the lockfile, the corresponding file will be fetched, hash checked, and then semgrep runs rules looking for "permission-like" behavior. If the # of observed permissions doesn't match the previous number, the package is considered changed.

This  could be fooled by manipulating things so the net count remains the same, and it doesn't address problems like compiled `pyc` files being malicious or other binaries, but it's probably a step in the right direction. During the evaluation I mentioned with a 4% TP rate, we considered only transitions of the `exec` permission from 0 -> 1 or more. Anyways let me know if you have feedback and/or would be interested in contributing to the project @Anders Kaseorg and @Jonathan Rudenberg!

**Riken Shah** · 2021-02-01 18:06 UTC

We can introduce `wait_for_type` function which will wait until (input) element is ready for typing.
```javascript
// frontend_tests/puppeteer_tests/16-settings.js
...
await page.waitForSelector("#change_password_modal", { visible: true})    
await common.wait_for_type(page, "#old_password");
await page.type("#old_password", test_credentials.default_user.password);
await common.wait_for_type(page, "#new_password");
await page.type("#new_password", "new_password");
...
```
Here is the `wait_for_type` function
```javascript
    async wait_for_type(page, selector, maxTime = 5000) {
        // This function is used to wait until element is ready for
        // typing.
        const type = async (text) => {
            await page.type(selector, text);
            return await page.$eval(selector, (el) => el.value);
        };
        await page.waitForSelector(selector, {visible: true});
        let value = await page.$eval(selector, (el) => el.value);
        const valueToCheck = "Zulip";
        const startTime = performance.now();
        // It should only run until maxTime.
        while (performance.now() < startTime + maxTime) {
            value = await type(valueToCheck);
            if (value === valueToCheck) {
                break;
            }
            // Cleaning the value if it has written partial value (eg: Zu).
            await page.$eval(selector, (el) => (el.value = ""));
        }
    }
```

            await page.$eval(selector, (el) => (el.value = ""));

**Dinesh Ch** · 2021-02-02 16:58 UTC

Hmm, I don't think we are introducing it as a wrapper function. A bit background on the issue in case you missed it or it wasn't clear in the above messages:
We have this code that tests changing password
```js
<click change password>
await page.waitForSelector("#change_password_modal", { visible: true})
await page.type("#old_password", test_credentials.default_user.password);
await page.type("#new_password", "new_password");
<click submit which checks if old password is correct>
```
This was flaky because some actual code in our codebase is calling `.focus()` on `#change_password_modal`. The `.focus` is sometimes called after puppeteer start typing. Puppeteer `.type` works as follows: focus on the text field, send keystrokes on after another. So, calling `.focus` on `#change_password_modal` after puppeteer starts typing shifts focus from the text field resulting in partially typing what we wanted to type.
(@Riken Shah does this clear you question about what exactly happens when `.focus` is called?)

To get rid of this flake, we want to use `page.waitForSelector("#change_password_modal:focus")` which works on chrome but not on firefox.

So, for firefox @Riken Shah is proposing `wait_for_type` above which tries to type a long string and checks if the whole string is typed else repeats the same till whole string is typed. We run this function just above the two `.type`'s in the above code as a workaround. (I think having actual `.type`'s for password fields would make it a wrapper function. Could you confirm?)

~~~ js
 983     // Don't warn if subscribers list of current compose_stream is
 984     // a subset of linked_stream's subscribers list, because
 985     // everyone will be subscribed to the linked stream and so
 986     // knows it exists.  (Just always warn Zephyr users, since
 987     // we may not know their stream's subscribers.)
 988     if (
 989         peer_data.is_subscriber_subset(compose_stream.stream_id, linked_stream.stream_id) &&

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-01-29 21:27 UTC

For reference, this is the [unicorn/no-lonely-if](https://github.com/sindresorhus/eslint-plugin-unicorn/blob/v27.0.0/docs/rules/no-lonely-if.md) rule. I already filed an [issue](https://github.com/sindresorhus/eslint-plugin-unicorn/issues/953) about its fixer swallowing comments, which after some drama was just [fixed](https://github.com/sindresorhus/eslint-plugin-unicorn/pull/1047) a few hours ago. You can of course manually put the comments back where you want them.
```js
if (
    can_access_streams &&
    // Zephyr is an exception due to bla bla
    !zephyr
) {
    do_stuff();
}
```

*2021-02-13 to 2021-03-24 · 12 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/43-automated-testing/topic/Unicode.20emoji.20sync/with/1117603)*

**Neil Pilgrim (neiljp)** · 2021-02-13 00:08 UTC

ZT, much like mobile I expect, needs to occasionally grab the server list of unicode<->name mapping. We have a script to grab this from GitHub, but are thinking of automating it - #T912 / #T918.
There's clearly no need to run this on every push/PR, or even fail CI due to it. Is there a good CI recipe for this already extant in Zulip? Perhaps around the discussion of moving the `<branch> failing` check from CircleCI to Actions? (ie. messaging to a topic when something could be fixed)

**Neil Pilgrim (neiljp)** · 2021-03-11 23:23 UTC

@Sarthak Garg 😊 has updated this to use Action secrets - this seems reasonable, with what I can tell an environment variable for added security.
We don't use any secrets right now - would a ZT repo secret be appropriate?
Any other thoughts on this?

**Sarthak Garg** · 2021-03-24 02:40 UTC

(Any thoughts?)

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-03-24 03:50 UTC

@Sarthak Garg 😊 what is the secret that would be involved in syncing unicode emoji?

**Sarthak Garg** · 2021-03-24 03:53 UTC

The secrets are bot credentials (email, api key) as of now

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2021-03-24 03:57 UTC

> would a ZT repo secret be appropriate?

Yeah, adding secrets in the repo settings is the recommended way to do it.

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2021-03-24 03:59 UTC

You need an incoming webhook bot to send message to a topic. See https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/master/tools/ci/send-failure-message for how to do that.

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2021-03-24 04:00 UTC

(Let me know if I am not reading your concern correctly here)

**Sarthak Garg** · 2021-03-24 05:31 UTC

## mypy with `lint --fix`

*2021-02-13 to 2021-02-13 · 28 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/43-automated-testing/topic/mypy.20with.20.60lint.20--fix.60/with/1117932)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-02-13 20:58 UTC

So, I think we should consider disabling `mypy` when running `lint --fix` -- it doesn't have any fixes it can actually run, and apparently ends up being quite slow in a way that makes running `black` to reformat a single file require extra arguments (or waiting 8s).

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-02-13 20:58 UTC

@Anders Kaseorg thoughts on that concept?

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-02-13 20:59 UTC

I feel like that should probably be the default behavior of `lint --fix` but we might want to print a notice about linters not being run if so.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-02-13 21:00 UTC

As in, don’t run any linters without a `fix_arg` or `check_arg`? Not sure. I think that would break expectations, especially since individual linters can still report errors that could not be automatically fixed when run with `--fix`.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-02-13 21:01 UTC

Yeah, that's my concern.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-02-13 21:01 UTC

One thing I'm not sure about is whether `mypy` is actually only checking the file in question in this context; 5s feels like a long time.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-02-13 21:01 UTC

At least, this has the same runtime:
```
(zulip-py3-venv) tabbott@coset:~/zulip$ time lint --only=mypy

real	0m5.475s
user	0m5.141s
sys	0m0.260s
```

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-02-13 21:02 UTC

So possibly we just have a bug here.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-02-13 21:02 UTC

It's also possible that the nature of `mypy`'s current caching is such that checking a single large file ends up doing similar work to checking the whole codebase to do type inference.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-02-13 21:02 UTC

`mypy` can’t be run only on specific files, because a type change in one file might cause an error somewhere else.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-02-13 21:03 UTC

If you really want to run `black` on one specific file, you can just run `black file.py`.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-02-13 21:04 UTC

I suppose we could add a `lint --fix-only` or something like that, that might feel a bit more abstract?  Like, I want to run `isort` too.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-02-13 21:04 UTC

(BTW, do we need to do something to make sure `isort` and `black` run in the right order?)

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-02-13 21:04 UTC

`isort` and `black` should commute.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-02-13 21:05 UTC

Because both agree on the 100 line length?

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-02-13 21:05 UTC

Among other things. This is why we configured `isort` with `profile = black`.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-02-13 21:07 UTC

And our lint check is for isort(code) == code && black(code) == code, not for isort(black(code)) == code or black(isort(code)) == code.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-02-13 21:09 UTC

The suggestion I documented was `tools/lint --only=black,isort --fix`, but I realize that’s a mouthful, which is why I also suggested editor integrations. I set up Emacs so I just press F5 for [format-all-buffer](https://github.com/lassik/emacs-format-all-the-code) and F6 for [py-isort-buffer](https://github.com/paetzke/py-isort.el).

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-02-13 21:17 UTC

Speaking of which, should we add a section to `docs/testing/linters.md` with instructions for editor setup?

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-02-13 21:18 UTC

I'll test emacs instructions if you write them, and then maybe we can do a call for other folks to write them for their favorite editors.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-02-13 21:18 UTC

My theory was that it’s better to link to the individual formatters’ instructions as I did, since there are a lot of editors.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-02-13 21:18 UTC

Do you think a `lint --fix-only` might be worthwhile as a shorter version that works on all files?

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-02-13 21:19 UTC

Yeah, instructions that are just a couple links are fine; I just prefer to write documentation and then test it when other people are likely to want to do the same thing.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-02-13 21:19 UTC

(Though I suppose it's possible you and I are some of the only emacs users here!)

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-02-13 21:19 UTC

Did you miss the links that are already there?

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-02-13 21:20 UTC

Oh, ok, great.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-02-13 21:21 UTC

I guess they’re in [contributing/code-style.md](https://zulip.readthedocs.io/en/latest/contributing/code-style.html).

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-02-13 21:25 UTC

If someone still wants `lint --fix-only`, it’s probably reasonable to add, as long as the documentation clears up the likely confusion.

## puppeteer robustness

*2021-02-18 to 2021-02-18 · 5 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/43-automated-testing/topic/puppeteer.20robustness/with/1120715)*

**Steve Howell** · 2021-02-18 16:22 UTC

I merged b4ab662442b71045b882a561cc990907c2c2b53a a little while ago, and I wanted to point out a possible pitfall with our tests (probably dating back to Casper).

**Steve Howell** · 2021-02-18 16:23 UTC

We want to be a little careful about assuming that an element we get from a test step will still be around after we perform some user action like a button click.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-02-18 16:26 UTC

Unless we explicitly re-verify that an element remains visible, we can get a **false positive** if we check a property of the element after waiting for some other symptom of the change, but the code has actually made the element invisible.

And we can also get a **false negative** if the code is replacing our row due to a live update.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-02-18 16:27 UTC

So I think our general strategy should just be to re-find relevant elements after each step.  Hopefully my commit provides a good example of this.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-02-18 21:14 UTC

Yeah, there's definitely a useful follow-up project to the puppeteer migration of trying to rewrite the existing puppeteer tests to be cleaner / more correct.
