## node test removal

*2021-03-05 to 2021-03-06 · 11 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/43-automated-testing/topic/node.20test.20removal/with/1127652)*

**Steve Howell** · 2021-03-05 15:20 UTC

I am working on killing off three or four node tests that are historically difficult to maintain and mostly redundant.  This is a heads up to @Anders Kaseorg that if he waits a day, I might make some of the final es6 cleanup a bit easier if @Tim Abbott agrees to this.

Probably the least controversial decision is to kill off `ui_init.js`.

Probably the most controversial decision will be to kill off `compose.js`, but I believe I can address Tim's possible concerns here by adding some more direct coverage to its dependencies.  That just takes a little bit of grunt work on my part.

Now that we've ported over Casper tests to puppeteer, I think we can shift some of our time investment to cleaning up puppeteer tests and extending their usefulness, rather than maintaining some of the more beastly node tests.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-03-05 18:39 UTC

I thought that `ui_init.js` was a useful check for ordering issues of our initialization code, even if it is annoying to maintain?

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-03-05 18:41 UTC

`compose.js` is like 2K lines of code, so I don't think I can quickly evaluate what it tests.  But certainly I'm on board with reworking older test modules to achieve our actual testing goals with more thoughtfully designed tests.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-03-05 18:45 UTC

(replying to Tim Abbott)
> I thought that `ui_init.js` was a useful check for ordering issues of our initialization code, even if it is annoying to maintain?

Yeah, that was its original purpose, but I think we will detect the same kinds of errors in our puppeteer tests.  And I'm not completely confident that the node tests will detect non-subtle problems.  I will push the PR hopefully by the end of today, and I try to be pretty thorough in my commit messages to explain the rationale.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-03-05 18:52 UTC

(replying to Tim Abbott)
> `compose.js` is like 2K lines of code, so I don't think I can quickly evaluate what it tests. But certainly I'm on board with reworking older test modules to achieve our actual testing goals with more thoughtfully designed tests.

So the actual module (`static/js/compose.js) is only 1318 lines of code, because it now delegates a lot of work to other modules.  But I think it probably has surpassed the 2k line at some point in its lifetime, which explains why the test is 1940 lines of code. The test shouldn't be **quite** that long, but some of its length is due to legacy.  It's basically just super-hard-to-maintain code for a variety of reasons, and I'm not convinced it actually catches many bugs.  What I'm totally convinced of is the opportunity costs it imposes on folks like me, Anders, and new contributors.

The key safeguards for eliminating `frontend/node_tests/compose.js` are the following:
* Most normal bugs with compose get reported pretty quickly on czo.
* We have a 230-line puppeteer test, which despite its flaws, tests the compose experience way more efficiently than node tests could ever possibly do.
* We have pretty solid unit tests on all the modules that `compose.js` delegates to.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-03-05 18:53 UTC

There are some use cases of the compose box that are easy to slip by us in czo testing.  The two main ones are right-to-left support and video support.  I intend to address those before killing off the compose test.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-03-05 23:35 UTC

https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/17504

@Tim Abbott If you merge this without even giving it two seconds of your attention, I promise you won't regret it.  But I do hope you spend at least a minute to read my carefully crafted commit messages.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-03-06 00:35 UTC

I think I'm not on board with deleting `compose.js` wholesale; e.g. there's a pretty reasonable looking unit test `test_wildcard_mention_allowed` for business logic and lots of cases that I do think is important for us to test systematically and would be a mistake to test in puppeteer.  I'm fine with a strategy that involves deleting tests from that suite that we think are low quality/value, but I don't think that description applies to the whole 2KLOC test module.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-03-06 00:36 UTC

For `ui_init.js`, I'm probably fine with removing it; it's probably not that hard to resurrect if we discover we have initialization bugs in the future.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-03-06 00:38 UTC

Can you flag a few key tests in compose.js to keep?  Please just kill ui_init.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-03-06 01:36 UTC

Primarily I want to keep the ones that are testing business logic for whether our settings are implemented correctly.

Feel free to merge the `ui_init` removal; am about to go AFK.

## node test leaks

*2021-03-16 to 2021-05-19 · 14 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/43-automated-testing/topic/node.20test.20leaks/with/1133928)*

**Steve Howell** · 2021-03-16 21:52 UTC

Out of 131 node tests, 126 now have these properties:
* you can run any `run_test` test back to back with itself
* you can run any two tests back to back in either order

This basically means that while the tests within the module may change some global state, they protect themselves from other tests by clearing their state or by calling code that doesn't depend on any global state.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-03-16 21:53 UTC

These are the five that are ugly:
* activity
* compose
* message_flags
* settings_user_groups
* stream_list

**Steve Howell** · 2021-03-16 21:55 UTC

The two worst ones have the `sloppy_$` flag set, because tests aren't even isolated in terms of their zjquery tests.  Both of these modules are hard to read and are probably due for a rewrite:
* compose
* settings_user_groups

**Steve Howell** · 2021-03-16 21:56 UTC

The `message_flags` test module is probably easy enough to fix, but it has one complicated function that it tests, which is `message_flags.send_read`, which has a queue inside an IIFE that we need to clear.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-03-16 21:58 UTC

The `stream_list` tests can probably be isolated by creating a `clear_for_testing` helper in `static/js/stream_list.js`.  It probably wouldn't be too much code.  I only punted on it due to `stream_list` having lots of moving parts.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-03-16 22:02 UTC

And then `activity` is something that would be a relatively easy rewrite, I think.  The history behind `activity.js` is that it used to do everything related to the right sidebar (aka "buddy list") without any helper modules.  So the original test for it does a lot of fairly deep testing.  Since then we've extracted a few smaller modules that are more amenable to unit testing:
* buddy_data
* buddy_list
* presence

If you temporarily remove `activity.js` from the node tests, it reveals some holes in direct coverage on those modules.  We could restore the coverage on those modules with more direct tests, and then basically rewrite the `activity` test from scratch to use better abstraction boundaries.  The `activity.js` module is only 374 lines of code.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-03-16 22:03 UTC

I don't have any immediate plans to fix these five modules, but I thought it might be helpful for folks to know that these five are arguably our most brittle modules.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-03-16 22:23 UTC

For folks making small changes to the compose box or buddy list or stream list, I doubt the intra-test leaks are going to present too many problems.  But if folks are making major feature changes, you can always create a new test module with clean setup.  One example of this is that we now test video-related features of the compose box inside of `frontend_tests/node_tests/compose_video.js`.  We generally map node test modules on a 1:1 basis with the actual modules, but this isn't a set-in-stone convention.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-03-16 22:42 UTC

Cool, yeah, thanks for doing this writeup!

**Steve Howell** · 2021-05-19 15:07 UTC

The `activity.js` test module is now leak-free.  (You can run the tests in any order.)

**Steve Howell** · 2021-05-19 15:11 UTC

Since my original post on this topic, we've introduced leaks into `message_list_view.js`, which I will investigate.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-05-19 15:20 UTC

Ok, MLV was a simple fix, so we're down to these four:

~~~
compose
message_flags
settings_user_groups
stream_list

**Steve Howell** · 2021-05-19 19:57 UTC

The `compose.js` tests no longer leak.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-05-19 20:45 UTC

Yay!

## test_subs

*2021-03-22 to 2021-03-26 · 15 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/43-automated-testing/topic/test_subs/with/1138669)*

**Sahil Batra** · 2021-03-22 11:57 UTC

I was going thorugh the tests in test_subs for testing the `create_stream_policy` and `invite_to_stream_policy`.

To give a bit more context about the code of these two policies first, we use two helper functions `can_create_streams` and `can_subscribe_other_users`in the stream creating and subscription logic to test whether the acting user is allowed to do the specified task or not. And these two helper  functions - `can_create_streams` and `can_subscribe_other_users`, do nothing but just call another function `has_permission`to do the main work on checking the role of user and the converned setting of realm to return whether the user can perform the specified task or not.

Now coming to the main part, the tests. For testing `create_stream_policy` we have two separate tests, one which tests `can_create_streams` by just checking the boolean value it returns by setting different user roel and realm setting of `create_stream_policy`. And then another tests which tests by mocking the `can_create_streams` helper and then using the required api endpoint.

But the tests for `invite_to_stream_policy` are different. For this also we have a test for only testing the `can_subscribe_other_users` function, but the cases which are checked in two tests (for `can_create_streams` and `can_subscribe_other_users`) are not same. I think we should have a consistent for such tests which can be like to just check the admin is allowed to do the change irrespective of policy and then setting the policy value one by one and just asserting that the concerned role can do the task and the user just below that cannot do. (like if setting is set to admin, then   checking admin can do the task and the role just below admin which is member cannot do (i.e. no need to cehck for roles below that) and having this consistent methods will not lead to confusion while adding tests for other settings in future and will look more concrete after we add a moderator role (I noticed this while working on adding moderator role settings only). 

`invite_to_stream_policy` also has a test which directly tests the behaior directly by calling the api endpoint. But instead of mocking the `can_subscribe_other_users` function, it actually changes the realm setting and user role, which I feel is not needed as we already have tests for `can_subscribe_other_users`. And if we think otherwise, we should atleast make it same for both the polices.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-03-22 12:25 UTC

For this kind of stuff, where there's a pretty clear boundary between the two layers of software, I prefer to have detailed testing on the lower layer, but then for the top layer it's fine to mock out the lower layer functions.  And then you want probably two end-to-end tests as a sanity check that the two layers are wired up correctly (which is probably also mostly enforced by mypy, but we want to be on the safe side).  And the end-to-end tests might do a bit more painful setup and take a bit longer to run, but they can catch bugs that mocking might allow in.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-03-22 12:27 UTC

For these particular tests, I trust your judgment on cleaning them up a bit.  If you find that one testing pattern in the existing code seems better than some other testing pattern, it's good to evolve us to the pattern that you actually find to be more readable/maintainable.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-03-22 12:28 UTC

(When I say two end-to-end tests, the "two" is fairly arbitrary.  It's fine to also have one end-to-end test that maybe tests both sides of a boolean or something.)

**Sahil Batra** · 2021-03-22 13:26 UTC

I have a small doubt regarding the end-to-end tests point. 
By also having end to end tests along with mocking, do you mean that we should also keep tests which directly check whether the user is allowed to create a stream by having different role and different stream policies, along with mocking, which will mean that in the above mentioned cases we would have three tests for each policy (`create_stream_policy` and `invite_to_stream_policy`) - one for testing the lower layer function (`can_create_streams` and `can_suscribe_other_users`), one for mocing the mentioned lower layer functions and one by not mocking but testing for different role and settings whether we allow the task or not, similar to what we have right now for `invite_to_stream_policy` [here](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/855ac26c4811c5ce2b11a392beccdeb8265453b9/zerver/tests/test_subs.py#L3235)

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-03-22 22:38 UTC

Yeah.  I think it's almost always better to avoid mocking lower-level checks in an end-to-end test, and instead do the right data setup such that functions like `can_subscribe_other_users` return the right value -- that's the general pattern we go for and is talked about a bit here: https://zulip.readthedocs.io/en/latest/testing/philosophy.html#integration-testing-or-unit-testing

## create_mock_message

*2021-03-25 to 2021-03-29 · 14 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/43-automated-testing/topic/create_mock_message/with/1143080)*

**Abhijeet Bodas** · 2021-03-25 11:02 UTC

206fe1ef3b9819268cf6fe1be6107c2d814e2ee8 introduced a new helper - `message_store.create_mock_message()` which does nothing but add a new `key: value` pair to the message store map - 
```js
export function create_mock_message(message) {
    // For use in tests only. `id` is a required field,
    // everything else is optional, as required in the test.
    stored_messages.set(message.id, message);
}
```

**Abhijeet Bodas** · 2021-03-25 11:05 UTC

The main objective was to avoid overriding things like `message_store.get()` etc, which is typically done because it's pretty tedious to create real message objects, considering `message_store.add_message_metadata` has so much validation involved in it.

**Abhijeet Bodas** · 2021-03-25 11:25 UTC

The idea was to pass whatever message fields were required for the test, and let the helper fill out the rest of the fields.
@Tim Abbott  [said](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/17440#discussion_r597298283)
> I think this function doesn't fully do what I'd had in mind -- the ideal version would populate values that were not provided in some reasonable way such that we end up with a message object with all the normal fields it should have. But I'm OK with merging this for now since this commit improves things by removing overrides.

I have a few questions, about adding these "default" fields in the helper.
- We want that, if some field is not passed to the helper, only then add a default value, right?
- How to deal with interdependent fields (for example, if `message.type = "private"`, then that message should not have a `stream` property)? If some test passes just, say the `stream: "general"` field (but not the type), should the helper infer that its a stream message and add other properties like `topic`? Wouldn't the helper become a huge tree of `if`s and `else`s in that case?
- How to handle cases where we want to test that some field was added/changed after some operation? (This scenario may not exist, please let me know if so.)

**Steve Howell** · 2021-03-25 11:30 UTC

I think the ideal scenario here would be to have a function in `frontend_tests/node_tests/lib` called `add_message`, and it would do things like adding reasonable default fields and sanity checking that you've at least provided the message type (and give you a clear error message if you don't).  And then that would call `create_mock_message` in its current form.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-03-25 11:31 UTC

I personally don't have a problem with overriding `message_store.get()` in these circumstances, though.  The API of `message_store.get` is very unlikely to change, and if your test's only interaction with `message_store` is through that API, then using `override` feels entirely appropriate to me.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-03-25 11:32 UTC

Obviously, if the code that you are testing has rich interactions with `message_store`, then it makes sense to just build a realistic, fleshed out message, and then go through the "real" code.

Makes sense. I'm not sure what the next steps are here though :thinking:

Let's just see if anybody else weighs in on the topic.

async function navigate_to(page: Page, click_target: string, tab: string): Promise<void> {

    await page.click(`a[href='#${CSS.escape(click_target)}']`);

    await wait_for_tab(page, tab);
}
...
await navigate_to(page, "narrow/is/private", "message_feed_container");
```
To,
```javascript
async function navigate_to(page: Page, parent_selector: string, click_target: string, tab: string): Promise<void> {
    console.log("Visiting #" + click_target);
    await page.click(`${parent_selector} a[href='#${CSS.escape(click_target)}']`);

    await wait_for_tab(page, tab);
}
...
await navigate_to(page, ".private_messages_header", "narrow/is/private", "message_feed_container");
```

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-03-28 23:43 UTC

We should definitely replace that.  Given the `navigate_to` interface, I wonder whether the intent is to just do navigation by changing the URL fragment?  But probably better would be to do something that has it click on the relevant element within the left sidebar, and rename it to `navigate_using_left_sidebar` (basically hardcoding `parent_element`?).  I think that's probably what that test is intending to verify.

**Riken Shah** · 2021-03-31 08:38 UTC

Opened a small [PR](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/17901) to fix this.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-03-31 13:01 UTC

Merged!  Thanks @Riken Shah (Riken-Shah)

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-04-19 19:53 UTC

**Riken Shah** · 2021-04-20 10:46 UTC

@Akshat (akshatdalton),  The reason it is failing is that the error is shown in `#admin-linkifier-status` instead of  `#admin-linkifier-pattern-status`. 

The linkifier form is capable of showing [errors in three different blocks](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/367cf897fa32262a41cbcd6527a3b319e73ec776/static/js/settings_linkifiers.js#L43).
As you have removed the `validators` option from the [pattern field](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/abcdcab16e63d1010dd3bc836f29e7768815327b/zerver/models.py#L936) and you are checking its validity through [clean function](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/abcdcab16e63d1010dd3bc836f29e7768815327b/zerver/models.py#L942) the [`error`](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/367cf897fa32262a41cbcd6527a3b319e73ec776/static/js/settings_linkifiers.js#L47) is classified as `__all__` instead of `pattern` which is causing the above situation.

The possible solution to this is either to update the `pattern` field to accept the `validators` option or update the puppeteer test.


P.S: If you decide to update the puppeteer tests (i.e checking for `#admin-linkifier-status` instead of  `#admin-linkifier-pattern-status`) please remove the relevant code to `#admin-linkifier-pattern-status` as I think so we are not using it elsewhere.

- I'm going to update the puppeteer tests (i.e. checking for `#admin-linkifier-status`).
- There is no need to remove the relevant code to `#admin-linkifier-pattern-status` as it still can show errors for the case like when the field is left blank, or the input is not a string.

**Dinesh Ch** · 2021-04-20 20:06 UTC

@Aryan Shridhar  I think there's some `.focus`or something similar being called somewhere in the actual code.  
* In the first case of the loop, only a few characters are being removed because: 
  - The loop types a few `backspace`s but not the required number.
  - There's some `focus` being called. Backspace won't work now in clearing the text.
* In second case, for odd order of text:
  - Puppeteer focuses on `input_field` and starts typing.
  - Halfway through, `.focus` or something is called on the `input_field` which moves the cursor to the start of text field but puppeteer continues to type the word resulting in a part of start of test to be in the end.

You might have to verify if my hypothesis is right and figure out a fix like waiting for the `.focus` to execute first and then test  whatever was intended to be tested.

Hope that helps.

## upgrading puppeteer to 9.1.1

*2021-05-12 to 2021-05-25 · 28 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/43-automated-testing/topic/upgrading.20puppeteer.20to.209.2E1.2E1/with/1179089)*

**Riken Shah** · 2021-05-12 06:59 UTC

I fixed almost all the flakes, the only thing blocking us from upgrading the puppeteer to 9.1.1 is the `scrolling bug (or we can also say scrolling race?)` (again).
This time it's in the settings modal. 

When we run `settings.ts`,
```typescript
async function settings_tests(page: Page): Promise<void> {
    await common.log_in(page);
    await open_settings(page);
    await test_change_full_name(page);
    -> await test_get_api_key(page); 
    -> await test_change_password(page);
```

First, it moves down the settings modal to test `api key` then it moves up to test `change password`.

The scrolling between them caused missed clicking on [`#change_password`](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/a87749b4789258bfacd23402f7541c335a378cc6/frontend_tests/puppeteer_tests/settings.ts#L54).

When it clicked on `#change_password`, it actually clicked on
[click_point.png](https://chat.zulip.org/user_uploads/2/2f/cquoWJNnwb3gNKvIe8Gl_v8h/click_point.png)

**Riken Shah** · 2021-05-12 06:59 UTC

I am proposing adding `common.scroll_to`,

```typescript

@@ -115,6 +115,24 @@ class CommonUtils {
         await page.type(selector, text);
     }
 
+    async scroll_to(page: Page, root_element_selector: string, selector: string): Promise<void> {
+        const previous_scroll_height = await page.evaluate(
+            () => (root_element_selector: string): number =>
+                document.querySelector(root_element_selector)!.getBoundingClientRect().y,
+            {},
+            root_element_selector,
+        );
+        await page.focus(selector);
+        await page.waitForFunction(
+            () => (root_element_selector: string, previous_scroll_height: number) =>
+                document.querySelector(root_element_selector)!.getBoundingClientRect().y !==
+                previous_scroll_height,
+            {},
+            root_element_selector,
+            previous_scroll_height,
+        );
+    }
+
     /**
```

This will helps us to solve the above bug, also possibly help us when we remove jQuery from puppeteer (#17833).

P.S: I am testing this function [here](https://github.com/Riken-Shah/zulip/runs/2563574809).

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-05-12 07:02 UTC

Sounds like a good set of goals (didn't read that function as I'm going to bed now)

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-05-12 19:54 UTC

That function doesn’t makes sense—if the element is already scrolled into view, there’s no reason to expect its scroll position to change.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-05-12 19:56 UTC

(Also, `previous_scroll_height` doesn’t make sense as a name for that variable, as “scroll height” has a completely [different meaning](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Element/scrollHeight).)

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-05-12 19:58 UTC

## Production Upgrade

*2021-05-26 to 2021-07-29 · 73 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/43-automated-testing/topic/Production.20Upgrade/with/1189083)*

**Gaurav Pandey (ligmitz)** · 2021-05-26 18:45 UTC

I am looking to start the work for #18346: Add an automated test for upgrading a Zulip server to current master. So the basic plan is to have Zulip's previous version (or oldest supported) be installed on an Ubuntu based distro, then perform an upgrade using a tarball for the latest commit and then perform a production verify check. The main point which can lead to this process being slow is the process of installing the previous release and then doing an upgrade; how should this be handled? Should it be a part of the already existing production test suite or we create a new workflow?

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-05-26 19:28 UTC

Yeah, the way I'd structure it is this:
* These tests would run like the `production-install` tests, i.e. after the `production-build` ones have made us a release tarball.
* Boot up a prebuilt docker container that's installed with a previous release (presumably which previous release would be parameterized for the test matrix); so we'd extend our `Dockerfiles` data set to just have installed images for each major release we support upgrading from.  (E.g. 2.1 on Bionic, 3.0 on Buster).
* Run `upgrade-zulip <tarball>`  on the system
* Run `production-verify` to check that the upgrade worked.

I think it makes sense for this to be part of the production workflow.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-05-26 19:30 UTC

Depending how fast these tests end up being, we can decide how many to do, but I'm imagining we'll just do one per old major release to get good coverage with limited cost.

Sounds good.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-06-01 19:11 UTC

For the node tests, the `css` function set/get semantics are as follows:

~~~ js
205         css(...args) {
206             if (args.length === 0) {
207                 return css || {};
208             }
209             [css] = args;
210             return self;
211         },
~~~

Continuing the discussion from #16083 about [puppeteer documentation](https://zulip.readthedocs.io/en/latest/testing/testing-with-puppeteer.html)
It is almost complete except for a few TODOs which might require some additional work like adding tools/extra code:
> TODO: Mention how to access Puppeteer screenshots in CI.

The screenshots generated on CI failure can be downloaded with the artifacts dropdown present at the top right corner of a failed run view. (This could probably go into the bullet point that already has a bit of info about these screenshots)

> TODO: Add an option for using the `headless: false` debugging mode of Puppeteer so you can watch what’s happening, and document how to make that work with Vagrant.

This would be easier on a non vagrant setup with requirements like node and puppeteer already installed. In any case, the things that would change are:
* port in `realm_url`. We use 9981 for test server but for headless we may want to change it to the dev server's 9991 as it's probably easier and faster(no webpack issue that makes the start up slow) 
* `headless` to be set to `false` obviously
It would probably be easier to set two env variables for those and load them in `puppeteer_lib/common.ts` to set those values and document that describing the setup instructions like installing node and puppeteer and asking to set those env variables. Then any test can be run with node <test_name>.js. Additionally, we could add a short script for doing those to make things easier.

> TODO: Document `--interactive`.

This runs tests in a loop like a normal run but when a test fails, it prompts `Tests failed. Press Enter to re-run tests, "q" to quit:` and pressing anything other than `q` and then clicking `Enter` reruns the failed test. This repeats in a loop allowing you to make changes to the test to see if your change works. If the test passes after you make some changes, the loop continues running other tests.

> TODO: Document how to run 100x in CI to check for nondeterminstic failures.

This involved adding a loop in `tools/test-js-with-puppeteer` and removing code irrelevant to puppeteer tests in gh actions to only run puppeteer tests. > TODO: Document any other techniques/ideas that were helpful when porting the Casper suite.

There are a few intended audiences for this piece of code, which is < 400 lines (even with imports and extensive comments).

**Steve Howell** · 2021-06-08 13:18 UTC

The first audience is developers who are new to Zulip, and possibly even a bit new to Django-style unit testing.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-06-08 13:19 UTC

Even new Zulip developers who have extensive experience on prior Django projects will need to learn about `ZulipTestCase` and `test_helpers.py`.  Obviously, it helps to just read the code for those, but it can be a bit daunting.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-06-08 13:20 UTC

The best place for new folks to start is still https://zulip.readthedocs.io/en/latest/testing/philosophy.html, but I think it's also nice to read actual code.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-06-08 13:21 UTC

(I should point out the code in `test_example.py` actually does get executed as part of our test suite, so it won't bitrot, and we'll need to maintain it if we change any of our core APIs.)

**Steve Howell** · 2021-06-08 13:22 UTC

The second audience is developers who have plenty of experience with Zulip, but who just can't remember basic idioms after they've been away from the Python side of the codebase for a couple months.  In other words, I'm talking about me.  But I think others can relate.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-06-08 13:22 UTC

So it's kind of a cheat sheet.

I am bumping this thread for GSOC students.  We're looking for folks who have stumbled upon a common testing API or a common testing technique to add examples to `test_example.py`.  Read above for more context.

This can be a nice three-hour project for somebody that has lots of leverage with relatively low effort.  If you find yourself using an interesting testing technique, you can take a half hour to think about how to construct a useful example, an hour to write it, an hour to polish it, and then maybe have a cup of tea.  It's actually a one-hour project if you stumble on something pretty simple that other folks would benefit from.

In the above thread we've also discussed opportunities for simplifying our testing API in some places.  This is another high-leverage opportunity.  If you spend a few minutes on thinking about a better API, and then a half hour on sweeping the test codebase to use the better API, your time will be reimbursed over and over again by future test writers being able to use the better API.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-07-06 14:49 UTC

Your test reminded me of another test pitfall!

**Steve Howell** · 2021-07-06 14:53 UTC

We should have a test example that covers non-determinism from unsorted lists.  When a function doesn’t have a deterministic sort order, we should either do a set comparison or sort the list in the test (if elements aren’t unique) or just have the real code sort the list (which may be hard to convey in test_example.py).

**Steve Howell** · 2021-07-06 15:04 UTC

Sorting any list that isn’t completely huge is generally cheap (because sorts are usually highly native and optimized), so I think we should encourage devs to have functions return sorted results for any non-huge list.  And then the testing idiom becomes self.assertEqual(result, sorted(result, key=…)).

**Steve Howell** · 2021-07-06 15:08 UTC

Sorting a list of a million rows is often faster than a linear operation that works in byte code.

## mock_template

*2021-06-11 to 2021-07-01 · 48 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/43-automated-testing/topic/mock_template/with/1207127)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-06-11 15:57 UTC

I think in general the model I'd want for testing template rendering is:
* We actually render the template, if it were the case that (1) it's cheap, which I'm pretty sure is true with handlebars, and (2) doing so resulted in an error if your code passed invalid valid input to the template, which I suspect isn't.
* We can hook things to run an HTML syntax checker on the output of template rendering, so that invalid HTML in a template rendered by our node tests throws an error.  (Possibly via just logging the HTML to files to keep the node tests fast, and then running a checker on the output in a separate tool / in CI if we have to).
* We have an easy way to wrap rendering so as to capture the parameters that were passed into the template, so that we can make assertions about which valid parameters were passed into the template, since that'd often be a useful correctness hook.
* We end up with coverage reporting for which templates are actually verified in this way by our node tests.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-06-11 16:09 UTC

It would be pretty easy to wire that through the new `mock_template` function.  Basically, `mock_template` could do this:

* call the actual template function
* verify the resulting HTML with some kind of syntax checker
* call the mock function (so that it can verify the data that was passed in correctly without having to wade through HTML soup)

And for tests where we are actually concerned about checking the exact HTML, I think we can call the mock function with two parameters:
* data (inbound data)
* html (outbound html)

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-06-11 16:11 UTC

Yeah, that sounds like a pretty nice design.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-06-11 16:15 UTC

I think there's some logic in us refusing to compile a template that hasn't been mocked, so that any code coverage that we get on a template has to actually be verified by the unit test for the sanity of the incoming data.  Otherwise, the tests don't really have any value over the `check_templates` tool.  If the author of the node test isn't conscientious enough to verify the sanity of the data that's passed into the template, then I doubt they'll be conscientious enough to try to fish out injection vulnerabilites.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-06-11 16:24 UTC

When we add the HTML-parsing piece, we could possibly rename `mock_template` to `add_template_spy` or something.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-06-11 16:36 UTC

I like the `mock_template` name in a world where mocking is optional, and we probably do want that to be possible for those tests that might render templates that the test isn't interested in.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-06-11 16:39 UTC

(replying to Tim Abbott)
> I like the `mock_template` name in a world where mocking is optional, and we probably do want that to be possible for those tests that might render templates that the test isn't interested in.

**Greg Price** · 2021-06-11 21:46 UTC

(replying to smalltext)
> As a general beginner question, I've been using Find All References, definitions, and implementations to understand things, but I still hit dead ends like this. Is there another tool/method I could be using to work this out?

@smalltext This is a good question! The most important tool to use here is to do a plain old string/text search for the identifier you're hitting a dead end on.

That will find references like the one Anders pointed out is involved here, where it's hidden behind a layer of dynamic code that the IDE feature can't trace through.

Here's what `git grep` finds for this example:
```
$ git grep template_stub
frontend_tests/zjsunit/handlebars.js:    window.template_stub = stub;
frontend_tests/zjsunit/handlebars.js:        "    if (window.template_stub !== undefined) {\n",
frontend_tests/zjsunit/handlebars.js:        "        return window.template_stub(",
```

**Greg Price** · 2021-06-11 21:48 UTC

Another popular tool for that kind of search is `rg` -- it has some annoying gotchas, but a slightly nicer output format and some useful features. That's what I most often use.

And VS Code has a feature to do this kind of search too, though I don't use that feature.

**Greg Price** · 2021-06-11 21:49 UTC

In general any time you're hitting a dead end in looking for the implementation of something, or the references to something, you should definitely do a plain-text search with one of these tools because there's a high chance that that'll find it.

**Greg Price** · 2021-06-11 21:51 UTC

Also if you're *not* hitting a dead end -- i.e. you are finding some results -- but anytime it's important that you find *all* the references, you should also do a plain-text search :smile:

E.g. when renaming something or otherwise changing its interface, be sure to do a plain-text search in addition to any fancy IDE smart search -- that way you catch dynamic references like this example, plus references in comments and docs that should be updated.

**Priyam Seth (Signior-X)** · 2021-06-12 10:50 UTC

What does  this mean and how to resolve?

**Abhijeet Bodas** · 2021-06-12 11:44 UTC

Here's some context from the test file for `zjquery`
```
Inorder to keep zjquery light, it only has stubs for the most commonly
used functions of jQuery. This means that it is possible that you may need to
stub out additional functions manually in the relevant test module.
```

**Abhijeet Bodas** · 2021-06-12 11:48 UTC

That probably means you'll have to create a stub for the `css` function. Here's an example from the `list_widget.js` tests:
```javascript
    container.css = (prop) => {
        assert.equal(prop, "max-height");
        return "none";
    };

```

**Priyam Seth (Signior-X)** · 2021-06-12 11:51 UTC

Thanks!

**Abhijeet Bodas** · 2021-06-12 11:54 UTC

As for the meaning of "stub" @Steve Howell (showell) can help way better than I can :smile:

**Steve Howell** · 2021-06-12 12:57 UTC

@Priyam Seth (Signior-X) I recommend reading this article:

https://circleci.com/blog/how-to-test-software-part-i-mocking-stubbing-and-contract-testing/

One thing that is a little confusing when you start testing with mocks and stubs is that people aren't very rigorous about distinguishing the two, including me. Part of the problem is that there's not much consensus about the exact definition of either.

I wouldn't worry too much about that, though.  Essentially whenever somebody talks about stubs or mocks, they are talking about some sort of test object that **simulates** behavior of a real function or class, or, in some case, simply keeps a record of how other code is calling it, so you can verify that the higher-level code is calling the lower-level code as expected, without you actually caring about the implementation of the lower code.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-06-12 12:59 UTC

I would also echo the recommendation to read https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/master/frontend_tests/node_tests/zjquery.js

**Steve Howell** · 2021-06-12 12:59 UTC

**Steve Howell** · 2021-06-12 16:24 UTC

I just pushed a change that moves the main zjquery pseudoclass implementation to its own file. If you ever need to read zjquery's implementation to figure out what it's doing, I suspect 99% of the time you'll go to [zjquery_element.js](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/master/frontend_tests/zjsunit/zjquery_element.js#L10).

**Steve Howell** · 2021-06-12 16:26 UTC

`FakeElement` isn't a true class.  We should make it into an es6 class at some point, but it does a few non-trivial things to build up the object.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-06-12 16:27 UTC

When you call `$("#foo)` in a node test that has zjquery enabled, you're essentially getting an object from the `FakeElement` function.  (You're actually getting a slightly proxied version of it, and that part of the implementation is still in `zjquery.js`.)

**Sahil Batra** · 2021-07-04 11:04 UTC

I had some questions regarding the structure and approach we follow in realm setting tests in `test_realm.py`.

1. For some of the settings, we have an individual test only for that setting in `RealmTest` class (for example `test_change_realm_default_language) and we also have `do_test_realm_update_api` which we call in loop for testing all the settings. Both the tests essentially do the same thing using the same API endpoint. And we have same for testing invalid value of these settings, we test invalid value in individual tests for settings and also have a separate test which tests invalid values for all settings. What is the reason for having same tests at two places?

2. In the `do_test_realm_update_api` function, we define a list of all possible values of settings which explains that all values are being tested, but that is not the case, we only test first two values. Usually that sort of issue results from either changes in `populate_db` (e.g. we adjusted the data in 4ad592ed4ffcbebfc31b432b273e0c6945c88a7c), or from caching that results in the order in which we run tests affecting how many queries are run.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-07-13 16:45 UTC

We generally aim to clear caches in the setUp methods for our test infrastructure in order to prevent this category of bug.

The correct thing to do in this situation is to figure out what 2 queries are occurring differently locally vs. in CI; I don't have a better way to do that than adding print statements in an environment where you get 88 queries and another where you get 86 and doing a `diff` on the output.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-07-19 16:58 UTC

Here:
```
def add_new_user_history(user_profile: UserProfile, streams: Iterable[Stream]) -> None:              
    """Give you the last ONBOARDING_TOTAL_MESSAGES messages on your public                           
    streams, so you have something to look at in your home view once                                 
    you finish the tutorial.  The most recent ONBOARDING_UNREAD_MESSAGES                             
    are marked unread.                                                                               
    """                                                                                              
    one_week_ago = timezone_now() - datetime.timedelta(weeks=1)                                      
                                                                                                     
    recipient_ids = [stream.recipient_id for stream in streams if not stream.invite_only]            
    recent_messages = Message.objects.filter(                                                        
        recipient_id__in=recipient_ids, date_sent__gt=one_week_ago                                   
    ).order_by("-id")                                                                                
    message_ids_to_use = list(                                                                       
        reversed(recent_messages.values_list("id", flat=True)[0:ONBOARDING_TOTAL_MESSAGES])          
    )                                                                                                
    if len(message_ids_to_use) == 0:                                                                 
        return                                                                                       
                                                                                                     
    # Handle the race condition where a message arrives between                                      
    # bulk_add_subscriptions above and the Message query just above                                  
    already_ids = set(                                                                               
        UserMessage.objects.filter(                                                                  
            message_id__in=message_ids_to_use, user_profile=user_profile                             
        ).values_list("message_id", flat=True)                                                       
    )                                                                                                
                                                                                                     
    # Mark the newest ONBOARDING_UNREAD_MESSAGES as unread.                                          
    marked_unread = 0                                                                                
    ums_to_create = []                                                                               
    for message_id in reversed(message_ids_to_use):                                                  
        if message_id in already_ids:                                                                
            continue                                                                                 
                                                                                                     
        um = UserMessage(user_profile=user_profile, message_id=message_id)                           
        if marked_unread < ONBOARDING_UNREAD_MESSAGES:                                               
            marked_unread += 1                                                                       
        else:                                                                                        
            um.flags = UserMessage.flags.read                                                        
        ums_to_create.append(um)                                                                     
                                                                                                     
    UserMessage.objects.bulk_create(reversed(ums_to_create))                                         
```

## outgoing webhook - fail_with_message

*2021-07-21 to 2021-07-25 · 8 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/43-automated-testing/topic/outgoing.20webhook.20-.20fail_with_message/with/1235538)*

**Gaurav Pandey (ligmitz)** · 2021-07-21 08:22 UTC

In #19248, I have written a test for the situation when the bot owner and bot gets deactivated just after the event triggering the web-hook pops an error. Since the owner and bot is deactivated, `send_response_message` throws an exception in `fail_with_message` and `notify_bot_owner` which is captured. This works as expected when I manually deactivate the user after the web-hook error, thus not sending any further messages from the bot since it is deactivated. But in the automated test, the `send_response_message` does not throw an exception and sends a message to the stream where the web-hook was triggered despite the fact that the bot owner and bot both after deactivated within the scope of the function. Not sure why it is so. Also, I don't get a no coverage error for the test considering that there is no exception hence the catch block after that is not executed.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-07-21 19:09 UTC

@Gaurav Pandey (ligmitz) that sounds like a caching bug of some sort -- e.g. there's a `user_profile` object that's already been fetched for the bot owner.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-07-21 19:09 UTC

Coverage errors only display when you run the entire test suite, so that's probably the issue there.

**Gaurav Pandey (ligmitz)** · 2021-07-21 19:26 UTC

Its a bit strange. The side effect for `fail_with_message` is also imposing that the bot owner is deactivated for `notify_bot_owner` although its not within the same scope. This leads to the message not being sent to the bot owner (which is actually expected).

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-07-21 22:18 UTC

This likely has to do with exactly when various local variables are fetched before the call that you're doing a `mock.patch` on.

**Gaurav Pandey (ligmitz)** · 2021-07-23 16:20 UTC

I took a dip into this again and found the following behavior (when the owner is deactivated just after the 408 response):

* If the bot is mentioned in a stream, `fail_with_message` works fine and send a message to the stream while `notify_bot_owner` does not send one as the owner is deactivated.

* If the bot is PMed, `fail_with_message` and `notify_bot_owner` both do not send any messages to either the PM or bot owner.

The reason I got the above behavior is because `mock_event` mocks a stream message. So I have created another function `mock_private_message_event` to test the second behavior. Should we rename `mock_event` to `mock_stream_message_event`?

Also there was no `message_id` with `near:` as `mock_event` has `id` for message as empty string.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-07-23 18:31 UTC

That renaming certainly sounds like a good idea.

**Gaurav Pandey (ligmitz)** · 2021-07-25 16:48 UTC

Updated #19248 with the suggestions.

## mock.call_args.args

*2021-07-26 to 2021-07-28 · 14 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/43-automated-testing/topic/mock.2Ecall_args.2Eargs/with/1238987)*

**Dinesh Ch** · 2021-07-26 18:35 UTC

Should we replace all `call_args[0][x]` with `call_args.args[x]`(similarly `kwargs`) for better readability in our mock objects? See https://docs.python.org/3/library/unittest.mock.html#unittest.mock.Mock.call_args. Apparently, this is new in python3.8

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-07-26 18:54 UTC

**Dinesh Ch** · 2021-07-28 16:15 UTC

**Alex Vandiver** · 2021-07-28 17:35 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-07-28 17:50 UTC

It's documented in this sorta hidden place in our CI configuration:
```
$ cat .github/workflows/zulip-ci.yml 
# NOTE: Everything test in this file should be in `tools/test-all`.  If there's a
# reason not to run it there, it should be there as a comment
# explaining why.

name: Zulip CI

on: [push, pull_request]

defaults:
  run:
    shell: bash

jobs:
  tests:
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        include:
          # Base images are built using `tools/ci/Dockerfile.prod.template`.
          # The comments at the top explain how to build and upload these images.
          # Bionic ships with Python 3.6.
          - docker_image: zulip/ci:bionic
            name: Ubuntu 18.04 Bionic (Python 3.6, backend + frontend)
            os: bionic
            is_bionic: true
            include_frontend_tests: true
          # Focal ships with Python 3.8.2.
          - docker_image: zulip/ci:focal
            name: Ubuntu 20.04 Focal (Python 3.8, backend)
            os: focal
            is_focal: true
            include_frontend_tests: false
          # Bullseye ships with Python 3.9.2.
          - docker_image: zulip/ci:bullseye
            name: Debian 11 Bullseye (Python 3.9, backend)
            os: bullseye
            is_bullseye: true
            include_frontend_tests: false
```

My PR is failing the CodeQL test for reasons I don't think are related to my changes: https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/19444/checks?check_run_id=3229606842.

**Akshat** · 2021-08-03 15:49 UTC

I'm also getting this.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-08-03 18:21 UTC

You can ignore those for your PRs; it's because CodeQL added new rules that make master fail.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-08-03 19:26 UTC

That’s not what happened. The rules are not new, and those errors have always been there. But the CodeQL action always flags errors *relative* to the current `master`. Since your PR has not been rebased past ad5f0c05b5d865fb6d3acfc333fa1d0625e91752, its tree has a slightly different version of the lines that trigger those errors, so the CodeQL action thinks that you have “fixed” three errors and “introduced” three different errors.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-08-03 19:35 UTC

This would be less visible if our `codeql-analysis.yml` workflow didn’t do `git checkout HEAD^2`. It looks like we’re [supposed](https://github.com/github/codeql-action/pull/297/files) to remove that now.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-08-03 19:47 UTC

#19481

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-08-03 23:00 UTC

Ahh, thanks for fixing.  The HEAD~2 thing was a super weird mechanism that I'd forgotten about.

## test coverage failing for continue

*2021-08-14 to 2021-08-16 · 6 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/43-automated-testing/topic/test.20coverage.20failing.20for.20continue/with/1246940)*

**Priyansh Garg (garg3133)** · 2021-08-14 09:33 UTC

The test coverage in my PR #19564 is showing that one line is missing from being covered in tests, while I'm pretty sure that I'm covering that line in my tests.

Upon further investigation, I found out that there seems to be some issue with the `continue` statement appearing alone within an `if` block. If I just keep the `continue` statement inside the `if` block, that line is shown as being missing from the test coverage.
[Screenshot-from-2021-08-14-14-57-25.png](https://chat.zulip.org/user_uploads/2/e7/KSNKO0ynVod97Ouy1pqGLOUg/Screenshot-from-2021-08-14-14-57-25.png) 

But, if I add some other statement before `continue`(say, a `print` statement), it passes the test coverage.
[Screenshot-from-2021-08-14-15-02-44.png](https://chat.zulip.org/user_uploads/2/a2/XeF3Oj2UAEHJv-B3txaV1GvL/Screenshot-from-2021-08-14-15-02-44.png)

**Abhijeet Bodas** · 2021-08-14 09:42 UTC

Yeah, there's a bug -> https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/stream/3-backend/topic/user.20group.20mentions/near/906609
Can you try to extract a function/variable and avoid the `continue`?

**Abhijeet Bodas** · 2021-08-14 09:44 UTC

Maybe we should also file an issue at https://github.com/nedbat/coveragepy/issues. I couldn't find a similar issue there.

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2021-08-14 09:45 UTC

@Priyansh Garg (garg3133) Ah, this is a  confusing consequence of how CPython optimizes this kind of  thing - https://github.com/nedbat/coveragepy/issues/198#issuecomment-399705984 and the rest of that thread have more details

@Abhijeet Bodas BTW, that's an issue for tracking this, apparently it's resolved in Python 3.10

**Steve Howell** · 2021-08-16 14:09 UTC

@Priyansh Garg (garg3133) It looks like your workaround here was to add `logging.info`, which seems reasonable to me.

I generally consider `continue` to be a code smell, as it's sort of a glorified `goto`.  In this particular code, there's a big loop over `message.get("channels", [])`, and it seems like it would be fairly difficult to extract a function here without having to pass in a lot of the shared data structures here.

So, I would probably just be sure to add a comment above the logging statement that it serves the side benefit of avoiding the CPython optimization so that the coverage reports aren't misleading.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-08-16 14:13 UTC

It's probably outside the scope of your PR, but making `process_messages` less than ~170 lines would probably be a worthwhile goal, although it may just be nature of the problem that leads to such a long function.

@Steve Howell (showell) , Do you remember i reported a bug while working on ` ListWidget` for alert-words that when we're trying to focus the element of input-search , it's not working! (though it's passing the node-tests in main and in every branch)

**Riken Shah** · 2022-04-21 16:36 UTC

It's been long time since I have debuged puppeteer test :sweat_smile:.

As we can see the issue is the [`button!.click()`](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/c2148dc4d9e2ba1ea96d8ee0c972fcf77af43e8d/frontend_tests/puppeteer_tests/subscribe_toggle.ts#L40) didn't work for some reason. 

I have seen this issue previously where `elem.click()` function doesn't work. 

As far as I  could think of there could be two possible explanation for this:
- The modal/window somehow lost focus and then `button!.click()` regain the focus of modal/window instead of clicking on the element. 
- As puppeteer can be very fast, it might be possible that the JS might be initializing or modal was not completely open and it clicked.  

I think so best solution for this is to use JS to click the button.

What do folks think?

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-04-21 19:10 UTC

The best solution is never to use JS to click the buttons. If Puppeteer is too fast, it’s because we’re not waiting for the right thing.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-04-21 19:46 UTC

Yeah, agreed, generally the solution in this situation is to add a wait for the component being ready before doing the click.

**Riken Shah** · 2022-04-22 17:07 UTC

> The best solution is never to use JS to click the buttons. If Puppeteer is too fast, it’s because we’re not waiting for the right thing.

Ohh! Yeah. 
You told me this before. 

Sorry, it's been long time.

It looks like the issue is the `click` action didn't go through for [reactivate button](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/f26479577061fcd599061f90f33c29d87d1e72ab/frontend_tests/puppeteer_tests/user-deactivation.ts#L86).

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-08-06 00:55 UTC

Yeah; so I'm guessing it's a recent regression.

**Riken Shah** · 2022-08-07 05:11 UTC

So `waitForSelector` with the `visible=true` option doesn't guarantee that the element is interactable.
Puppeteer only checks [if the element exists in the node and it's visible (after computing its style)](https://github.com/puppeteer/puppeteer/blob/eb6470931bda13d6e3aad8ae386181cacf6d2106/src/common/util.ts#L342-L384).

One thing we can do to check if the element is read to be interactable is to hover over the button and wait until `$(button).is(":hover")` evaluate to be `true`.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-08-07 05:15 UTC

That sounds plausible; do we understand why this specific button would not be interactable?

**Riken Shah** · 2022-08-07 05:19 UTC

I am just considering an improbable race condition where the chrome is still processing the table page while the puppeteer initiated the click function.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-08-07 05:26 UTC

JavaScript is single-threaded. How would that be possible?

**Riken Shah** · 2022-08-07 09:49 UTC

~~Oh, So puppeteer runs on the same thread as the browser?~~

  actual: 0,
  expected: 1,
  operator: 'strictEqual'
}
```

It is not a non-deterministic failure, It would fail for everyone I believe. It was introduced from this commit https://github.com/zulip/zulip/commit/56b2b838ee17cbce191f40704df4cfec710a2ece. 

The issue was,
```typescript

async function test_narrow_public_streams(page: Page): Promise<void> {
    await page.click(await get_stream_li(page, "Denmark"));
    await page.waitForFunction(() => $(".recipient_row:visible").length >= 3);
// Here it checks for bookend which is not there by default.
   assert.equal(await page.evaluate(() => $(".stream-status:visible").length), 1);
...
}
```


To fix this, I have raised PR #22692 which first unsubscribes from the Denmark stream and then checks for a bookend.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-03-16 18:50 UTC

From the Node.js Build Working Group Slack channel:

> Ah okay, so in theory this is what is happening:
>
> - our server is being hammered with requests
> - Because of try_files it tries certain conditions, like the $uri then the $uri with .html etc
> - Our rules need to be optimised a little bit
> - But because of the amount of requests, at one point our fs exhausts the simultaneous open() requests basically timing out
> - As nginx is not able to know if the file exists or not, it gives a 404
> - CloudFlare caches that
>
> That’s why the behaviour is also random. In the past this would actually show a 500 internal server error, because in the past we didn’t have try_files $uri =404:

Seems like they’re having a fun day.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2024-02-21 17:27 UTC

Have we considered using [`django-linear-migrations`](https://adamj.eu/tech/2020/12/10/introducing-django-linear-migrations/) to make migration conflicts into git file conflicts?

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-02-21 17:30 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-02-21 17:30 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-02-21 17:31 UTC

It does look like it prevents us from doing merge migrations without some hackery, and we do need to do those when we backport a migration, but that's fairly rare and probably not that hard to manage given that the tool does support mergemigrations having occurred in the past, but that's probably the main risk.

**Riken Shah** · 2024-06-12 16:19 UTC

(replying to Prakhar Pratyush)
> How to run it 100x in CI to check for nondeterministic failures? -- This is currently documented as TODO in [puppeteer docs.](https://zulip.readthedocs.io/en/stable/testing/testing-with-puppeteer.html#debugging-puppeteer-tests)

Sure, it's pretty straight forward, you just need to update the GH action config (`zulip-ci.yml`) to run the test 100x in loop. 

Comment out all tests blocks except puppeteer and add `--loop 100 'test file name'` to `./tools/test-js-with-puppeteer` command.

You can reference this [commit](https://github.com/Riken-Shah/zulip/commit/81c3027ea3b1328501092eaf34f2da48ebbfcbe3).

Feel free to DM me is you need help :)

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-11-01 18:46 UTC

That does seem like a test setup design failure; sending a message just before midnight will indeed have it show up as sent yesterday a few seconds later. Usually the mechanism one uses it to control time in the test. I don't see a puppeteer option to mock time. Possibly the right answer is to ignore if we're thinking about migrating to PlayWright, which does have https://playwright.dev/docs/clock, and set that after we do.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-11-01 20:04 UTC

Messages go through the server and get marked with the backend’s time.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-11-01 21:03 UTC

Oh right, so maybe we just need to mock time in the server; that is probably easier.

**Sahil Batra** · 2024-12-06 04:58 UTC

The failure is where the test is expected to fail but it passes. The test for checking the case when an invalid ID is passed to "old" value.

The "old" value passed in the test is `"direct_members": [hamlet.id], "direct_subgroups": [1111]` while the expected value is `"direct_members": [hamlet.id], "direct_subgroups": [marketing_group.id]`. 

So, since the test is passing when it should not, I think somehow `marketing_group.id` is equal to "1111", which I think is happening as we have settings that has stream creator and group creator as default, so might be the case that we are actually creating these many groups while running the full test suite. Maybe we should just make the invalid ID "11111".

Or can we just remove the test since we do not check ID validity while checking the old value, we just compare it with the setting value?

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-12-06 21:45 UTC

Yeah removing the test seems reasonable, or you can change it to -1 if we think it's worth ensuring there's a "This is an integer" validator.

    if stat.frequency == CountStat.DAY:

```

Is causing the `count_stat` to be captured for the next month instead of the current. Makes me feel like we should use `ai_credit_usage::month` instead of `ai_credit_usage::day`.

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2025-02-28 05:50 UTC

So, we have no issue with the usage being capture in the wrong month? I can image that being confusing to self hosted customers.

I was preparing a solution along the lines of 

```python
    if stat.frequency == CountStat.DAY:
        end_time = ceiling_to_day(event_time)
        # Since we set monthly usage limits on AI credit usage,
        # we want to capture the usage here in the current month
        # if the event_time is in the current month.
        if stat.property == "ai_credit_usage::day" and end_time.month != event_time.month:
            # Shift the `end_time` back 1 minute to bring it back
            # to the current month.
            end_time -= timedelta(minutes=1)

```

**Tim Abbott** · 2026-05-19 00:56 UTC

I'll just echo that `main` bring broken ends up wasting time on every PR that gets rebased past that version of `main`. 

Most issues with `main` being broken involve code we just merged, and can be pretty easy/quick to fix. (E.g., a linter error because we merged a PR written before a new linter rule). But some, like this one, involve some change in our dependencies that can be tricky to debug. I think the decision tree on `main` consistently failing CI should look like this:
- If you see how to fix it, post that you're working on it here and be willing to immediately merge a PR potentially without waiting for CI to finish. We can write a bit more of a process doc on this.
- If you don't feel you're making progress debugging it, flag down someone who might to help out within 5 minutes of your being aware of the problem.

We can write a doc on the workflow.

Quoting from the docs:
> - Merging a pull request with API changes without running
  `tools/merge-api-changelogs` to allocate a feature level number. CI
  should complain, and you can then run the merge command in a
  follow-up commit. If the commit history has many separate feature-level
  commits when merging a PR that stacked several API changes from
  different commits in a feature level, it's not a big deal. (But
  typically, we squash the `merge-api-changelogs` commit when there's
  only one commit in a PR touching the API, to keep the history clean).

## playwright

*2021-11-15 to 2021-11-16 · 6 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/43-automated-testing/topic/playwright/with/1281739)*

**Yash RE** · 2021-11-15 15:05 UTC

This is super old news at this point, but interesting story about puppeteer developers moving to Microsoft to become the playwright team. Also interesting how playwright offers cross-browser testing by patching firefox and webkit.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-11-15 19:24 UTC

Puppeteer has firefox support without forking the browser, though it's beta enough that we aren't running our tests with it.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-11-15 19:25 UTC

Structurally, one doesn't want to need a forked browser to run one's automated tests; ideally the browser codebase would support the features you need and just require configuration.  So I expect/hope the plan for Playwright is to delete the forked versions of browsers, and this is just a temporary strategy until upstream has the APIs they need.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-11-15 19:26 UTC

That said, even with puppeteer, running the tests does download a copy of the browser to run just for the tests, so the cost of using a forked version is a lot less than if it were a system designed to run with whatever browser you happen to have installed.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-11-15 21:53 UTC

My main concern in choosing Puppeteer was to bet on a technology that wouldn’t become unmaintained and stuck on old browser versions like CasperJS did. Relying on [forked browsers](https://github.com/microsoft/playwright/tree/master/browser_patches) increases that risk substantially. However, the Playwright team appears to be well-resourced and is making an effort to upstream their patches (at least [for WebKit](https://github.com/microsoft/playwright/blob/master/browser_patches/webkit/upstream_status.md)), so I expect this will get better with time.

**Yash RE** · 2021-11-16 05:41 UTC

Here's a detailed reply relating to their firefox patch, CDP and general philosophy: https://github.com/microsoft/playwright/issues/1765.
Things seem to be much better now, as compared to early 2020, in terms of upstreaming their patches.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-11-19 01:45 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-11-19 01:45 UTC

Which is done in `puppet/zulip/files/postgresql/pgroonga_setup.sql` via the puppet application.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-11-19 01:46 UTC

This output kinda looks like it was only displaying a `noop` mode:
```
+ /home/zulip/deployments/current/scripts/zulip-puppet-apply
Notice: Compiled catalog for 2b0de88a1bdd.b3qsmdnmz0tudpq43p2gswzmkf.xx.internal.cloudapp.net in environment production in 1.33 seconds
Notice: /Stage[main]/Zulip::Apt_repository/Exec[setup_apt_repo]/returns: current_value 'notrun', should be ['0'] (noop)
Notice: Class[Zulip::Apt_repository]: Would have triggered 'refresh' from 1 event
Notice: /Stage[main]/Zulip::Camo/Service[camo]/ensure: current_value 'stopped', should be 'running' (noop)
Notice: Class[Zulip::Camo]: Would have triggered 'refresh' from 1 event
Notice: /Stage[main]/Zulip::Postgresql_base/Package[postgresql-10-pgdg-pgroonga]/ensure: current_value 'purged', should be 'present' (noop)
Notice: /Stage[main]/Zulip::Postgresql_base/File[/usr/share/postgresql/10/pgroonga_setup.sql]/ensure: current_value 'absent', should be 'file' (noop)

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-11-19 01:46 UTC

I think you may be missing `-f` in that command.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-11-19 01:46 UTC

Yeah, I think that's the bug; without `/home/zulip/deployments/current/scripts/zulip-puppet-apply -f` the lack of a connected shell is defaulting to the `N` option (you can see the prompt if you look carefully).

@Priyansh Garg (garg3133) Read the code for `most_recent_usermessage`.  In your test I suggest that you explicitly star somebody's message and then track down the relevant `UserMessage` rows and then do assertions on them.  You will probably want to do something like send a message to both Hamlet and Cordelia, but then only Cordelia stars the message, so that you test both sides of your assumptions.

def enforce_proper_coverage(coverage_json: Any) -> bool:
    all_js_files = set(
        glob.glob("static/js/*.js")
        + glob.glob("static/js/*.ts")
        + glob.glob("static/shared/js/*.js")
        + glob.glob("static/shared/js/*.ts")
        + glob.glob("static/js/billing/*.js"),
    )
    enforce_fully_covered = all_js_files - EXEMPT_FILES

    coverage_lost = False
    for relative_path in enforce_fully_covered:
        path = ROOT_DIR + "/" + relative_path
        if not (path in coverage_json):
            coverage_lost = True
            print_error(f"{relative_path} has no node test coverage")
            continue
        line_coverage = coverage_json[path]["s"]
        line_mapping = coverage_json[path]["statementMap"]
        if not check_line_coverage(relative_path, line_coverage, line_mapping):
            coverage_lost = True
    if coverage_lost:
        print()
        print("It looks like your changes lost 100% test coverage in one or more files.")
        print("Ideally, you should add some tests to restore coverage.")
        print("A worse option is to update EXEMPT_FILES in `tools/test-js-with-node`.")
        print("To run this check locally, use `test-js-with-node --coverage`.")
        print()

    coverage_not_enforced = False
    for path in coverage_json:
        relative_path = os.path.relpath(path, ROOT_DIR)
        if relative_path in EXEMPT_FILES:
            line_coverage = coverage_json[path]["s"]
            line_mapping = coverage_json[path]["statementMap"]
            if check_line_coverage(relative_path, line_coverage, line_mapping, log=False):
                coverage_not_enforced = True
                print_error(f"{relative_path} unexpectedly has 100% line coverage.")

    if coverage_not_enforced:
        print()
        print("One or more fully covered files are miscategorized.")
        print("Remove the file(s) from EXEMPT_FILES in `tools/test-js-with-node`.")

    problems_encountered = coverage_lost or coverage_not_enforced
    return problems_encountered

**Statuspage** · 2022-04-05 16:44 UTC

**PyPI Down**:
* State: **postmortem**
* Description: At approximately 15:00 UTC, the TLS certificates that PyPI’s internal deployment tooling uses to secure access to Vault expired. This led to a cascading failure within the PyPI infrastructure that caused running pods to lose access to secure credentials and stopped new instances from being launched.  
  
Under normal circumstances, this would have been resolved as the Vault instances restarted and retrieved a new TLS certificate, but an abnormally large backlog of expired leases caused the new Vault instances to crash on startup and required manual intervention to cleanup extraneous leases.  
  
The initial remedy will be to upgrade our Vault instances to a version that resolves the crash on launch issue when the quantity of expired leases is too high, which would allow for this outage to have been recovered in a more automated fashion. Longer term, research and development time will be allocated to improving the automation around detection of instances nearing expiration as well as mechanisms to securely automate the unseal process for our secure storage.

**Statuspage** · 2022-06-03 12:29 UTC

**Newly uploaded files are returning 403 from files.pythonhosted.org**:
* State: **postmortem**
* Description: ## Summary

The cloud infrastructure that runs PyPI is managed via an automation tool, terraform, which allows for configuration changes to be version controlled, reviewed, and deployed automatically. This tool includes multiple backends for state sharing and locking to facilitate collaboration between multiple contributors. While migrating the remote state backend and locking features to a more robust hosted platform an error was made when setting the credentials that grant our CDN access to the object storage where uploaded files to PyPI are hosted.  
  
The result was that newly uploaded files as well as files that had expired from our CDNs cache were unavailable. The outage began 2022-06-022 20:28 UTC and was initially mitigated 2022-06-02 22:38 UTC by rolling back the configuration to a previous version. The configuration issue in the hosted platform was confirmed and corrected 2022-06-02 12:00 UTC and a corrected new version of the CDN configuration was deployed. Future deploys will include this value and will regress.

## Details

As the Infrastructure team at the PSF onboards a new hire and the clunkiness of collaborating on our terraform configuration led to only two people having the ability to deploy changes, a decision was made to migrate all state, sensitive variables, and locking to a hosted backend for terraform. This will allow all those with appropriate access \(PyPI Admins and PSF Infrastructure Staff\) access without having to pass around plaintext secrets necessary to plan and apply changes to the infrastructure.  
  
During the migration from S3 state storage and DynamoDB locking to Hashicorp Terraform Cloud, the Infrastructure staff lead made an error in copying the value for the GCS secret access key that grants Fastly, our CDN, access to read the Cloud Storage bucket where PyPI uploads are stored.  
  
Because the value was marked as sensitive in Terraform Cloud via a setting, it wasn’t obvious to the staff member when planning the changes what would change, and it was assumed to be an artifact of that setting. As a confirmation and for assurances, the staff member configured the changes to Fastly configuration to _not_ auto activate the new configuration.  
  
After applying the changes which would not be automatically activated in Fastly it is unclear why the incorrect change was not identified when diffing service configurations, but ultimately it was missed and the services were activated.

Impact lasted 140 minutes until enough signal from users was raised to alert PyPI admins and affected all new uploaded files as well as any files that had expired from our CDN caches.

## Future Mitigation

This outage highlighted two key areas where improvements can be made to ensure timely response

1. **More thorough automated monitoring of file access via our CDN.** Due to the caching nature of our CDN, it was not detected that this error was occurring as the file checked never expired from cache. We will implement a monitor that checks for a file that is explicitly not cached to ensure that the entire system from client to object-store is working appropriately
2. **Improvements to secrets handling in our infrastructure automation.** We carried some legacy practices for storing secrets/configuration in our systems that led to pertinent configuration value being obscured in a complex object rather than an individual key. We’ll refactor this to make detecting changes to values more obvious to contributors to the project.
