**Statuspage** · 2022-06-10 16:32 UTC

**Redirect Loops on JSON API endpoints.**:
* State: **postmortem**
* Description: ## Summary

PyPI's JSON API experienced an incident that caused redirect loops to occur for all clients when requesting many of the endpoints available on the service. These endpoints provide JSON documents describing projects and specific releases of projects hosted on [pypi.org](http://pypi.org).

This incident was initiated by changes intended to make the JSON API more performant and less of a burden on the PyPI backends.

Specifically, the combination of [this change to the warehouse codebase](https://github.com/pypa/warehouse/pull/11546) and [this change to the CDN configuration for PyPI](https://github.com/python/pypi-infra/pull/87) update the canonical locaiton for accessing the JSON documents deterministic. This allows for deeper cache efficiency and the ability to move redirects to the canonical URL out to the CDN edge. The result is faster response times for clients and reduced load on the PyPI backends.

The redirect updates specifically had an unintended consequence that led to this outage. Namely the existing elements in cache for the "normalized" project names redirected to the verbatim names of projects.

Example:

* Before

    * `/pypi/pyOpenSSL/json` "verbatim" project name url returns a `200` with the document and is canonical.
    * `/pypi/pyopenssl/json` "normalized" project name url `301` redirects to canonical URL.
    
* After

    * `/pypi/pyOpenSSL/json` "verbatim" project name url returns a `301` redirect to canonical URL.
    * `/pypi/pyopenssl/json` "normalized" project name url returns a `200` with the document and is canonical.
    

The issue at hand is that what is intended to the new canonical URL using the "normalized" project name was cached for _many_ projects, and that cache included a redirect to the "verbatim" project name, which... redirected back.

## Impact

This impacted any client of the PyPI JSON API. These include the `poetry` tool for installing and managing Python dependencies, mirroring tools such as `bandersnatch`, and even our own internal service that redirects legacy file URLs on [files.pythonhosted.org](http://files.pythonhosted.org) to their new locations.

The outage began with the deployment of [this change to the warehouse codebase](https://github.com/pypa/warehouse/pull/11546) and [this change to the CDN configuration for PyPI](https://github.com/python/pypi-infra/pull/87) at approximately 2022-06-10T10:50 UTC and continued to impact some URLs in a "long-tail" fashion through to 2022-06-10T16:00 UTC. Most notably project names beginning with `p` were the last to be affected as it is the most common first letter for projects uploaded to PyPI.

## Mitigation

The changes described that led to this outage have been actively being attempted for over 6 weeks after more than a year of being aware of the problem. When faced with a system that was functioning correctly, but required purging of cache to be fully established the PyPI administrator managing the deployment chose to roll forward rather than roll back, knowingly extending the impact of this incident in favor of getting PyPI to a more maintainable state for serving the JSON API into the future.

Because of the massive scale of PyPI's caches it was untenable to specifically purge bad URLs, leading to a need to clear the entire PyPI cache. This was undertaken by kicking off pools of processes that would iterate over individual first letters of project names to purge the entire project cache in parallel over a 1-2 hour duration. This duration was required as purging the entire cache would have overloaded the backends for PyPI in such a way that even with massive temporary scale up/out the load would have been too much for _many more hours_ than even this incident.

While most of the purges completed within the two hour estimate, the letter `p` was the final sgement, taking nearly 4 hours due to the popularity of the `py` prefix on the index.

While the purges were ongoing PyPI's backends even in a scaled out state provided lackluster response times and performance as the caches were slowly refilled.

## Future work

Issues have been filed to create better tooling to safely and expediently purge the caches and to limit the blast radius of purges in the future.

We will also begin to research ways to build more confidence and expose these kinds of errors in our review process for changes to the configuration of our CDN.

**Statuspage** · 2022-06-28 14:37 UTC

**Queue delay affecting CDN purges and emails**:
* State: **postmortem**
* Description: ### Summary

PyPI initially experienced delays in features which used a centralized task queue \(such as purging the CDN cache and sending emails\) due to a poorly performing task type. This was followed by an outage due to the combination of the steps taken to mitigate the queue issue and unrelated changes that affected PyPI’s performance, resulting in PyPI becoming unavailable via the web or for installations.

### Details

On Thu, 23 Jun 2022 at 04:55 UTC, PyPI admins deployed a change which introduced a new periodic task designed to aggregate statistics about 2FA usage on PyPI. This task was designed to run every 5 minutes and sampled multiple counts of different characteristics of 2FA usage.

This task used a database query that attempted to count a large number of rows, and had poor performance, causing high database utilization and a long processing time for the task. However, while long-running, the task was finishing and publishing metrics, and so PyPI admins were unaware of its poor performance. Over time, however, the tasks that workers were actively working on began to include more and more of these poorly-performing tasks, exhausting the number of available workers to process other tasks.

On Sun, 26 Jun 2022 at 17:29 UTC, PyPI admins deployed an unrelated change which replaced the JSON serializer used by PyPI from the standard library JSON serializer to a third-party JSON serializer, with benchmarks indicating that this would result in a 6x savings on time to serialize JSON, and thus a significant savings on response time for PyPI’s various JSON-rendering endpoints. 

At 21:06 UTC, PyPI admins began to receive reports that newly published versions were not being immediately updated in the web frontend for PyPI, not installable, and that emails were delayed. However, because the queue backlog was sufficiently small at this point, this small number of early reports were resolved within an hour and attributed to transient errors.

Over the course of the following 12 hours, which coincided with the US EST evening, night and early morning, PyPI admins received an increasing stream of user reports that emails were delayed and project pages were not updating.

On Mon, 27 Jun 2022 at 15:43 UTC, PyPI admins determined that PyPI’s task queue had a significant backlog, with more than 46K pending tasks, with the oldest task being more than 14 hours old, and began attempting to mitigate the backlog.

PyPI admins determined that the backlog correlated with an increase in CPU usage by the database, and that there were at least two poorly-performing queries: one which had been introduced in the task for the 2FA metrics, and another which was due to a historical implementation detail of how PyPI projects are modeled in the database, where normalized project names are not stored in the database, but generated upon request based on the un-normalized project name

To mitigate the load on the database, PyPI admins immediately began canceling the long-running database queries that resulted from the poorly performing task, in an attempt to remove as many as possible from the queue and free up workers to complete other tasks. Simultaneously, admins prepared two separate changes to mitigate the two poorly-performing queries: one to temporarily disable the poorly performing metrics task, and a second to add a column in the database which stored the normalized project name.

At 15:53 UTC, PyPI admins deployed the first change that disabled the 2FA metrics task, which resulted in stopping additional long-running queries from being created. Admins continued to manually reap the poorly performing query as PyPI’s workers began to drain the backlog of other tasks. At this time, the size of the queue began to decrease.

At 16:19 UTC, PyPI admins deployed the second change which added a column for the normalized project name. This included a large migration which unexpectedly locked PyPI’s database for a significant amount of time, resulting in PyPI backends being unable to create new database connections, becoming unhealthy, and causing responses to fail.

At 16:45 UTC, the migration finished and PyPI backends began to recover, however PyPI still continued to intermittently return errors and did not become fully healthy, which was not explicable based on the previous mitigations.

After investigation, PyPI admins determined that workers were crashing due to exceeding their allotted memory usage. Admins determined that the natural increase in requests after having an outage resulted in a large amount of memory being consumed by the new JSON serializer, which had higher memory footprint than the previous JSON serializer.

At 17:41 UTC, PyPI admins deployed a change reverting the new JSON serializer back to the original serializer, and backends eventually returned to healthy status.

### Impact

As a result of the task queue becoming increasingly large, user-facing tasks such as CDN purges and emails became more and more delayed. Delayed CDN purges meant that the PEP-503 ‘simple’ API was not getting updated and installers were unable to become aware of newly-published packages or new versions of existing packages. Additionally, the web frontend was not displaying new versions or new packages. Users attempting to create accounts and verify email addresses were unable to do so as well.

At the peak, the task queue had nearly 50K pending tasks, and the oldest task in the queue was more than 14 hours old, whereas this queue normally has less than 100 pending tasks on average and tasks are completed in less than 1 second.

![](https://dustingram.com/assets/images/pypi-incident-jun-27-2022/1.png)
![](https://dustingram.com/assets/images/pypi-incident-jun-27-2022/2.png)
As a result of the locked migration, PyPI backends became unhealthy and served 500-level errors to users, preventing much of the web traffic, API traffic and uploads from succeeding for approximately 40 minutes.

![](https://dustingram.com/assets/images/pypi-incident-jun-27-2022/3.png)
![](https://dustingram.com/assets/images/pypi-incident-jun-27-2022/4.png)
As a result of the increased memory usage due to the new JSON serializer, the PyPI backends did not fully recover from the prior outage and continued to return intermittent errors as pods consumed their available memory and were terminated.

During the entire process, PyPI deployments were delayed due to their dependence on a successful run of a shared CI pipeline which had a significant backlog at the time changes were attempting to be introduced. This impacted the delivery times for changes to mitigate the issues.

### Future work

During the outage, it was identified that the service PyPI uses for alerting and monitoring was insufficiently configured to notify the team of an excessively large task queue, which would have given administrators early warning that the 2FA metrics task was failing to complete and that delays were increasing. Additionally, the monitoring system lacked alerts for high CPU utilization in the database which was indicative of poorly performing queries. Alerts for both of these have already been added.

When PyPI admins re-enable the 2FA metrics task, it will be redesigned to speed up queries by denormalizing counts rather than naively counting rows.

In order to mitigate delays in PyPI’s CI pipeline, PyPI admins will migrate PyPI’s source repository to a separate organization, in order to ensure that the CI queue remains small and changes can be quickly deployed.

In order to prevent long-running migrations from locking the database for extended periods of time, PyPI’s migration runner will be modified to make migrations safer, including adding timeouts after a certain short period of time rather than block for an arbitrarily long time.

In order to mitigate complications when attempting to recover from an outage, PyPI admins will implement a policy to ensure that changes which are not directly related to the recovery efforts will not be merged until the outage has been resolved.

**Statuspage** · 2022-10-24 16:05 UTC

**PyPI Backends are unavailable.**:
* State: **postmortem**
* Description: ## Summary

The cluster that hosts PyPI’s backends as well as multiple ancillary services experienced an outage during maintenance that interrupted access to services over HTTPS.

## Details

From 2022-10-24 14:43 UTC until 2022-10-24 15:03 UTC, PyPI’s backends were not accessible over HTTPS. This interfered with our CDNs ability to fetch pages, made uploads to [uploads.pypi.org](http://uploads.pypi.org) impossible, and interrupted other services such as our legacy file redirect service.  
  
PyPI services run as deployments in a Kubernetes cluster and are exposed via Ingress with the AWS Elastic Load Balancer \(ELB\) integration. The TLS certificate that this load balancer uses is managed via Amazon’s Certificate Manager \(ACM\). When initially deploying our Kubernetes cluster, the Ingress managed ELB was configured to use an existing ACM TLS certificate.  
  
Earlier today, regular maintenance of our Kubernetes cluster required a rolling restart of all nodes in the cluster to distribute upgrades and new configurations to all nodes. During this rolling restart as the Kubernetes API server hosts were deployed, Kubernetes validated and refreshed the Ingress configurations we had previously defined.  
  
Since the most recent rolling upgrade, an additional hostname was needed for PyPI’s Ingress. PyPI administrators created a new ACM TLS certificate including that hostname and updated the Ingress managed ELB to use this new certificate. As a result, the new Kubernetes API servers were unable to find the previous ACM TLS certificate and disabled the HTTPS listener for the Ingress configuration that serves PyPI and associated services as they came online.  
  
Once identified, the PyPI admins updated the Ingress configuration to point to the new ACM TLS certificate and Kubernetes restored the HTTPS listener on the Ingress managed ELB, restoring access to all services.

## Mitigation

We will investigate mechanisms by which the hostnames needed on ACM TLS certificates for PyPI’s Ingress configurations can be managed via Kubernetes resources rather than manually via the AWS console. By managing resources all via the Kubernetes API, drift between desired state and reality will be less likely to occur and surface during similar maintenance in the future.

**Statuspage** · 2022-10-26 20:05 UTC

**PyPI Database Upgrade**:
* State: **scheduled**
* Description: PyPI's databases will be undergoing a major version upgrade during this period. At the beginning of the maintenance window, PyPI will be set to a read only mode to ensure database consistency as data is migrated to a new database instance running the upgraded version.

We anticipate that PyPI will remain in read only mode for approximately 60-90 minutes. During this time, uploads will not be allowed and changes that would result in any database write will not succeed via the web UI. All client APIs (simple, JSON, XMLRPC) will remain online and fully available during the maintenance.

During this time, uploads will not be allowed and changes that would result in any database write will not succeed via the web UI. All client APIs (simple, JSON, XMLRPC) will remain online and fully available during the maintenance.

If you notice an impact that is not consistent with the above, please report it to admin@pypi.org.

**Statuspage** · 2022-10-28 17:37 UTC

**PyPI Database Upgrade**:
* State: **postmortem**
* Description: While successful and without error, this database maintenance took a little over 200% of the time we expected and communicated.  
  
In analyzing the performance of the dump/restore process necessary for upgrading major versions of our database, we noted that one table in particular \(our largest\) took nearly four times longer than in initial testing of the procedure while all other tables performed as observed in tests.  
  
We identified two differences between our trial runs and the actual final migration:  
  
- PyPI’s codebase being in read-only mode  
- Upgrades to the database client utilities  
  
We have nothing to indicate that changing our codebase to stop database writes would have impacted performance, and are reasonably confident that using different versions of the dump/restore utilities may have impacted our estimates.  
  
We will consider other methods for this kind of maintenance in the future and apologize for the extended duration of this maintenance. After our previous major database upgrade in December 2021, we are satisfied with the minimized impact on installers in this maintenance window but have a goal of reducing the duration that PyPI needs to be in read-only in the future.

**Statuspage** · 2023-04-11 09:27 UTC

**PyPI: Object Storage Migration**:
* State: **scheduled**
* Description: The object storage for PyPI (pypi.org) and Test PyPI (test.pypi.org) are being migrated to new redundant storage. We anticipate that this maintenance will about two days to fully complete, but have worked to ensure that it should have minimal, if any perceptible impact on users.

During the migration, files not found in our new bucket will be fetched from the bucket we are migrating away from. This is the only *expected* impact and may incur additional latency for misses. We will be monitoring for this latency.

While we do live in the blessed days of error code correction ram being the status quo, we cannot rule out that some objects may be inconsistent. The tools used for migrating objects perform checksumming, but we will be doing a full reconciliation sweep after the migration has completed to ensure that all files currently known to the databases were stored with the correct checksum.

If you experience any unexpected behavior with file downloads from files.pythonhosted.org during this migration, please file an issue at https://github.com/pypi/support/issues.

**Statuspage** · 2024-08-22 20:48 UTC

**PyPI Simple Index Timing Out**:
* State: **postmortem**
* Description: **What happened?**

PyPI experienced an outage which resulted in serving 500-level responses for certain requests, including requests to a subset of the [Simple Repository API](https://peps.python.org/pep-0503/), from approximately 19:00:00 UTC to 20:15:00 UTC. As a result, some packages were uninstallable during this period. While such outages are not entirely uncommon and generally easy to recover from, this outage was more severe due to PyPI becoming un-deployable as a result of its own outage.

**Impact**

At its peak, PyPI served errors at approximately 25 responses per second and in total nearly 100K requests during this ~1hr 15m period resulted in an error. This represents approximately 0.04% of usual traffic to the affected services.

**Background**

PyPI is served by a Python web application named ‘Warehouse’, with several dependencies on Python packages that are hosted on PyPI. As part of the deployment pipeline, Warehouse and its dependencies are built into a series of container images that are ultimately deployed into a container orchestration service.

At the time of the incident, PyPI contributors were working on adding new functionality, which included introducing a new service to the service layer used with PyPI’s web framework. While the actual details of this new functionality is unrelated, a misconfiguration of this new service resulted in views that depended on this service failing to successfully serve a response, which was missed by PyPI’s unit test suite and by manual testing of the feature branch.

**Investigation**

PyPI administrators were notified of a production error approximately 10 minutes after it was introduced, and immediately after a faulty request was served:

* 2024-08-21T18:48:29 UTC - The feature branch is merged into the \`main\` branch of the Warehouse repository
* 2024-08-21T18:55:42 UTC - The container image is built and deployed to production
* 2024-08-21T18:58:37 UTC - PyPI admins are notified of an exception in production affecting a Simple Repository API view

At this point, PyPI administrators began working on a fix.

**Root Causes and Trigger**

PyPI administrators immediately determined that the recent merge was at fault due to timing and clear signals from the error observed.

As a result of PyPI’s container orchestration and deployment service not explicitly supporting rollbacks, issues like this are generally resolved by introducing a new pull request which reverts the problematic commit, which in turn is merged and [deployed.](http://deployed.In)

In this instance, a revert commit was prepared, however the decision was made to wait for a forward fix to be prepared instead. This was partly because it was thought that this fix would be a trivial change and could be prepared as quickly as a revert, thus saving time overall.

However, additionally, the introduction of the new feature included a database migration which had already been applied in production. This migration could not be reverted simply by reverting the commit, as deployment would fail when it would attempt to bring the database up to date with the migration history, and find that the current migration version was no longer present. This instead would require an additional migration to migrate the database forwards to a state that would be compatible with the reverted commit, which would potentially take more time than introducing a fix.

The fix was prepared, merged and deployed, however it contained an additional issue that resulted in it not ultimately resolving the root cause. An additional pull request to rectify the issue with the forward fix was prepared.

At this time, PyPI administrators noted that PyPI’s CI/CD suite was failing to build the containers required to run the test suite on new pull requests, due to the \`/simple\` detail page for one of PyPI’s dependencies being unresolvable due to the outage. As a result, the team decided to pursue a full revert of the feature instead, hoping to leverage our container layer cache to ensure that external requests to PyPI would not be necessary to build. An additional pull request to fully revert the faulty commit was prepared.

While the container image build on the new PR was successful, a CI/CD check which did not use the container image, namely a check that ensures Warehouse’s dependency lock files are up-to-date, failed due to the outage. PyPI administrators attempted disabling the required status of these checks in branch protection for the repository, however the failed dependency check caused the remaining tests to be canceled before completion, which prevented the deployment pipeline from picking up on the new commit and triggering a deployment.

At this time, PyPI administrators determined that overriding the build/deploy service to manually revert the deployed container image back to a known good image, bypassing the release phase that included migrations, was required.

**Mitigation**

Mitigation required bypassing PyPI’s build and deploy pipeline to manually re-deploy a previously built image, without running the release phase which included migrations. This allowed PyPI to successfully respond to previously failing requests, allowing the reverted pull request to build and be deployed, fully resolving the issue in production.

* 2024-08-21T20:17:58 UTC - The revert was fully deployed to production and errors subsided

Additionally, after the production incident was resolved, it was determined that although the final deployment to TestPyPI had been reported as successful, it had not succeeded due to the database migration failing to get a lock, highlighting that there was additionally a logic error in our deployment reporting when deployments fail.

**Lessons Learned**

* Until additional protections are in place, when an outage affects \`/simple\`, reverts must be immediate or they run the risk of requiring manual intervention.
* It is clear that a lack of functional testing is a gap in assurances against production outages.

**Things That Went Well**

* Maintaining cached container image layers proved potentially useful for recovering from issues where new container images could not be built due to the outage.

**Things That Went Poorly**

* PyPI used to maintain a mirror of itself on a third-party service to prevent incidents like this, however this is no longer used due to maintenance of the mirror becoming an issue due to on-disk size.
* The decision to not revert and fix forward instead proved to not work out. While the additional time to do the additional work to revert could have still resulted in a stuck merge, waiting for the forward fix, which had additional issues, resulted in enough time passing for one of PyPI’s dependencies to be affected by the outage.
* A popular dependency, which was also a Warehouse sub-dependency, quickly fell out of cache. PyPI’s CDN is configured to serve stale responses while it revalidates for 5 minutes, and to serve stale responses while the backends are returning errors for 1 day, so the CDN should not have served an error for any of these pages.
* The lack of a mirror and a production dependency on PyPI allowed for an ‘ouroboros’ style paradoxical outage that could not be resolved by a simple revert.
* A subset of CI/CD checks in the critical path to deployment reach out to PyPI directly as part of their tests, and as a result they will likely fail in conditions like this outage.
* Failing CI/CD checks that were not strictly required by branch protection rules were preventing the deployment pipeline from proceeding with the deployment due to setting \`cancel-in-progress: true\` on the parent workflow, causing the workflow to fail when they failed or were canceled.
* The Warehouse codebase has extensive unit testing which depends on stubbing/mocking which masked the root cause. The codebase only recently gained the ability to perform functional testing, but the problematic PR did not add additional functional tests, and the limited functional testing that did exist missed this issue.

**Where We Got Lucky**

* At the time of the incident, all of PyPI’s administrators were online and able to contribute towards mitigating the outage, including the sole administrator that was capable of performing the manual rollback.

**Action Items**

* Determine why the sub-dependency fell out of cache more quickly than expected based on the CDN configuration, and how that could have been prevented.
* Add functional testing to cover the Simple Repository API, with a focus on critical code paths that can cause similar outages.
* Update the deployment pipeline to correctly report on deployment status.
* Introduce rollback functionality for the deployment pipeline so that a rollback does not require manual intervention or specific knowledge.
* Re-introduce a mirror \(either static or a caching proxy\) for PyPI that would not be affected by production outages.
* Revisit the CI/CD dependency check and determine how it be hardened against a production outage to not block a deployment.

* Description: We have identified a flood of requests from a cluster using the `python-requests/2.32.3` User-Agent which do not include a trailing slash to the JSON api endpoints.

## node tests parallel

*2022-01-05 to 2022-01-06 · 12 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/43-automated-testing/topic/node.20tests.20parallel/with/1304579)*

**Steve Howell** · 2022-01-05 15:56 UTC

What do folks think of running node tests serially by default, so that they're easier to debug?  In my setup the parallelization has kind of a disappointing speedup, and I don't really love the idea of fielding questions for the next couple years about interleaved output.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-01-05 21:10 UTC

Hmm, for me it's currently: 10s when run parallel vs. 14s serial with hot cache -- definitely lower than I'd have expected.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-01-05 21:11 UTC

There's probably some sort of bug hidden in it helping as little as it does.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-01-05 21:11 UTC

OK it finishes in like 7s with `--parallel=2`.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-01-05 21:11 UTC

And a bit faster with 3 or 4.  So I think the bug is that it is using too many processes.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-01-05 21:12 UTC

Hmm, 4 is the default -- that's weird.  And indeed, now if I run it with no options it finishes in 6s.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-01-05 21:12 UTC

So I think the core issue is there's some sort of caching detail that means you need to run it 3x in a row to have it be at full speed.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-01-05 21:12 UTC

You’re probably seeing the Babel cache.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-01-05 21:13 UTC

In any case, what I was going to say is that if `--parallel=1` is too annoying to type, you can create an alias; and if multiple folks want that we could make a dotfile setting to adjust the default, but I think it's probably worth optimizing for runtime in the default setting?

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-01-05 21:14 UTC

Our naïve parallelism strategy does not interact well with Babel. Lots of compilation will be duplicated between processes, and it might be that only the compilation from the slowest process gets propagated to future runs.

**Steve Howell** · 2022-01-06 23:56 UTC

(replying to Tim Abbott)
> In any case, what I was going to say is that if `--parallel=1` is too annoying to type, you can create an alias [...]

My concerns here aren't my own convenience, but that newbies will get confused by the parallel output just for a modest speedup.  But it's probably something that we don't have a ton of data on, so maybe not a big deal.

**Steve Howell** · 2022-01-06 23:58 UTC

see also #**tools>test-js-with-node**

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-02-25 18:44 UTC

When you change your password, we destroy all existing browser sessions, so it is expected that there is a brief race where `GET /events` requests will fail with a 401 error -- basically if the request begins before the old session is deleted.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-02-25 18:45 UTC

We have some special logic that runs in that situation:
```
    args.error = function wrapped_error(xhr, error_type, xhn) {                                          
        remove_pending_request(xhr);                                                                     
                                                                                                         
        if (reload_state.is_in_progress()) {                                                             
            // If we're in the process of reloading the browser,                                         
            // there's no point in running the error handler,                                            
            // because all of our state is about to be discarded                                         
            // anyway.                                                                                   
            blueslip.log(`Ignoring ${args.type} ${args.url} error response while reloading`);            
            return;                                                                                      
        }                                                                                                
                                                                                                         
        if (xhr.status === 401) {                                                                        
            if (password_change_in_progress || xhr.password_changes !== password_changes) {              
                // The backend for handling password change API requests                                 
                // will replace the user's session; this results in a                                    
                // brief race where any API request will fail with a 401                                 
                // error after the old session is deactivated but before                                 
                // the new one has been propagated to the browser.  So we                                
                // skip our normal HTTP 401 error handling if we're in the                               
                // process of executing a password change.                                               
                return;                                                                                  
            }                                                                                            
```

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-02-25 18:45 UTC

Though that's primarily directed towards avoiding throwing exceptions unexpectedly; it doesn't do a retry.

## ci pipelines

*2022-03-14 to 2022-03-16 · 6 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/43-automated-testing/topic/ci.20pipelines/with/1344257)*

**Vitaliy** · 2022-03-14 20:06 UTC

Hi. My name is Vitaliy. I live in Dublin and I'm studying Software development in DevOps. Zulip project was selected as an object for research. The research I'm currently working on is to investigate the efficiency of the CI/CD pipeline. I need to find the weakest places in the CI/CD pipeline and propose improvements or fixes. Investigate if the best DevOps practices are applied.  After I've read the Zulip documentation I did not find some information, so I'm asking my questions here. The  'update-oneclick-apps.yml'  file describes the workflow to upload the built Docker image with the latest Zulip App. Why this is always marked as not successful? How the chat.zulip.org server is being updated after the software was released? Is it a manual update or there are third-party tools that deploy the latest software? How do you gather, if so, the statistic of successful and not successful Ci/CD runs? I would much appreciate any help or information.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-03-14 21:47 UTC

@Vitaliy the `onclick-apps` build is not part of the main CI; it builds an image used only for Digital Ocean which had some technical issues at the time of the last couple releases.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-03-14 21:48 UTC

Statistics are probably available in GitHub Actions UI somewhere, but I don't think they're interesting for us; our goal is to fix all nondeterministic CI failures in `main`, and we debug those via responding to the automated notifications #**automated testing>main failing**.

**Vitaliy** · 2022-03-16 20:48 UTC

Thank you, Tim, for your replies.  I have some more questions. I know you are very busy with the Zulip project and I'm sorry for distracting you. My first question is about the release process. Why you did not automate this process. As an example, there might be one more workflow that reacts to the word 'Release' in the commit comments while pushing the code to the main branch. This will trigger the release process. My second question would be about automated deployment. I did not see any deployment workflow in the Zulip repository. Is the Zulip server on chat.zulip.org being upgraded manually? Or how do you do this? Thanks and sorry for distracting you.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-03-16 20:53 UTC

@Vitaliy here are some thoughts:
* We often want to be doing chat.zulip.org deployments explicitly, both because we test things that are not in `main` on this server, and because some changes are migrations that we want to watch run for QA or other reasons. It doesn't take much time and automatically triggered deployments there (rather than the manual ones we do like 4x/week) would not help my workflow. (The actual deployment is just pushing a branch and running `upgrade-zulip-from-git`, so it's automated in that sense).
* For releases, it's also the case that most of the work is communication that is not possible to automate. There's a few bits of added automation that we'd like to add. This checklist is complete if you're interested: https://zulip.readthedocs.io/en/latest/subsystems/release-checklist.html#executing-the-release

**Vitaliy** · 2022-03-16 20:58 UTC

Thanks, Tim. I'll look at how the release can be automated, but after I'll finish my research paper. It's worth trying.

    def request(self, **request):

        signal_uid = "template-render-%s" % id(request)

        # Capture exceptions created by the handler.
        exception_uid = "request-exception-%s" % id(request)
        got_request_exception.connect(self.store_exc_info, dispatch_uid=exception_uid)
        try:
            response = self.handler(environ)

            signals.template_rendered.disconnect(dispatch_uid=signal_uid)

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-04-26 17:04 UTC

At least one bug is just that the `EmailLogBackEnd` used by that test when `settings.DEVELOPMENT_LOG_EMAILS`  is enabled uses a fixed `EMAIL_CONTENT_LOG_PATH`:
```
        # Read in the pre-existing log, so that we can add the new entry                                 
        # at the top.                                                                                    
        try:                                                                                             
            with open(settings.EMAIL_CONTENT_LOG_PATH) as f:                                             
                previous_emails = f.read()                                                               
        except FileNotFoundError:                                                                        
            previous_emails = ""                                                                         
                                                                                                         
        with open(settings.EMAIL_CONTENT_LOG_PATH, "w+") as f:                                           
            f.write(new_email + previous_emails)                                                         
```

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-04-26 17:06 UTC

That can likely be fixed using the test runner logic, which sets a unique `TEST_WORKER_DIR` for each worker.
```
def initialize_worker_path(worker_id: int) -> None:                                                      
    # Allow each test worker process to write to a unique directory                                      
    # within `TEST_RUN_DIR`.                                                                             
    worker_path = os.path.join(TEST_RUN_DIR, f"worker_{_worker_id}")                                     
    os.makedirs(worker_path, exist_ok=True)                                                              
    settings.TEST_WORKER_DIR = worker_path                                                               
                                                                                                         
    # Every process should upload to a separate directory so that                                        
    # race conditions can be avoided.                                                                    
    settings.LOCAL_UPLOADS_DIR = get_or_create_dev_uuid_var_path(                                        
        os.path.join(                                                                                    
            "test-backend",                                                                              
            os.path.basename(TEST_RUN_DIR),                                                              
            os.path.basename(worker_path),                                                               
            "test_uploads",                                                                              
        )                                                                                                
    )                                                                                                    
    settings.SENDFILE_ROOT = os.path.join(settings.LOCAL_UPLOADS_DIR, "files")                           
```

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-04-26 17:06 UTC

So probably if we make `EMAIL_CONTENT_LOG_PATH` a function of `TEST_WORKER_DIR` in tests using that feature, it'll help.

## duplicate CI runs

*2022-07-07 to 2022-07-07 · 4 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/43-automated-testing/topic/duplicate.20CI.20runs/with/1400843)*

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-07-07 00:46 UTC

Until now, we’ve always been running CI on both `push` events and `pull_request` events, which means it ran twice for commits that are pushed to a pull request. I’ve just fixed this in #22385. CI will run for all pull requests, but will only run on push for branches named `*.x`, `chat.zulip.org`, and `main`.

If you want to run our CI on another branch that isn’t in a pull request, you can [manually run a workflow](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/managing-workflow-runs/manually-running-a-workflow).

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-07-07 20:00 UTC

CodeQL is now giving this warning after this change:
```
Warning: 1 issue was detected with this workflow: Please make sure that every branch in on.pull_request is also in on.push so that Code Scanning can compare pull requests against the state of the base branch.
```

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-07-07 20:01 UTC

Probably it's fine to enable `pull_request` only for `codeql-analysis.yml`?

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-07-07 20:26 UTC

`pull_request` is enabled; that’s not its complaint. Its complaint is that someone could theoretically open a pull request for a target branch that isn’t `*.x`, `chat.zulip.org`, or `main`, and CodeQL wouldn’t have a base state to compare with. This is harmless, but I’ll appease it in #22415.


## override_rewire

*2022-07-13 to 2025-01-06 · 13 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/43-automated-testing/topic/override_rewire/with/1404367)*

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-07-13 23:45 UTC

With #22450 I’ve made an initial effort toward the project of removing `__Rewire__`, `override_rewire`, and friends from the Node tests: 315 uses → 109 uses. This will mean that we need to be a bit more controlled in the way we mock things, but when we’re done we should be able to speed up the Node tests substantially, while hopefully making them easier to understand and maintain. Please avoid adding new uses, feel free to help removing existing uses, and ask if you have any questions about avoiding them.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-11-08 12:28 UTC

#32296 proposes the strategy of adding explicit setters for all rewired variables and using those instead of `__Rewire__`.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-11-08 18:41 UTC

Ooh, interesting!

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-11-08 18:54 UTC

This strategy seems like a solid way to get rid of that mess.

I think given that this class of bulk-created setter functions aren't intended to be used outside tests, probably a good naming scheme might be `override_{function}` or `rewire_{function}` rather than `set_{function}`. While there may be a few that we want to eventually clean up by changing to a `set_value` setter, I expect that at least half the time, the correct way to do the sweep will instead be to just do more data setup; at least several of the `people.ts` ones seem like they'd be better replaced with just creating an additional mock user. 

So having a naming scheme for these potentially undesirable test overrides that sticks out a bit from normal code that we're happy with is net helpful. In particular, I think I can write up a meta-issue or batch of issues for that follow-up sweep using `grep` rules or whatnot. One can always find them through this sort of tactic:

```
$ git grep sub_store | grep rewire
web/tests/drafts.test.js:    override_rewire(sub_store, "get", (stream_id) => {
web/tests/drafts.test.js:    override_rewire(sub_store, "get", (stream_id) => {
web/tests/drafts.test.js:    override_rewire(sub_store, "get", (stream_id) => {
```

But I think it'll be nice if we have a recognizable token in the production code piece as well.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-11-08 20:14 UTC

Yeah sounds good. We use the term “override” for the mechanism that auto-reverts the change at the end of each subtest; I’ll go with `rewire_`.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-11-08 20:38 UTC

Sweet, merged!

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-11-08 20:39 UTC

I still have a TODO to write up a master issue for the follow-up cleanups.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-11-12 02:45 UTC

Opened #32326 to track that. I think it'd make a good GSoC project but not necessarily a good first/starter project, so not adding the "help wanted" label to it.

**Steve Howell** · 2024-12-25 19:57 UTC

There used to be a huge taboo with adding code to the "production" files to support testing.  This latest PR shows why the taboo was always kind of silly (granting the fact that things have changed since then).  I like the hooks in the source code to allow test to override things for mocking purposes.  I assume babel is smart enough these days to omit the source-code test helpers from the production payload, but even if it's not, they're so tiny.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-01-02 17:50 UTC

The main thing I like about this mechanism is that it's really obvious which code is the testing rewire logic; it'd be a major code smell to do that sort of rewiring in production, so it's nice to be able to easily distinguish the two categories.

**Steve Howell** · 2025-01-05 10:57 UTC

See #**frontend>test passes locally but not in CI** for one possible pitfall of the new approach.  The magic behind `override_rewire` is that it restores old values after `run_test` completes, so you don't leak settings out to other tests.  Do we lose this functionality now?

**Steve Howell** · 2025-01-06 13:21 UTC

Disregard ^^^.

The pitfall here is that the linter didn't prevent Evy from calling `common.rewire_has_mac_keyboard` directly in the test.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-01-06 17:24 UTC

Ahh, yeah, we probably should add a lint rule for that.


## adding bookends to test data via populate_db

*2022-08-10 to 2022-08-10 · 2 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/43-automated-testing/topic/adding.20bookends.20to.20test.20data.20via.20populate_db/with/1417852)*

**Adam Sah** · 2022-08-10 04:56 UTC

PR #22691

I was recently working on a bug in bookends (#22651) when I noticed that there were no bookends in the sample data, either in dev or in the automated test suite. As an experiment, I forced some (half by default) of the messages created by `populate_db` to be historical ([code here](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/commit/0723461df19fd47ebac59c61df5f33c0f8c0c3b5#diff-0df8376e2f4653b9a4149e01ec9008bdfc002134c26d5c7b6246d8abb7ebd183)) and then fixed the one unittest that broke.

thoughts?  cc @Tim Abbott  (co-author on #22651 and mentioned that hacking populate_db was risky)

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-08-10 05:48 UTC

Yeah, I have a few thoughts. 
* Messages with the `historical` flag are rare in practice, so 50% seems like it'd be unrealistic in a way that's unfortunate (I think we'd have a lot of bookends in normal streams, and that might appear to be a bug!)
* I worry a bit about other tests failing nondeterministically. Generally, we guard this kind of feature behind an option that is used only for the manual testing dev environment, not automated tests.

I think a good compromise might be to pick a specific stream like `social`, modify its name to something like `historical test` and add a description about the `historical` flag, and set the historical flag precisely on messages sent within a particular time window to that stream, to simulate everyone being unsubscribed during that time period.

Another sensible option is to just make what you're doing an option, so one can run `populate_db --historical-percentage=10` to have some messages have the flag.

## changes to cache hash

*2022-08-29 to 2022-08-29 · 1 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/43-automated-testing/topic/changes.20to.20cache.20hash/with/1427115)*

**Vipul Sharma** · 2022-08-29 18:14 UTC

With [22797](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/22797) we've shifted to using a single hashFiles key in all actions/cache steps in our CI. hashFiles supports passing multiple filenames, and using this feature results in much cleaner keys.

We can check the new single hash keys created in the post restore steps of this workflow run - https://github.com/zulip/zulip/runs/8076415837?check_suite_focus=true
Any future workflow run like these - https://github.com/zulip/zulip/runs/8076938136?check_suite_focus=true will use these single hash keys from now onwards. (Can be checked in the save step)

## links broken until merge but CI fails

*2022-08-31 to 2022-09-01 · 11 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/43-automated-testing/topic/links.20broken.20until.20merge.20but.20CI.20fails/with/1428390)*

**Yash RE** · 2022-08-31 04:31 UTC

I was wondering if there was anything we could do about CI failing on PRs when we add new sections in the docs or when we rename sections in the docs. (CI fails because the links do not exist until the changes are merged, but check links fails because they do not exist.)

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-08-31 22:26 UTC

@Yash RE it'd be helpful to have an example, since the answer may vary with the situation. Sometimes we need to add a redirect, sometimes the right thing is to do two PRs / merges, with the first one linking to a the old URL (which redirects).

**Yash RE** · 2022-08-31 22:37 UTC

just to make sure we're on the same page: I'm asking if there's anything we can change in how we're testing links (which I think would be spiders.py)

**Yash RE** · 2022-08-31 22:39 UTC

#20459 could be an example, but I think this is most annoying when adding a new feature with docs

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-09-01 18:10 UTC

Right, so the solution is to use relative links, for example, link to /help/foo rather than say `https://zulip.com/...`

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-09-01 18:10 UTC

The tests can verify those links correctly.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-09-01 18:11 UTC

We have a relatively small number of absolute links in the project, largely when we are linking from one deployment area to another, say from ReadTheDocs to the Help Center or vise versa.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-09-01 18:11 UTC

For those, you're likely to see test failures if you, say, make a change that links from ReadTheDocs to a zulip.com /help/ page that doesn't exist yet.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-09-01 18:12 UTC

Those generally represent real bugs in the PR, in the sense that if the PR is merged, those links will be broken until your PR is deployed to Zulip Cloud.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-09-01 18:14 UTC

The opposite direction, links from /help/ pages to ReadTheDocs, generally require a 3-step merging process:
* First, make a PR that changes the page and all relative links to it. That PR will pass CI and can be merged.
* Immediately after that merged PR is built on ReadTheDocs, I add a redirect in the ReadTheDocs administrative panel from the old page URL to the new one. This means existing links to the old URL will keep working once the ReadTheDocs production build completes; if this is not done, CI will fail on PRs that are rebased onto the target commit, for example.
* Then, make a new PR that changes all absolute links to the new URL.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-09-01 18:16 UTC

@Yash RE so for #20459 in particular, if you can rebase the PR and drop the second commit changing absolute links, it can be merged. And then we can do a quick PR to update the absolute links shortly after.

**Riken Shah** · 2022-10-04 12:16 UTC

So `wait_for_fully_processed_message`, verifies that by checking the last visible row id and if star is present or not,

```js
 const $row = zulip_test.last_visible_row();
            if (zulip_test.row_id($row) !== last_msg.id) {

Specifically:
- For some reason `corporate/urls.py` is still in effect, despite the app having been removed from `INSTALLED_APPS` via `self.modify_settings(INSTALLED_APPS={"remove": "corporate"})`, and its view gets called. ## dependabot auto-merge philosophy

*2023-01-03 to 2023-08-25 · 11 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/43-automated-testing/topic/dependabot.20auto-merge.20philosophy/with/1484674)*

**Josh Klar** · 2023-01-03 21:04 UTC

Context: here's the current state of `main` on https://github.com/zulip/github-actions-zulip, wherein the most recent 15 commits, all from the past two weeks, are Dependabot bumps: [screenshot-2023-01-03-205609Z.png](https://chat.zulip.org/user_uploads/2/89/xNrzFfbudsu4CHYUQYQU_8V7/screenshot-2023-01-03-205609Z.png) 

Setting aside any commentary on whether this frequency of dependency updates is great or terrible or neither or both (as great of a convo as that might be), what I *do* want to open a discussion about is whether others think getting to a world where we trust auto-merging dep-bumps like this, perhaps for minor/patch releases (or just patch releases), is a goal worth going after.

I've worked in orgs where Dependabot (or whatever the other one I used was called) PRs piled up for months to years and just ate up space in the pulls list, and by the time those dependencies did finally need updated, the migration paths were generally unpleasant to take in a single swing. I'd like to avoid that wherever I can (thus why I've been tackling these for this particular repo immediately as they show up in my notifications), *however* if 15 such PRs in two weeks is going to be the typical rate of change, that's well into "difficult to keep up with manually" territory, and I'm inclined to argue for beefing up test suites where necessary and enabling auto-merge-on-passing-tests for these.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-01-03 21:21 UTC

My opinion is that although Dependabot serves as a useful reminder when important updates are available, there’s not much utility in taking these updates one-by-one. It’s less noisy and more complete to run `npm upgrade` and `npm outdated` every so often.

**Josh Klar** · 2023-01-03 21:33 UTC

(this made me wonder if Dependabot itself supported grouped/batched updates. [sadly not](https://github.com/dependabot/dependabot-core/issues/2265))

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-01-03 21:35 UTC

In the case of github-actions-zulip, even after merging the outstanding Dependabot PRs, there would still be updates to take for @babel/runtime 7.13.9 → 7.20.7, ci-info 3.6.2 → 3.7.1, es-abstract 1.20.4 → 1.20.5, fastq 1.13.0 → 1.15.0, ignore 5.2.0 → 5.2.4, internal-slot 1.0.3 → 1.0.4, mime-db 1.46.0 → 1.52.0, mime-types 2.1.29 → 2.1.35, regenerator-runtime 0.13.7 → 0.13.11.

Are any of these important? Individually, probably not. Collectively, leaving a bunch of packages behind just because nobody bothered marking the updates as important can lead to a lot of outdated packages, which might then hold back other updates.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-01-03 21:35 UTC

Yeah, I agree, I find the Dependabot updates primarily useful as a reminder that we should do an update, not as something I'd want to merge directly.

**Josh Klar** · 2023-01-03 21:37 UTC

Cool - seems reasonable to me to spend 5 minutes manually running the underlying tool to not spend half an hour spamming `@dependabot rebase` to a dozen PRs a week and managing the ordering/merge train drama

**Josh Klar** · 2023-01-03 21:38 UTC

Wonder if an even better move (for the future) would be to rig up a Zulip bot on a cron job to notify us of these types of outdated dependencies, and turn off Dependabot itself to spare us the sea of GitHub notifications :thinking: Anyway, that's a thing for Some Other Day, not important today.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-01-03 21:43 UTC

Renovate has some kind of configurable [grouping](https://docs.renovatebot.com/configuration-options/#groupname)—maybe it can be configured in a more useful way?

**Greg Price** · 2023-07-10 18:11 UTC

(replying to Josh Klar)
> (this made me wonder if Dependabot itself supported grouped/batched updates. [sadly not](https://github.com/dependabot/dependabot-core/issues/2265))

An update on this bit: that issue was deduped against this one:
https://github.com/dependabot/dependabot-core/issues/1190
and the latter seems to be making active progress — just last week they announced the feature was in "public beta".

**Alex Vandiver** · 2023-07-10 18:15 UTC

## grouping jobs & testing all commits #T1295

*2023-02-11 to 2023-02-23 · 8 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/43-automated-testing/topic/grouping.20jobs.20.26.20testing.20all.20commits.20.23T1295/with/1507201)*

**Neil Pilgrim (neiljp)** · 2023-02-11 00:23 UTC

I'm seeking some wider feedback here on #T1295, to simplify and improve the ZT CI.

I initially wanted to split jobs into:
- basic overall linting/testing
  - focus contributor attention on passing basic CI tasks
  - if they don't pass, running tests on other platforms/runtimes are of little worth, and distracting
- cross-platform testing
  - unnecessary on every early WIP push to a PR
  - still useful to confirm before final merges

In addition, last year I wrote up a simple `tools/check-branch` tool for ZT, which followed discussion in #**mobile-team>running tests on all commits** in the last few years and was merged last year. I've used that frequently before merging, and pointed contributors to it when they work on more complex PRs. This doesn't guarantee *coherent* commits, but at least that they are isolated/independent - and if CI now fails there, it can point contributors to a different aspect of the PR to improve, without requiring reviewer feedback.

So the overall flow of CI after #T1295 will be:
- Basic linting/tests -> Ensure isolated PR commits -> Pytest matrix on other platforms
(eg. https://github.com/zulip/zulip-terminal/actions/runs/4148515619)

Our linting and tests are not optimized to avoid unchanged files right now, which could certainly be a speed improvement, but does keep things simple - and the repo is relatively small right now so CI times are relatively low in any case. Ruff may help for speed, or grouping linting jobs, though separate jobs can be helpful as-is to indicate which parts are failing. However, pytest is the speed blocker when running all tests, particularly on slower platforms, though these are now in the final group of jobs.

One challenge in this PR was identifying commits to use for the isolated-commit job, since pull requests provide a quasi-merge commit as the head SHA by default. I resolved that, but ran into some discussion of the benefits of the merge commit, so particularly wondered if anyone has thoughts on if avoiding that would be an issue, though it's a little difficult to avoid as one specifically wants to assess each commit in turn. Is that something that require features like in bors or github merge-queues to resolve properly?

**Greg Price** · 2023-02-23 01:12 UTC

(replying to Neil Pilgrim (neiljp))
> One challenge in this PR was identifying commits to use for the isolated-commit job, since pull requests provide a quasi-merge commit as the head SHA by default. I resolved that, but ran into some discussion of the benefits of the merge commit, so particularly wondered if anyone has thoughts on if a …

If you're already running tests on each commit in the branch, then one approach to this would be:
* Run tests on each commit in the PR branch itself.
* Also run tests on the PR merge commit, in the case where that's different from the tip of the branch itself (i.e., when the PR branch isn't atop the latest `main`.)

That way you assess each commit in turn, and also assess how the whole branch integrates with `main`.

(But I'm not sure I'm correctly understanding the question.)

**Neil Pilgrim (neiljp)** · 2023-02-23 02:01 UTC

I plan to merge the commits for grouping the tests soon, as that seems like a good standalone first step, for the reasons I mentioned above (this would make the dependency be `basic linting/tests` -> `pytest matrix`).

**Neil Pilgrim (neiljp)** · 2023-02-23 03:27 UTC

(replying to Greg Price)
> If you're already running tests on each commit in the branch, then one approach to this would be: * Run tests on each commit in the PR branch itself. * Also run tests on the PR merge commit, in the case where that's different from the tip of the branch itself (i.e., when the PR branch isn't atop the …
@Greg Price Thanks - that sounds like it might address what I was concerned about :+1:
- the new job added in the last commit in the PR should handle the first bullet point, which may well be optimized later but works for pull requests, checking each commit;
- we run tests on different python platforms already, which I suspect will already be always testing the PR merge commit, since we don't pick a specific commit or range of commits for that.

That said, the merge commit is presumably determined when the action is run, and so main can change subsequently, before the PR is merged - and I got the impression that something like bors/merge-queues could potentially help with that kind of issue.

**Greg Price** · 2023-02-23 19:13 UTC

(replying to Neil Pilgrim (neiljp))
> That said, the merge commit is presumably determined when the action is run, and so main can change subsequently, before the PR is merged - and I got the impression that something like bors/merge-queues could potentially help with that kind of issue.

Yeah, a merge queue, like what bors does, solves that problem.

It comes at some cost in slowing things down. If your test suite takes 10 minutes to run, and you hit merge on a couple of different PRs, then it'll be 10-20 minutes (depending on just how the merge queue works) before their code lands in main.

So you have to weigh that cost against the benefit — against how big of a problem, for your project, is the problem it solves. How often does it happen that you have a PR that
* looks good in review, so that you're happy to merge it;
* also passes all the tests;
* and when merged/rebased to main there are no Git merge conflicts;
* but there was some kind of conflict Git didn't detect, such that the tests fail after merge?

**Greg Price** · 2023-02-23 19:14 UTC

Speaking for zulip-mobile, those cases are extremely rare — like once a year, or less. So for us there isn't a practical problem that a merge queue solves.

**Greg Price** · 2023-02-23 19:17 UTC

In a larger project with many different teams working on separate but interdependent parts, it can be crucial. At Dropbox we introduced such a thing (Commit Queue, we called it), and it was a big help in keeping the tree green with hundreds of engineers working in the same codebase.

**Neil Pilgrim (neiljp)** · 2023-02-23 20:37 UTC

Thanks @Greg Price, that's very informative :+1:

**Joseph Ho** · 2023-04-07 04:02 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-04-07 17:30 UTC

Just a note that you can always restart tests by doing a Git update to the branch, often an option via just rebasing your PR onto `main` again.

**Joseph Ho** · 2023-04-07 17:39 UTC

Would there be another option if I had already rebased my PR to `main`?

**Joseph Ho** · 2023-04-07 17:41 UTC

Also thank you @Aman (amanagr)!

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-04-07 17:59 UTC

Anything that changes the commit hash; so you can do a trivial `git commit --amend` to add a space and then do it again and remove the space (the combination will change the timestamp in the commit hash); that's probably still faster than asking for someone else to restart the job, and then you don't have to wait :).

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-04-07 18:02 UTC

No need to add a space; just `git commit --amend` without changes will bump the committer timestamp.

**Joseph Ho** · 2023-04-07 18:14 UTC

Ahh, that's interesting. I kind of just thought that only new code changes are able to be pushed up, didn't think a simple bump on the timestamp will do.

**Steve Howell** · 2023-04-26 11:16 UTC

In the most recent video I talk a lot about the general structure of a test, and I will transcribe some notes to here:

General structure of a single test
- clear out irrelevant data
- set up pertinent data
- create any necessary mocks or stubs
	- some mocks simulate behavior
	- other mocks simply short-circuit deep function calls
	- some mocks actually capture behavior
- make the BEFORE assertions
- perform the action
- make the AFTER assertions
- clean up

**Steve Howell** · 2023-04-26 11:17 UTC

Writing process (very similar to reading process)
- assert BEFORE state
- assert END state (sort of like test-first)
- perform the action between those assertions
- see what breaks
- if it's YOUR code causing the failure, debug it of course
- verify original data setup was as you predicted
- decide whether to stub functions or not
- consider whether your test reveals structural problems in existing code

**Steve Howell** · 2023-04-26 11:19 UTC

And, toward the very end of the video, I talk a little bit about how test can reveal **possible** code smells, and I call out this interaction:

~~~ js
    override(message_lists.current.view, "show_message_as_read", () => {});
    override(message_lists.home.view, "show_message_as_read", () => {});
~~~

**Steve Howell** · 2023-04-26 11:22 UTC

The latter is possibly a symptom that `message_lists` needs to have some kind of wrapper interface above it to make it a little easier for other modules to have one-stop shopping for these kind of things.  I know that Tim and I discussed this at least a little bit, but I don't remember many details.  It's entirely possible that the APIs have evolved since I wrote the test example, or even that I ignored an existing better API at the time, which I talk about in the video.  Obviously, if that's the case, then there is an opportunity to clean up the example a bit.  On the other hand, this example is toward the end, and it will probably always reflect some of the real-world complexity in writing tests toward higher levels of the API.

 - `zulip/ci:jammy`

**Alex Vandiver** · 2023-05-08 21:01 UTC

That resolved this.

AFAICT this was caused by the `apt-get upgrade` process installing a new `erlang-base` which killed `epmd` but not `rabbitmq-server` -- so when `epmd` got started later, it had no `rabbitmq-server` registered, so thought it needed to be started, but rabbitmq couldn't start up because it couldn't claim its ports.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2023-05-08 21:03 UTC

We're now side-stepping this by building the upgraded pacage into the new Docker image.  Which also speeds up the CI runs.


## production tests with auto-merge

(replying to Alex Vandiver)
> Peeling off the last commit, which apparently failed production tests, and "auto-merge" does not block on them.

Oh, is this because those tests are optional or something? I'm kinda surprised that would be the case.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2023-05-19 00:13 UTC

Correct, because those tests don't run on every change, they can't be included in the set that block auto-merge, so they're free to fail all over the place and the auto-merge will carry on.

I see, it's very annoying in that the thing you obviously want in the presence of both "block on these checks" and "optional checks" as features is to be able to configure checks to be blocking only if they were going to be run.

dcb5e0d610a59cf8d855d4075b7d1210506f7a89 introduces `threaded` for queue workers, which is used to determine if a consume timeout should be signaled.

Here's the script we use for pulling things down:
``` bash
./manage.py makemessages --all
tx pull -a -f --mode=translator --minimum-perc=5 "$@"
# For readability, we prefer UTF-8, not ascii, in these JSON files.
find ./locale \
    -regextype sed \
    -regex '^\./locale/.*/\(mobile\|translations\).json$' \
    -exec ./tools/i18n/unescape-contents {} \;

./manage.py compilemessages --ignore='*'
./tools/i18n/process-mobile-i18n
```

## date-related flakes

*2023-07-10 to 2023-07-11 · 16 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/43-automated-testing/topic/date-related.20flakes/with/1606818)*

**Steve Howell** · 2023-07-10 09:07 UTC

I recently broke one of my builds with a date-related flake.  Our backend test setup does not guarantee how old the pre-populated messages are going to be, as it depends on how recently you have re-built your test database.  So if you have a test that exercises something like `add_new_user_history`, which finds messages from the last week to put in the user's feed, then the test is going to break depending on timing.

**Steve Howell** · 2023-07-10 09:11 UTC

I know that I have brought this up before, and I think one simple remedy is to make it easier for somebody running tests locally to know that they have a pretty old copy of the test database.

**Steve Howell** · 2023-07-10 09:14 UTC

I think my suggestion last time was to simply to refuse to run the tests and tell folks to rebuild the test database. On my droplet this takes 63 seconds, which certainly isn't an onerous thing to do a couple times a year.  It would have saved me about 20 minutes of debugging today.

**Steve Howell** · 2023-07-10 09:15 UTC

The test that failed for me wasn't obviously date-related, as I was doing query counts on a function that indirectly called `add_new_user_history`, but I wasn't actually working on the function, so I wasn't on high alert to look for date flakes.

**Steve Howell** · 2023-07-10 09:16 UTC

This suggestion got pushback last time due to the "convenience factor".  Maybe there is some compromise here, like a prominent warning.  Or maybe others can chime in about similar pain, and we can reconsider the decision.

**Steve Howell** · 2023-07-10 09:18 UTC

(The reason it took me 20 minutes to debug was that I couldn't reproduce the bug locally, since once I had passed a certain amount of time not building the test database, the test very reliably found no recent messages for `add_new_history` to process.)

**Steve Howell** · 2023-07-10 09:22 UTC

For the particular flake on `add_new_history`, I always try to ask if a test failure is telling me something a little out-of-the-box about the code itself.  In this case I wonder why we are even using a one-week window.  One week on some projects feels like a year; on others it feels like a day.  Does it make sense to keep it simple and just find the last N messages?

**Steve Howell** · 2023-07-10 10:19 UTC

It actually feels very counterproductive to limit on-boarding messages to a week.  It can be quite difficult to bootstrap a Zulip community, and in the first couple months of launching it, you may have very low traffic.  Is it better to try to engage users with slightly old content or give them no content at all?  Neither is ideal, but the latter certainly seems worse to me.

**Steve Howell** · 2023-07-10 10:25 UTC

For super-busy sites, the week limit is moot, because we do cap the number of messages that we set to unread at 20.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-07-11 17:53 UTC

I think generally we want to write tests that are not deeply dependant on the starting messages in the test database; what I'd do to fix that test in particular is to have the new user only be subscribed to a single stream, which is newly created and populated in the test.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-07-11 17:54 UTC

I think it's possible that 1 week value is not the right product approach; but I'm not sure I'd want no limit; it might feel pretty weird to show up and get 20 unreads that are all 1+ year old? A month is likely a better value, though.

**Steve Howell** · 2023-07-11 18:15 UTC

(replying to Tim Abbott)
> I think it's possible that 1 week value is not the right product approach; but I'm not sure I'd want no limit; it might feel pretty weird to show up and get 20 unreads that are all 1+ year old? A month is likely a better value, though.

I think a month is good.  It's still reasonably current but longer than most people go on vacation for (or even get distracted by other work-related or project-related tasks).

**Steve Howell** · 2023-07-11 18:16 UTC

I can do a quick PR on that if I get the thumbs up.

**Steve Howell** · 2023-07-11 18:17 UTC

(replying to Tim Abbott)
> I think generally we want to write tests that are not deeply dependant on the starting messages in the test database; what I'd do to fix that test in particular is to have the new user only be subscribed to a single stream, which is newly created and populated in the test.

Yeah, I agree with strategy in general, but the problem is when you don't even know that you're dealing with a moving target.  I agree that my situation is a little unique, since I was dealing with query counts.

## mocking browser events?

*2023-07-24 to 2023-07-25 · 11 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/43-automated-testing/topic/mocking.20browser.20events.3F/with/1614868)*

**Karl Stolley** · 2023-07-24 18:26 UTC

One of the things I'm trying to understand is what the Zulip philosophy is regarding mocking browser events in the JS unit tests. Different tests seem to take different tacks, including something as basic as just mocking an object literal like this:

```js
const event = {
  target: ".some-class-selector",
  preventDefault: noop, // defined as an empty arrow function
}
```

**Karl Stolley** · 2023-07-24 18:27 UTC

Others, like [the `copy_and_paste.test.js` file](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/main/web/tests/copy_and_paste.test.js) in particular, go as far as loading up jQuery and use it in tandem with the native `window.Event` object:

```js
const {JSDOM} = require("jsdom");

const jquery = require("./lib/real_jquery");
const {window} = new JSDOM("<!DOCTYPE html><p>Hello world</p>");

const {document} = window;
const $ = jquery(window);

const createPasteEvent = function () {
    const clipboardData = new DataTransfer();
    const pasteEvent = new window.Event("paste");
    pasteEvent.clipboardData = clipboardData;
    return new $.Event(pasteEvent);
};
```

The issue with that approach is that, as with a true `Event` object, properties like `currentTarget` become read-only, making them impossible to mock without a bunch of other DOM-manipulation setup.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-07-24 18:27 UTC

I'm not sure we have one other than trying to avoid writing tests for functions that take an event as a parameter.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-07-24 18:28 UTC

One thing to note is that `jsdom` is very expensive/slow, so ideally we want to avoid using it in tests where it's not required. (E.g. if you can just extract a function that will be 98% of a click handler's code and accepts data and does computations, and test that, it's often going to be better than testing a full click handler end-to-end)

**Karl Stolley** · 2023-07-24 18:28 UTC

Thanks, Tim. So I guess, in situations where some logic is really event-dependent, could that paste-mocking function not just as well be mocked up like this? Are there good reasons for doing more than that to create/mock events in the JS unit tests?

```diff
 const createPasteEvent = function () {
     const clipboardData = new DataTransfer();
-    const pasteEvent = new window.Event("paste");
-    pasteEvent.clipboardData = clipboardData;
-    return new $.Event(pasteEvent);
+    const pasteEvent = {
+        currentTarget: ".my-fake-textarea",
+        originalEvent: {
+            clipboardData: clipboardData,
+        },
+        preventDefault: noop,
+        stopPropagation: noop,
+    };
+    return pasteEvent;
 };
```

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-07-24 18:29 UTC

I am perfectly happy for us to do that sort of mocking if it's sufficient to verify the logic. (If we have some test for complicated DOM manipulation logic, that would be a good place to use jsdom).

**Karl Stolley** · 2023-07-24 18:30 UTC

(replying to Tim Abbott)
> One thing to note is that `jsdom` is very expensive/slow, so ideally we want to avoid using it in tests where it's not required. (E.g. if you can just extract a function that will be 98% of a click handler's code and accepts data and does computations, and test that, it's often going to be better th …

Got it. I think the issue with the copy-and-paste logic is that it's more than a click handler or the like.

**Karl Stolley** · 2023-07-24 18:31 UTC

(replying to Tim Abbott)
> I am perfectly happy for us to do that sort of mocking if it's sufficient to verify the logic. (If we have some test for complicated DOM manipulation logic, that would be a good place to use jsdom).

That makes sense. I think the code currently in the copy-and-paste file is overkill; it's using JSDOM just to create a window object. None of the DOM's contents there even matter to the test suite.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-07-24 21:11 UTC

Yeah that seems like logic best deleted.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-07-24 21:14 UTC

My take is that if we want to test logic, we should write that logic in the form of a pure function that can be tested without extra layers of meaningless mocks that only serve to test that we call the functions whose names are the names of the functions that we call.

In this case, it looks like we’ve already extracted that pure function as `paste_handler_converter`, so that’s the one we should be testing, not the event handler.

**Steve Howell** · 2023-07-25 21:25 UTC

It's a bit unfortunate that a lot of our tests that use mocks are essentially just trying to get test coverage on existing code that may not have been written in the cleanest way.

Ideally, any time you see code that's difficult to test (whether with mocks or not), the tests are telling you that there's a better way to write the actual code, and extracting `paste_handler_converter` is probably a good example of that.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-08-11 16:34 UTC

https://github.com/nedbat/coveragepy/issues/251

**Steve Howell** · 2023-08-11 16:37 UTC

Oy vey. 10 years old and the latest activity is silly naming jokes.

**Steve Howell** · 2023-08-11 16:39 UTC

Once the basic infrastructure is in place, it is surely no more difficult to report an unexpectedly covered line than an unexpectedly non-covered line.

**Steve Howell** · 2023-08-11 16:47 UTC

**Steve Howell** · 2023-08-11 16:47 UTC

Or darn it, it's me! f86823f82f6fc80deeaafafa0c78429b427e7ce3

Am I correct that when you raise an `AssertionError` there is no need for `nocoverage`?

**Steve Howell** · 2023-08-11 16:53 UTC

~~~

zerver/tests/test_compatibility.py:                raise AssertionError  # nocoverage
zerver/tests/test_compatibility.py:                raise AssertionError  # nocoverage
zerver/tests/test_events.py:            except AssertionError:  # nocoverage

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-08-11 16:55 UTC

We have a custom list of regexes to exclude in `tools/coveragerc`, one of which is `raise AssertionError`. (Incidentally, that file claims that `nocoverage` is the standard coverage pragma, but the standard is actually `# pragma: no cover`.)

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-08-14 17:36 UTC

That comment was probably accurate when written. But I also I feel like "pragma: no cover" is less readable, so don't feel like switching is gonna help. We can update the comment.

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2023-10-10 17:34 UTC

**Prakhar Pratyush** · 2023-10-10 17:40 UTC
